217d6a477d95.title: Frame Interpolation: FILM
217d6a477d95.metaDescription: ComfyUI FILM frame interpolation workflow to smooth low-FPS videos. Load, interpolate with FILM VFI, and export with VideoHelperSuite.
217d6a477d95.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow upgrades choppy, low frame‑rate videos into smooth playback using FILM (Frame Interpolation for Large Motion). It uses VideoHelperSuite to handle I/O and the ComfyUI-Frame-Interpolation extension to synthesize in‑between frames. VHS_LoadVideo decodes your source clip into a frame sequence, while VHS_VideoInfo reads the clip’s original FPS and resolution so you can choose a suitable interpolation factor. The FILM VFI node then generates the intermediate frames between each input pair, leveraging FILM’s large‑motion handling to reduce judder without changing the video’s look or color. Finally, VHS_VideoCombine assembles the expanded frame sequence into a new video at your chosen output FPS.

Technically, the FILM VFI node inserts 1 or more in‑between frames for every adjacent pair of source frames (for example, 2× or 4×). That increases temporal resolution and smooths motion without upscaling or style transfer—no Stable Diffusion models are involved. The workflow is lightweight and predictable: decode frames (VHS_LoadVideo) → analyze original timing (VHS_VideoInfo) → interpolate with FILM VFI → re‑encode (VHS_VideoCombine). This makes it ideal for restoring old footage, improving AI‑generated or screen‑captured clips, or preparing content for platforms that expect higher FPS.
howToUse: Install requirements: update ComfyUI and add both custom node packs—ComfyUI-Frame-Interpolation (for FILM VFI) and ComfyUI-VideoHelperSuite (VHS nodes). Restart ComfyUI.
Load the workflow JSON. In VHS_LoadVideo, set the path to your source video. Leave other options at defaults unless you need to trim or resize upstream.
Run VHS_VideoInfo (or preview its output) to confirm the source FPS and resolution. Use this to decide your interpolation factor (e.g., 2× to go from 15→30 FPS, 4× to go from 12→48 FPS).
Open the FILM VFI node and set the interpolation factor (e.g., 2×, 4×). Keep other settings default for a first pass; higher factors create more frames but increase processing time.
In VHS_VideoCombine, set the output FPS. A common choice is source_FPS × factor (e.g., 24×2=48 FPS). Choose your output path/filename and encoding quality parameters.
Queue and run the workflow. When complete, open the saved file from the specified output directory and review smoothness. If motion still looks uneven, try a higher factor or adjust the target FPS.
suggestedUseCases: Smoothing old phone footage or archival clips shot at 12–24 FPS.
Improving AI-generated or diffusion-based videos that render at low FPS.
Making screen recordings and UI demos feel more responsive at 48–60 FPS.
Polishing stop-motion or time-lapse sequences while preserving their look.
Upgrading gameplay captures recorded at variable frame rates.

faqItems.question: What’s the difference between setting a factor and setting the output FPS?
faqItems.answer: The FILM VFI node controls how many in‑between frames to synthesize (e.g., 2×, 4×). VHS_VideoCombine sets the final playback FPS. A typical workflow is to pick a factor in FILM (e.g., 2×) and then set output FPS to source_FPS × factor to preserve real‑time speed.

faqItems.question: Can I keep the original audio?
faqItems.answer: If your VideoHelperSuite version and wiring support audio passthrough, connect the audio output from VHS_LoadVideo to VHS_VideoCombine to mux it back. If not, export the silent video and re‑mux the original audio with a tool like ffmpeg.

faqItems.question: Will interpolation fix motion blur or compression artifacts?
faqItems.answer: No. FILM synthesizes intermediate frames to smooth motion but does not deblur, denoise, or upscale. For best results, start from the cleanest source you have and consider separate denoise/deblur steps before interpolation if needed.

faqItems.question: How do I choose a good target FPS?
faqItems.answer: Match your delivery platform and content: 30 or 60 FPS for web and gameplay, 48 FPS for cinematic smoothness, or simply source_FPS × 2 for a natural improvement. Extremely high FPS can look unnatural on some content and increases file size.

21e4b651f816.title: SAM 3D Body: 3D Human Mesh Extraction From Video
21e4b651f816.description: Extract a full-body 3D human mesh from a single video frame using SAM 3D Body, guided by a text prompt to refine pose and shape estimation. The workflow loads one video and one text prompt, then outputs a reconstructed video showing the recovered human rig. Ideal for motion capture prototyping, biomechanics analysis, and character animation previsualization.
21e4b651f816.metaDescription: Extract a 3D human mesh from video in ComfyUI using SAM3. Detect boxes, track subjects, optional MoGe FoV, add face expressions, smooth, render, and export.
21e4b651f816.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow extracts a full-body 3D human mesh from a video and outputs a reconstruction video plus an optional animation/pose file. It starts by reading your clip with LoadVideo and, if needed, trimming it with Video Slice. Person regions are auto-detected with RTDETR_detect to generate bounding boxes (highly recommended for accuracy), while your text prompt is embedded via CLIPTextEncode to guide the SAM 3D Body estimator on ambiguous frames (for example, the simple prompt "person"). The SAM3DBody_Loader loads the SAM3 model (Comfy-Org/sam3.1), and SAM3DBody_Predict reconstructs a per-frame body mesh and skeletal rig. For multi-person clips, SAM3_VideoTrack improves identity consistency, helping the predictor lock onto the intended subject across frames.

To keep the recovered rig aligned with the original camera, the optional Get FoV group estimates field-of-view using LoadMoGeModel, MoGeInference, and MoGeGeometryToFOV; this can noticeably improve pose scale and alignment. Face expression signals are added by SAM3DBody_FaceExpression (SAM3 itself does not estimate expressions), and temporal stability is enhanced with SAM3DBody_Smooth. Finally, SAM3DBody_Render produces the overlay frames, CreateVideo compiles them, and SaveVideo writes the reconstructed video. If you need motion data downstream, BuildPoseFile creates a 3D animation/pose file for previsualization or mocap prototyping.
howToUse: Load the template and set the input video path on LoadVideo (e.g., input/woman_holding_water_glass.mp4). Optionally use Video Slice to trim the frame range and GetVideoComponents to confirm FPS/size.
Enter a simple subject prompt in CLIPTextEncode (e.g., "person"). Keep it generic and descriptive to help the model disambiguate the target in challenging frames.

Improve detections with RTDETR_detect in the Detect Bounding Boxes group. For clips with more than one person, enable the Multiple People Detection group and use SAM3_VideoTrack to maintain identity across frames.

Optionally enable the Get FoV group: load the model with LoadMoGeModel, run MoGeInference, and convert with MoGeGeometryToFOV. Connect the FoV output to the SAM 3D Body nodes to improve scale and camera alignment.

Load the SAM model with SAM3DBody_Loader, then run SAM3DBody_Predict using the video frames, prompt embeddings, bounding boxes, and optional FoV. Add SAM3DBody_FaceExpression for facial cues and stabilize results with SAM3DBody_Smooth.
Preview with SAM3DBody_Render, then assemble with CreateVideo and export via SaveVideo. If you need motion data, use BuildPoseFile to generate a 3D animation/pose file for your DCC or mocap pipeline.
suggestedUseCases: Motion capture prototyping for indie animation or previz before full studio capture
Biomechanics and form analysis for sports or rehab using single-camera footage
Character animation blocking with fast, camera-aligned body reconstructions
AR/VR avatar tests and retargeting from quick reference videos
Crowded-scene tracking experiments using multi-person detection and tracking

faqItems.question: Do I need bounding boxes for good results?
faqItems.answer: They’re optional but strongly recommended. RTDETR_detect narrows the subject area, which improves pose stability, handles occlusions better, and reduces identity switches—especially in busy scenes.

faqItems.question: Can this handle multiple people in the same clip?
faqItems.answer: Yes—enable the Multiple People Detection group and use SAM3_VideoTrack. This improves identity consistency across frames so you can focus the 3D reconstruction on the intended person.

faqItems.question: What does the MoGe FoV step do, and is it required?
faqItems.answer: MoGeInference with MoGeGeometryToFOV estimates the camera’s field of view from the clip. It’s optional but helps align the reconstructed mesh to the source video’s scale and perspective. Without it, a default FoV is used.

faqItems.question: Does SAM 3D Body capture facial expressions?
faqItems.answer: SAM3D Body does not estimate expressions by itself. The workflow adds them via SAM3DBody_FaceExpression using MediaPipe face detection. Results depend on face visibility, resolution, and lighting.

223bd1e21b66.title: Kling 4.0: Video Edit
223bd1e21b66.description: Edit an existing clip in one pass with Kling 4.0: name the change and list what must survive, and the model rewrites only that part while keeping the subject, costume, shot count, camera work and timing intact. Output inherits the input's length and aspect ratio, and stereo audio is regenerated to match the new scene. Ideal for swapping environments, wardrobe or style on footage that is already cut.
223bd1e21b66.metaDescription: One-pass video edits in ComfyUI with Kling 4.0. Swap environment or style while preserving subject, shot count, timing, and aspect ratio—with regenerated audio.
223bd1e21b66.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI tutorial workflow shows how to make precise, one-pass edits to an existing clip with Kling 4.0 while preserving what matters. The pipeline is intentionally minimal: LoadVideo brings your source clip into the graph, Kling4EditVideoNode sends a natural‑language edit request to the Kling 4.0 API, and SaveVideo writes the edited result. You describe a single change in plain English, then list what must survive. The model rewrites only that part, keeping the subject, costume, shot count, camera work, and timing intact. The output inherits the input’s aspect ratio and duration, and stereo audio is regenerated to match the new scene.

Technically, LoadVideo streams the input frames (and timing) that act as the structural anchor for the edit. Kling4EditVideoNode takes a prompt that must start with "Edit @Video1:" to bind your instructions to the loaded clip. It performs a temporally coherent rewrite constrained by your "must survive" list, helping maintain identity and continuity across cuts. Finally, SaveVideo collects the edited frames and the newly generated stereo audio from the edit node and muxes them into a single file. A MarkdownNote on the canvas summarizes prompt rules and best practices so you can iterate quickly and surgically.
howToUse: Open the workflow in ComfyUI and verify the LoadVideo path points to your clip (default example: input/kling4_gown_input.mp4, 5 s). Replace it with your own footage if desired.

Read the MarkdownNote on the canvas for prompt rules. In Kling4EditVideoNode, write your edit prompt starting with: Edit @Video1: <describe one change>. Then add a clear "must survive" list (identity, wardrobe, camera work, shot count, timing).

Example prompt: "Edit @Video1: Replace the ballroom environment with a modern art gallery. Must survive: same woman, same white gown, same number of shots, same camera moves and pacing, keep choreography and expressions consistent, do not change framing or duration."
If the node requires credentials, add your Kling API key in the node or ComfyUI preferences as instructed by your installation. Leave other parameters at defaults for your first run.
Queue and run the workflow. Kling4EditVideoNode will process the edit in one pass; progress appears in the ComfyUI console/status bar.

Inspect the output from SaveVideo. The result will keep the original length and aspect ratio with regenerated stereo audio. If needed, refine the prompt to be more specific about what should stay the same and re-run.
suggestedUseCases: Environment swaps (e.g., ballroom to forest or art gallery) while preserving performance and timing.
Wardrobe or style adjustments that keep the same subject and choreography.
Lighting and mood re-skins (day-to-night, warm-to-cool) without altering camera work.
Seasonal or set-dressing changes (summer to winter, add decorations) across existing cuts.
Localized details (signage, posters, on-screen text) with continuity intact.

faqItems.question: Do length and aspect ratio change after the edit?
faqItems.answer: No. The output inherits the input clip’s duration and aspect ratio. The model preserves shot count, camera work, and timing, so don’t request changes to pacing or framing.

faqItems.question: What’s the correct prompt format for the edit node?
faqItems.answer: Begin with "Edit @Video1:" to bind your instructions to the loaded video, then state one specific change, followed by a clear "must survive" list (e.g., subject identity, costume, number of shots, camera moves, timing, framing).

faqItems.question: Can I keep the original audio?
faqItems.answer: This template regenerates stereo audio to match the new scene. If you need the original soundtrack, export the edited video and replace the audio in your NLE after rendering.

faqItems.question: Can I make multiple big changes in one pass?
faqItems.answer: Keep edits surgical. One themed change with a strict "must survive" list yields the most reliable identity and continuity. For broader transformations, iterate with multiple runs, verifying results after each pass.

224442d3423c.title: Tripo P2: Multiview to Model
224442d3423c.description: Generate production-ready 3D models from up to four reference views using Tripo P2.0 Preview, which reconstructs geometry with native quad topology and triangle meshes up to 50,000 faces. Ideal for game characters and props ready for rigging, hard-surface mechanical assets, and high-volume real-time pipelines.
224442d3423c.metaDescription: Turn up to four photos into a riggable, textured 3D model with Tripo P2.0 Preview in ComfyUI. Includes multiview reconstruction, PBR texturing, rigging, and export.
224442d3423c.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI tutorial workflow turns up to four reference images into a production-ready 3D asset using Tripo P2.0 Preview. Starting with LoadImage nodes for front/back (and optionally side) views, the TripoPSeriesMultiviewToModelNode performs multiview reconstruction to produce a clean base mesh. The node supports native quad topology and a triangle mesh variant, with a face budget up to 50,000 for real-time use. From there, the graph branches into texturing, rigging, retargeting, conversion, and export—so you end with a usable asset, not just a mesh.

After geometry is built, TripoTextureNodeV2 creates a PBR texture set from your inputs, while TripoRigNode generates a basic rig to articulate the model. If you need to match an existing animation skeleton, TripoRetargetNode maps the auto-rig to your target rig. TripoConversionNode handles practical details—axis/origin alignment, scaling to real-world units, quad/tri conversion, and optional decimation—before Save3DAdvanced writes the final GLB/OBJ with textures. The nodes are grouped under Tripo Toolset (select and Ctrl+B to enable) for a clean, end-to-end pipeline that’s ideal for characters, props, and hard-surface assets in real-time and game workflows.
howToUse: Open the workflow in ComfyUI and enable the Tripo Toolset group: select the group and press Ctrl+B so its nodes (TripoPSeriesMultiviewToModelNode, TripoTextureNodeV2, TripoRigNode, etc.) are active.
Provide your Tripo API credentials if required by your Tripo nodes (either in the node’s settings or global config). Without valid credentials, remote processing will fail.

Load your reference images using the provided LoadImage nodes. Start with the included worker_doll_front.png and worker_doll_back.png; optionally add left/right views for up to four total angles with consistent framing and lighting.

Configure TripoPSeriesMultiviewToModelNode: set Model to Tripo P2.0 Preview, connect your 2–4 image inputs, and keep the face budget at or below 50,000 for real-time targets. Execute the graph to generate the base mesh (quads and tri variant).

Optional refinement: connect the mesh to TripoTextureNodeV2 to generate a PBR texture set (e.g., base color, normal, roughness/metallic as available). For animation, run TripoRigNode to auto-rig, then use TripoRetargetNode to match your studio skeleton if needed.

Finalize and export: use TripoConversionNode to set scale, axis (e.g., Y-up/Z-up), and quad/tri output. Then export with Save3DAdvanced (e.g., GLB or OBJ). Open the saved file in your DCC or engine to verify shading, scale, and orientation.
suggestedUseCases: Game-ready characters and stylized props with clean topology and a 50k-face budget for real-time engines.
Hard-surface mechanical assets quickly reconstructed from front/back references for prototyping and previs.
E-commerce turntables and AR catalog assets built from limited product photos.
Rapid kitbashing: convert sketch or maquette photos into textured meshes for concept blocking.

faqItems.question: How many reference images can I use?
faqItems.answer: The TripoPSeriesMultiviewToModelNode accepts up to four views. Two (front/back) will work, but adding left/right improves occluded areas and texture coverage.

faqItems.question: What topology and face count should I expect?
faqItems.answer: The node outputs native quads and a triangle mesh, with reconstruction targeted up to 50,000 faces. Use TripoConversionNode to decimate further or switch between quads and tris as your pipeline requires.

faqItems.question: Do I need perfectly clean backgrounds?
faqItems.answer: Not strictly, but consistent lighting, a plain background, and centered framing help reconstruction and texture quality. Keep subject scale and camera distance consistent across views.

faqItems.question: Which formats can I export?
faqItems.answer: Use Save3DAdvanced to write common formats like GLB or OBJ. Texture embedding or external file output depends on your Save3DAdvanced settings and chosen format.

228fef3dbe05.title: Bira: Remove Image Background
228fef3dbe05.description: Upload an image to automatically remove its background using the Bria API. The workflow processes the request asynchronously and returns the edited image with a transparent background.
228fef3dbe05.metaDescription: Automatically remove image backgrounds using the Bria API with ComfyUI. Efficiently process images for design and e-commerce needs.
228fef3dbe05.extendedDescription:
This workflow, titled 'Bira: Remove Image Background,' is designed to automate the process of removing backgrounds from images using the Bria API. It is particularly useful for users looking to streamline their image editing tasks, especially when dealing with large batches of images. The inclusion of the 'ImageCompare' node allows users to verify the quality of the background removal by comparing the original and edited images side by side, ensuring that the results meet their standards before finalizing the output.
howToUse: Load the 'Bira: Remove Image Background' workflow in ComfyUI.
Use the 'LoadImage' node to upload your image file.
Configure the 'BriaRemoveImageBackground' node to connect with the Bria API.
Run the workflow to process the image asynchronously.
Review the results using the 'ImageCompare' node to ensure quality.
Save the edited image with a transparent background using the 'SaveImage' node.

Graphic design projects that require isolated subjects for creative compositions.
Social media content creation, allowing for quick and professional-looking posts.
Marketing materials where the focus is on the product without background distractions.
Batch processing of images for large-scale projects, saving time and effort.

faqItems.question: What types of images work best with this workflow?

faqItems.question: How long does the background removal process take?

faqItems.question: Can I use this workflow for batch processing?

faqItems.question: Is there a way to preview the results before saving?

2318d5c3d250.title: Huyuan3D: Model Retopology and UV Unwrapping
2318d5c3d250.description: Input a dense mesh (from AI generation or photogrammetry scans) and create a light weight model with good topology and unwrapped UV. Great for 3D game assets optimization.
2318d5c3d250.metaDescription: Optimize 3D models with Huyuan3D for game assets using retopology and UV unwrapping. Efficiently prepare dense meshes for real-time rendering.
2318d5c3d250.extendedDescription: The Huyuan3D workflow is designed to streamline the process of optimizing 3D models, making it particularly beneficial for game developers and 3D artists. This workflow focuses on retopology and UV unwrapping, two critical steps in preparing models for efficient rendering in real-time environments. By utilizing the Hunyuan3D model, this workflow takes a dense mesh—often generated through AI or photogrammetry—and transforms it into a lightweight model with optimized topology and unwrapped UVs. This is achieved through a series of specialized nodes including the TencentModelTo3DUVNode and TencentSmartTopologyNode. The TencentModelTo3DUVNode is responsible for converting complex models into a format suitable for UV processing, while the TencentSmartTopologyNode ensures the model's topology is optimized for performance without sacrificing detail. Finally, the SaveGLB node allows users to export the processed model in a widely compatible format, and the Load3D node facilitates the initial import of the dense mesh.
howToUse: Load your dense 3D mesh into the workflow using the Load3D node.
Apply the TencentModelTo3DUVNode to convert the model for UV processing.
Use the TencentSmartTopologyNode to optimize the model's topology.
Execute the HUNYUAN 3D UV UNWRAP group to unwrap the UVs efficiently.
Export the optimized model using the SaveGLB node to save it in a GLB format.
Review the final model in your preferred 3D software to ensure it meets your requirements.
suggestedUseCases: Optimizing 3D game assets for better performance in real-time rendering engines.

231992fee1a6.title: AI on the Lot 2026 - QwenVL - i2t
231992fee1a6.description: The third workflow released for AI on the Lot 2026, made available for ComfyUI 101 workshop attendees to open and follow along if they choose. A simple image-to-text prompt creator using Qwen VL, useful for generating prompts from reference images.
231992fee1a6.metaDescription: ComfyUI tutorial: Convert images to high-quality captions or answers using Qwen-VL with AILab_QwenVL, LoadImage, and PreviewAny for fast image-to-text.
231992fee1a6.extendedDescription:
This workflow turns any image into descriptive, instruction-following text using Qwen-VL inside ComfyUI. It’s a simple, reliable chain: LoadImage brings your source frame or photo into the graph, AILab_QwenVL runs the Qwen-VL vision-language model to generate captions or answers based on your instruction, and PreviewAny displays the resulting text directly in the UI. Because AILab_QwenVL accepts both an image and a prompt, you can steer the output toward concise alt text, detailed scene breakdowns, tags, or even OCR-style transcriptions.

Technically, AILab_QwenVL encodes the visual content and decodes text conditioned on your instruction (e.g., "Describe this scene in one sentence" or "List objects with counts"). You can typically adjust generation behavior (such as temperature or maximum output length, if exposed by your node build) to balance creativity vs. precision. The minimal node graph keeps it fast and teachable—ideal for creating consistent captions, production notes, or metadata without extra post-processing nodes. PreviewAny then renders the string output so you can copy it straight from ComfyUI.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and confirm the three-node chain: LoadImage → AILab_QwenVL → PreviewAny.
In LoadImage, select or drag-and-drop the image you want to describe (frame, product shot, storyboard panel, etc.).
Open AILab_QwenVL and choose your installed Qwen-VL model variant if selectable. Enter a clear instruction, e.g., "Provide a concise caption highlighting setting, main subjects, and actions."
Optionally fine-tune generation settings (e.g., temperature for determinism, maximum tokens for length) if those controls are available in your AILab_QwenVL node.
Queue/Run the workflow. When it finishes, read the generated text in PreviewAny and copy it for your use.
Iterate: refine the instruction (e.g., ask for bullet points, tags, or verbatim transcription), swap the image in LoadImage, and re-run until you get the desired output.
suggestedUseCases: Automatic alt text and SEO-friendly image captions for websites and CMSs.
Shot descriptions and continuity notes for film/TV production stills or on-set frames.
E-commerce product summaries and tag extraction from catalog photos.
Social media caption starters tailored to mood, setting, or call to action.
Quick OCR-style transcription from signs, menus, and posters in images.

faqItems.question: What exactly does AILab_QwenVL do in this workflow?
faqItems.answer: AILab_QwenVL runs a Qwen-VL vision-language model on the input from LoadImage. It takes your instruction (prompt) plus the image, then generates text—such as a caption, list of objects, or an answer to a question about the image—which PreviewAny displays.

faqItems.question: Do I need an internet connection or API key to run this?
faqItems.answer: It depends on how AILab_QwenVL is configured in your environment. Many setups load local model weights and run fully offline. If your node is configured to call a remote backend, you may need network access or credentials. Check your node’s model selection and documentation.

faqItems.question: How can I control the style and length of the output?
faqItems.answer: Guide the model with explicit instructions (e.g., "One-sentence caption," "Return keywords separated by commas," or "Output JSON with fields: setting, subjects, actions"). If your node exposes settings like maximum tokens or temperature, use them to limit length and make results more deterministic.

faqItems.question: How do I get more accurate results (especially for text in images)?
faqItems.answer: Use clear, specific prompts (e.g., "Transcribe all legible text exactly, line by line"), provide sufficiently large, sharp images, and reduce temperature for factual tasks. If the scene is busy, crop to the relevant area before running LoadImage so the model focuses on what matters.

Ideal for poster and cover design, product and brand visuals, or multi-scene character workflows.
23226868cf80.metaDescription: ComfyUI tutorial: precise image edits and short-text rendering with Grok Imagine 2.0 (Aurora). Use up to 3 references, 1K/2K output, and 14 aspect ratios.
23226868cf80.extendedDescription:

The workflow is intentionally simple: LoadImage brings in your source and up to three optional reference images, GrokImageEditNodeV2 interprets your natural-language instructions to apply precise edits (like background swaps, restyling, or adding short text), and SaveImage writes the final render to disk. You can target 1K or 2K output and pick from 14 aspect ratios, making it easy to generate poster-ready or platform-specific visuals.

Under the hood, GrokImageEditNodeV2 conditions the edit on the provided base image plus any reference images to maintain visual identity and style. This enables strong character consistency across scenes, reliable product look alignment, and crisp short-text rendering for cover titles or label callouts—without manual masking. Because the node centralizes key settings (prompt, aspect ratio, and resolution), you can iterate quickly: refine the prompt, swap a reference, and re-render until the composition and typography meet your needs.

Connect the base image (and any reference images) to GrokImageEditNodeV2. In the node, write a clear prompt describing the desired changes (e.g., “Swap to a sunset beach background, cinematic lighting, preserve subject identity”).

Set output parameters in GrokImageEditNodeV2: choose 1K or 2K resolution and select an aspect ratio from the 14 available options that matches your target use (poster, cover, widescreen, square, etc.).

For text rendering, include exact wording in your prompt and be specific about placement and styling (e.g., “Add title ‘DAWN RISING’ in bold uppercase, centered at top, high contrast”). Keep text short for best legibility.
Execute the graph. Review the preview output and adjust the prompt or references to refine composition, identity, style, or text clarity.
When satisfied, connect the GrokImageEditNodeV2 output to SaveImage and run to export the final image to your output directory.

Product photography updates (background swaps, lighting/style harmonization) for e-commerce
Brand and campaign visuals that maintain consistent color, style, and iconography
Multi-scene character workflows where identity must remain consistent across settings
Social media and ad creatives that need fast aspect-ratio variants at 1K or 2K quality

faqItems.question: Do I need a mask to swap backgrounds or restyle part of the image?
faqItems.answer: No mask is required. GrokImageEditNodeV2 applies edits from natural-language instructions. For tighter control, use precise prompts (e.g., describe the subject and the background separately) and start from a well-framed base image.

faqItems.question: What resolutions and aspect ratios are supported?
faqItems.answer: The node renders at 1K or 2K resolution and offers 14 aspect ratios. Choose the aspect ratio that matches your output target (e.g., poster, square, vertical) to avoid unwanted cropping later.

faqItems.question: How do I get the best text rendering quality?
faqItems.answer: Keep text short (titles, labels, or brief slogans), specify the exact string, case, and placement in the prompt, and request high contrast against the background. If needed, generate a clean background or reserved space first, then iterate on type styling.

24c4f6954d46.title: Bria: Guided Background Removal
24c4f6954d46.description: Remove the background from an image with Bria while keeping whatever a text prompt describes, so one subject can be cut out of a busy scene instead of losing everything that is not background. The original pixels come back at full resolution with a new alpha channel. Ideal for product cutouts, portrait isolation and compositing prep.
24c4f6954d46.metaDescription: ComfyUI tutorial: Use Bria to remove backgrounds by prompt—keep one subject from busy scenes and export full‑resolution PNGs with alpha transparency.
24c4f6954d46.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow uses the BRIA model via the BriaGuidedRemoveBackground node to remove backgrounds while preserving only what you describe in a text prompt. Instead of a general background-erase that risks deleting important subjects, you explicitly tell Bria what to keep (for example, "red sneaker" or "woman with headphones"). The node returns the original pixels at full resolution with a clean alpha channel, so you get a precise cutout ready for compositing or design work without upscaling artifacts.

Technically, the pipeline is straightforward: LoadImage brings in your source asset, BriaGuidedRemoveBackground performs text-guided foreground isolation and outputs an RGBA image, ImageCompare provides a quick side-by-side or overlay check against the original, and SaveImage writes the final file with transparency preserved (use PNG to keep alpha). The MarkdownNote in the graph documents the intended behavior and guidance for crafting effective keep-prompts. This setup excels at product cutouts, portrait isolation, and prepping assets for layouts where clean transparency is essential.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and inspect the MarkdownNote for a quick overview of the node chain and the guidance note about describing what to keep.
Open the LoadImage node and select your source image (ideally high-resolution for best edge detail).
In the BriaGuidedRemoveBackground node, enter a concise description of the subject you want to keep (e.g., "blue ceramic mug," "gold wristwatch on hand," or "person in red jacket").
Run the workflow and use the ImageCompare node output to visually check the result against the original, focusing on edges like hair, fabric, and small accessories.
If needed, refine the keep-prompt for clarity (add color, material, or pose details) and run again until the isolation looks clean.
Use the SaveImage node to export the result as a PNG to preserve the new alpha channel for compositing in your editor or design tool.
suggestedUseCases: E-commerce product cutouts from busy lifestyle photos while retaining only the specific product.
Portrait isolation for social banners, thumbnails, and profile images with transparent backgrounds.
Compositing prep for motion graphics or print layouts where the subject must sit cleanly over new backgrounds.
Catalog and marketplace listings that require consistent, background-free assets.
Quick mockups and design iterations where fast, high-quality subject extraction speeds up workflows.

faqItems.question: How should I write the prompt to get the best cutout?
faqItems.answer: Be specific and concrete. Name the main subject and add discriminators like color, material, or distinctive features (e.g., "red running shoe with white logo" or "woman in yellow raincoat"). Avoid vague terms like "object" or broad scene descriptions.

faqItems.question: Does the workflow change my image resolution?
faqItems.answer: No. The BriaGuidedRemoveBackground node returns the original pixels at full resolution with a new alpha channel. The SaveImage node preserves this resolution when you export.

faqItems.question: Which format should I use to keep transparency?
faqItems.answer: Use PNG when saving with the SaveImage node to preserve the alpha channel. JPEG does not support transparency.

faqItems.question: How can I verify the result before saving?
faqItems.answer: Check the ImageCompare node output to view the original and the cutout result side-by-side. Pay close attention to fine edges (hair, fur, thin straps) and refine the keep-prompt if needed.

25c14ca59910.title: Pixal3D: Multi Views to 3D
25c14ca59910.description: Upload your own separate view images, or use one mixed multi-view turnaround sheet. The workflow prepares front, back, left and right views, then reconstructs a textured 3D model with Pixal3D Multi-View.
25c14ca59910.metaDescription: Convert 4-view turnarounds into a textured 3D mesh with Pixal3D Multi-View. Clean backgrounds, generate shape, and bake textures with a Trellis2-based pipeline.
25c14ca59910.extendedDescription:
Pixal3D: Multi Views to 3D turns a 4-view character or product turnaround into a textured 3D mesh. The Preprocess Multiview Images group takes either a single multi-view sheet or separate front, back, left, and right images. It can optionally remove the background (LoadBackgroundRemovalModel + RemoveBackground) to isolate the subject and improve consistency. CLIPVisionLoader provides vision conditioning from the views that drives the multi-view reconstruction.

Under the hood, the workflow builds shape first, then texture, and finally bakes it to a UV map. Sparse Structure Generation initializes a 3D latent with EmptyTrellis2LatentStructure. Shape Generation uses Trellis2ShapeStage with ModelSamplingSD3 and KSampler to refine the latent volume into geometry, while CFGOverride and RescaleCFG keep guidance behavior aligned with the original pipeline. VaeDecodeStructureTrellis2/VaeDecodeShapeTrellis turn the latent into a dense voxel grid, VoxelToMesh converts it to a watertight mesh, and DecimateMesh reduces polygon count. Texture Generation uses Trellis2TextureStage (optionally boosted by Trellis2UpsampleStage) and VaeDecodeTextureTrellis to predict appearance, with VAELoader loading the trellis_2_texture_vae_bf16.safetensors VAE. Finally, UnwrapMesh creates UVs and BakeTextureFromVoxel transfers colors to a texture atlas. PreviewImage nodes provide quick visual checks throughout.

The result is a practical, view-consistent 3D model built directly from your turnaround sheet—ideal when you need a clean starting mesh and texture without manual modeling. The multi-view conditioning keeps silhouettes aligned across views and reduces guesswork compared to single-image reconstruction.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI, then load required models: VAELoader → trellis_2_texture_vae_bf16.safetensors, CLIPVisionLoader (vision encoder), and optionally LoadBackgroundRemovalModel if you plan to remove backgrounds.

Add your inputs: either one 4-view turnaround sheet into the Preprocess Multiview Images group or separate front/back/left/right images. Verify the view mapping is correct so each perspective is assigned to the right slot.
Optional cleanup: enable RemoveBackground to isolate the subject. Use PreviewImage nodes in the preprocess group to check alignment, scale, and crop consistency across views.

Generate shape: keep CFGOverride and RescaleCFG at their provided defaults (to match the reference behavior). Set KSampler steps, sampler/method, and seed, then run Sparse Structure Generation + Shape Generation. Inspect the decoded shape output and mesh (VoxelToMesh) and, if needed, adjust seed or steps.
Generate and refine texture: run Trellis2TextureStage (optionally enable Trellis2UpsampleStage for higher fidelity), then VaeDecodeTextureTrellis. Use PreviewImage to verify appearance across views.

Bake and post-process: run UnwrapMesh followed by BakeTextureFromVoxel to produce a texture atlas. Use DecimateMesh to lower polycount if needed. Right-click image previews to save baked textures; use the mesh output from VoxelToMesh/DecimateMesh for export in your preferred way.
suggestedUseCases: Turn character concept turnaround sheets into a textured base mesh for rigging or further sculpting.
Create quick 3D product/packaging previews from front/back/side photography.
Block out stylized props for games from orthographic sketch sheets.
Generate printable base meshes from multi-view toy or figurine references.
Educational demos showing how multi-view constraints improve 3D reconstruction.

faqItems.question: Do I have to use all four views? Will a single view work?
faqItems.answer: The workflow accepts a single mixed turnaround sheet or separate views. It works with fewer views, but geometry becomes more ambiguous. For best results, provide front, back, left, and right views with consistent scale and pose.

faqItems.question: My mesh looks warped or has holes. How can I improve shape quality?
faqItems.answer: Ensure all views are aligned and similarly scaled, remove complex backgrounds (LoadBackgroundRemovalModel + RemoveBackground), increase KSampler steps, try a different seed, and keep CFGOverride/RescaleCFG at the provided defaults. Consistent, clean inputs yield more stable geometry.

faqItems.question: How do I control polycount and texture detail?
faqItems.answer: Use DecimateMesh to reduce polygon count after VoxelToMesh. For textures, enable Trellis2UpsampleStage for higher fidelity and set your desired texture size in BakeTextureFromVoxel. Inspect results with PreviewImage before exporting.

faqItems.question: What models are required, and why is VAE loading important?
faqItems.answer: VAELoader should load trellis_2_texture_vae_bf16.safetensors so the Trellis2 decoders (VaeDecodeStructureTrellis2/VaeDecodeTextureTrellis) can correctly decode shape and texture latents. CLIPVisionLoader provides vision conditioning from your views, and ModelSamplingSD3/KSampler control the diffusion sampling steps.

faqItems.question: What types of videos work best with this workflow?

faqItems.question: Can I use this workflow for live streaming?

faqItems.question: What output formats are supported?

faqItems.question: How can I improve the accuracy of background removal?

2620e5135442.title: Gemini Omni Flash: Video Edit
2620e5135442.description: Edit videos with natural language using Gemini Omni Flash, transforming a single input video into one edited output based on your descriptive instructions. Specify the duration and aspect ratio in your prompt, and leverage Omni's world knowledge for intuitive edits like changing backgrounds or adding atmosphere. Ideal for quick social media remixes, cinematic scene adjustments, and iterative video refinements without technical prompts.
2620e5135442.metaDescription: Edit videos with natural language in ComfyUI using Gemini Omni Flash. Load a clip, set duration/aspect ratio, preview, and export an AI-edited video.
2620e5135442.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI tutorial workflow lets you edit a single input video using natural language instructions powered by the GeminiVideoOmni node. The graph is straightforward: LoadVideo ingests your source clip, the Prompt Constructor subgraph (node id 331103d2-d660-4a88-abf0-1117dc46b2df) builds a well-formed prompt with the required duration and aspect ratio, GeminiVideoOmni sends the video plus prompt to the Gemini Omni Flash API, and the results are displayed with PreviewAny and saved with SaveVideo. A MarkdownNote in the canvas provides quick tips and reminders.

Technically, LoadVideo decodes frames and metadata, then the Prompt Constructor concatenates your natural language edit with explicit settings like "duration: 5s" and "aspect ratio: 9:16". GeminiVideoOmni uses these to guide the model: the aspect ratio determines the output canvas, and the duration constrains the target clip length. The model returns an edited clip that adheres to your instructions (e.g., background changes, mood/atmosphere adjustments, reframing), which you can quickly review in PreviewAny and export via SaveVideo. For best results, keep prompts concrete, always include duration and aspect ratio, and iterate in short passes.
howToUse: Load the workflow JSON in ComfyUI. You should see LoadVideo, the Prompt Constructor subgraph (331103d2-d660-4a88-abf0-1117dc46b2df), GeminiVideoOmni, PreviewAny, SaveVideo, and a MarkdownNote.

Configure GeminiVideoOmni: add your Gemini API key (in the node or via the node’s documented environment setting) and pick the intended model variant if exposed. Ensure you have internet access and valid API quota.
Open LoadVideo and select your source clip. Short clips (e.g., a few seconds) and moderate resolutions tend to return faster, more consistent edits.

Open the Prompt Constructor subgraph. Set duration (e.g., 5s) and aspect ratio (e.g., 16:9, 1:1, or 9:16). In the instruction field, describe the edit clearly, for example: "Make it dusk with light fog, keep the subject sharp, add a soft cinematic grade, crop to 9:16." The subgraph outputs a complete prompt string.

Run the graph. Use PreviewAny to review the generated clip. If framing or length isn’t as expected, refine the aspect ratio and duration in the Prompt Constructor and be explicit in your wording (e.g., "keep original motion," "center the subject," "trim to first 5 seconds").
When satisfied, set filename/codec options in SaveVideo and execute to export. Iterate by adjusting your prompt or the Prompt Constructor inputs to produce improved or alternate edits.
suggestedUseCases: Social media remixes: reframe to 9:16, shorten to 5–8 seconds, and add a quick mood/grade for Shorts/Reels/TikTok.
Cinematic adjustments: change time of day, add atmosphere (fog, haze), and apply a consistent color tone for scene polish.
Background tweaks: request subtle background replacements or cleanups for B‑roll and product shots.
Reframing and focus: center the subject, apply gentle crop/zoom, and maintain composition across a short highlight clip.
Promo snippets: trim a longer clip into concise, platform-ready teasers with clear aspect ratio and duration.

faqItems.question: Do I have to specify duration and aspect ratio?
faqItems.answer: Yes. The GeminiVideoOmni node expects both in the prompt so the model knows the output canvas and time budget. Use clear formats like "duration: 5s" and "aspect ratio: 9:16" in the Prompt Constructor.

faqItems.question: Does this workflow keep audio?
faqItems.answer: No. This setup focuses on visual edits, and the output from SaveVideo is typically silent. If you need audio, re-sync your original track or music in a video editor after export.

faqItems.question: Does my video stay on my machine?
faqItems.answer: GeminiVideoOmni calls the Gemini API, so your media and instructions are sent to the service provider. Avoid sensitive content and be mindful of your API’s usage, privacy, and content policies.

faqItems.question: How can I get more reliable results?
faqItems.answer: Keep clips short (a few seconds), be explicit and constrained in your instructions, always include duration and aspect ratio, and iterate. Use concrete guidance like "keep the subject centered," "subtle fog only," or "retain original motion" to reduce ambiguity.

2652985596d8.title: Wan2.1 VACE Control Video
2652985596d8.description: Generate videos by controlling input videos and reference images using Wan VACE.
2652985596d8.metaDescription: Turn a source video into a stylized clip using Wan2.1 VACE. Guide with text and a reference image, control edges with Canny, and export MP4/WebP in ComfyUI.
2652985596d8.extendedDescription:
Wan2.1 VACE Control Video is a guided video-to-video workflow that preserves the motion and timing of a source video while restyling or re-characterizing it with a text prompt and a reference image. It loads Wan2.1 VACE checkpoints (1.3B or 14B) via UNETLoader and VAELoader, encodes your text with CLIPTextEncode, and conditions generation with control signals derived from simple image preprocessing (Canny by default). GetVideoComponents reads frames and FPS from the input clip, and TrimVideoLatent keeps the latent sequence aligned with your chosen frame range and resolution before sampling.

Under the hood, ModelSamplingSD3 configures the expected sampler schedule for Wan2.1 VACE, and KSampler performs denoising on a sequence of video latents assembled by WanVaceToVideo using your control video, prompt, and reference image. VAEDecode converts the final latents back to frames, CreateVideo assembles them at the desired FPS, and you can export either MP4 (SaveVideo) or animated WebP (SaveAnimatedWEBP). An optional CausVid LoRA (LoraLoader) can accelerate or stabilize motion with very low steps, though you may need to tune its strength. The 14B model yields higher fidelity (and supports 720p) but runs slower and uses more VRAM; the 1.3B variant is faster and suited to 480p outputs.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and point the UNETLoader, VAELoader, and CLIPLoader nodes to the Wan2.1 VACE model you want to use (1.3B for speed at 480p, 14B for higher quality up to 720p). If you plan to swap the preprocessor, install comfyui_controlnet_aux.

In the Load control video group, connect your source clip with LoadVideo. GetVideoComponents will extract frames, FPS, and dimensions. If needed, use TrimVideoLatent to crop the frame range and ensure the target resolution matches the chosen model’s capability.

In the Load reference image group, add your style/identity image with LoadImage. In Image preprocessing, the Canny node generates edge guidance (you can replace it with another preprocessor such as Lineart or Depth). Adjust Canny thresholds to control how strictly edges are followed.

Open the Prompt group and enter your main prompt (and, if provided in the template, a negative prompt). Set the sampling parameters in Sampling & Decoding: for default generation use steps=20 and cfg=6.0; if using the CausVid LoRA, start with steps=2–4 and cfg≈1.0. Load the LoRA in LoraLoader and set its strength between 0.3 and 0.7, or bypass it to disable.

Run the graph. WanVaceToVideo assembles the conditioning, KSampler performs denoising using ModelSamplingSD3, and VAEDecode turns latents into frames. Use PreviewImage to sanity-check frames, then CreateVideo to compile them at the detected or chosen FPS.

Export your result from Save Video(Mp4) with the SaveVideo node, or from Save Video(WebP) with SaveAnimatedWEBP. If you see shake or blur, try lowering LoRA strength, slightly increasing steps, reducing CFG to 5–6, or relaxing the Canny thresholds.
suggestedUseCases: Character restyling: Keep a performer’s motion from a source clip while swapping to a new character look defined by a reference image.
Cinematic re-grading: Apply a prompt-driven aesthetic to B‑roll footage while using Canny to preserve scene structure and composition.
Product visualization: Retain camera moves from a control video and change materials or colors according to a prompt and reference swatch.
Animated concept previews: Quickly explore variations of a scene at 480p with the 1.3B model, then upscale fidelity with the 14B model for selects.
Consistent series outputs: Use the same reference image and prompt across multiple control clips to maintain a unified style.

faqItems.question: Should I choose the 1.3B or 14B Wan2.1 VACE model?
faqItems.answer: Use 1.3B for faster iteration and 480p outputs. Choose 14B if you need higher fidelity or 720p. The 14B model is slower and requires more VRAM but typically yields cleaner detail and temporal stability.

faqItems.question: My video looks shaky or blurry when using the CausVid LoRA. How can I fix it?
faqItems.answer: Lower the LoRA strength toward 0.3–0.5, slightly increase steps (e.g., from 2 to 3–4), and keep CFG near 1.0 for the LoRA preset. If artifacts persist, bypass the LoRA entirely or relax the Canny thresholds so edges are less constraining.

faqItems.question: How do I change duration or FPS?
faqItems.answer: TrimVideoLatent lets you limit or align the frame range. GetVideoComponents reads FPS from the source; you can keep it or override during CreateVideo. Shorter clips and moderate FPS will reduce VRAM and speed up sampling.

faqItems.question: Can I use a different preprocessor instead of Canny?
faqItems.answer: Yes. Replace the Canny node with another comfyui_controlnet_aux preprocessor (e.g., Lineart or Depth) and route its output to the same control input used by WanVaceToVideo. Different preprocessors change how strictly structure is preserved.

268307c5793e.title: GIMM Frame Interpolation
268307c5793e.description: Generate intermediate frames between existing video frames to create smoother motion. Input a video and receive a fluid, higher-frame-rate output without changing the total duration.
268307c5793e.metaDescription: ComfyUI tutorial: GIMM VFI frame interpolation to boost FPS without changing video length using VHS_LoadVideo and VHS_VideoCombine.
268307c5793e.extendedDescription:
This workflow performs video frame interpolation in ComfyUI to make motion look smoother without changing the total playback time. It uses the comfyui-videohelpersuite for I/O and the comfyui-gimm-vfi custom node to synthesize in-between frames. VHS_LoadVideo ingests your source clip and exposes its frames and native FPS. Those frames are passed to the GIMM VFI interpolator node (UUID: 8d69124f-cc0e-4891-b9ca-9c1b04432c40), which inserts synthetic frames between each pair of originals according to an interpolation factor you set (for example, 2x or 3x). Finally, VHS_VideoCombine assembles the expanded frame sequence back into a video file.

Technically, the GIMM VFI node estimates motion between consecutive frames and generates temporally consistent intermediate frames. The MarkdownNote in the graph spells out the key timing rule: output_fps = input_fps × interpolation_factor. By multiplying the output FPS in VHS_VideoCombine to match the factor, the clip’s duration remains identical while motion appears more fluid. No diffusion or checkpoint models are required; everything hinges on the VFI node and reliable video read/write via the Video Helper Suite.
howToUse: Install the required custom nodes: comfyui-gimm-vfi and comfyui-videohelpersuite. Restart ComfyUI, then load the "GIMM Frame Interpolation" workflow JSON.
Open the VHS_LoadVideo node and select your input video. Confirm it loads correctly and note the displayed input FPS.

Select the GIMM VFI interpolator node (UUID: 8d69124f-cc0e-4891-b9ca-9c1b04432c40) and choose an interpolation factor (commonly 2x or 3x). Higher factors increase smoothness but also computation time and potential artifacts.
In VHS_VideoCombine, set the output FPS to input_fps × interpolation_factor (for example, 30 × 3 = 90). Choose your container/codec and quality settings (CRF/bitrate) as desired.
Set the output file path in VHS_VideoCombine. Optionally, if your Video Helper Suite build supports it, configure audio passthrough or plan to remux audio afterward.
Queue and run the workflow. Inspect the output video for smoothness and artifacts. If needed, adjust the interpolation factor or encode settings and rerun.
suggestedUseCases: Smoothing handheld footage or gimbal shots to reduce micro-judder without altering runtime.
Upgrading screen captures or UI pans/scrolls to higher FPS for clearer motion.
Converting cinematic 24/30 fps material to 48/60+ fps for fluid playback on high-refresh displays.
Increasing temporal density before further processing (e.g., stabilization or denoising) that benefits from more frames.
Enhancing animation or game recordings where consistent frame pacing improves perceived quality.

faqItems.question: Will my video get longer after interpolation?
faqItems.answer: No. The workflow multiplies the output FPS to match the interpolation factor (output_fps = input_fps × factor), so total duration remains the same. This rule is highlighted in the MarkdownNote.

faqItems.question: What interpolation factor should I use?
faqItems.answer: Start with 2x for most footage. Use 3x if you need extra smoothness and the motion is not too complex. Very high factors increase compute time and can introduce ghosting or artifacts on fast action and occlusions.

faqItems.question: Can I keep the original audio?
faqItems.answer: If your VHS_VideoCombine node supports audio passthrough, point it to the original audio or enable the appropriate option to mux it into the output. If not, export the video and remux the audio with a tool like ffmpeg using the original track.

faqItems.question: How do I make slow motion instead of keeping the same duration?
faqItems.answer: This workflow is set up to preserve duration by raising the FPS. For slow motion, keep the output FPS equal to the original (or another lower value) while using a >1x interpolation factor so the added frames extend playback.

26e1f4eddd7e.title: Krea2: Text to Image
26e1f4eddd7e.description: Input a text prompt describing your desired scene. Generate four aesthetic, high-quality images that interpret your prompt with creative variety.
26e1f4eddd7e.metaDescription: Generate four varied, high-quality images from a text prompt in ComfyUI using Krea2ImageNode, then auto-save them with SaveImage for fast iteration.
26e1f4eddd7e.extendedDescription:
This workflow turns a text prompt into four high-quality, stylistically varied images using the Krea v2 image generation service. At its core is the Krea2ImageNode, which sends your prompt (and any optional parameters the node exposes) to the Krea API, returning a batch of images in one run. The SaveImage node then writes those images to your ComfyUI output directory with your chosen filename prefix.

Technically, ComfyUI orchestrates the request/response cycle while compute happens remotely on Krea. You supply the prompt in Krea2ImageNode and, if available in your installation, can set options like seed (for reproducibility), aspect/size, and the number of images. The workflow is preconfigured to produce four outputs for creative variety. The SaveImage node receives the image batch directly from Krea2ImageNode and saves each item as a separate file, which makes iterating and curating results straightforward.

Because generation runs in the cloud, this setup is fast to iterate on without a local GPU. It’s ideal for quickly exploring multiple visual directions from a single prompt, then narrowing in by locking a seed (if exposed) or refining the prompt. The minimal node graph—Krea2ImageNode plus SaveImage—keeps the process simple while still letting you manage output naming and batching inside ComfyUI.
howToUse: Load the workflow JSON in ComfyUI and ensure the Krea2ImageNode is installed and visible in the graph.
Open Krea2ImageNode and add your Krea API key (either in the node’s API key field or via the method documented for your install).
Enter your text prompt. If the node exposes options like negative prompt, aspect/size, seed, or batch size/num_images, set them (use 4 for four outputs or leave as preconfigured).
Configure SaveImage (set a clear filename_prefix so results are grouped; leave other defaults unless you have a custom output path).
Queue the prompt and run. Watch the images appear in the ComfyUI preview; the batch will also be written to your output directory.
Iterate: refine the prompt for style/subject accuracy; if available, lock a seed for reproducible tweaks or leave it blank for more variety.
suggestedUseCases: Rapid concept exploration for characters, environments, or products from a single prompt.
Moodboards and look-dev: generate four stylistic variations to compare tone and composition.
Thumbnail and social post ideation where multiple layout/style options are useful.
Client review sheets: produce a small set of distinct takes to discuss direction before refining.

faqItems.question: Do I need a local GPU to use this workflow?
faqItems.answer: No. Krea2ImageNode sends your prompt to the Krea API and generation runs in the cloud. ComfyUI orchestrates the request and saves the returned images.

faqItems.question: Why am I not getting four images?
faqItems.answer: Check the Krea2ImageNode settings. If your version exposes a batch size or num_images parameter, set it to 4. If not, the node may be preconfigured; update the node or refer to its docs.

faqItems.question: How can I reproduce a specific result?
faqItems.answer: If the node exposes a seed parameter, record and reuse that seed with the same prompt and settings. Without a fixed seed, each run may produce different images.

faqItems.question: Where are my images saved?
faqItems.answer: SaveImage writes files to your ComfyUI output folder (by default, ./output). Set a filename_prefix in SaveImage to keep runs organized or change the path if your setup allows.

faqItems.question: Is it possible to edit the generated video further?
