3427fd6e0fa8.title: Wan2.1 VACE Outpainting
3427fd6e0fa8.description: Generate extended videos by expanding video size using Wan VACE outpainting.
3427fd6e0fa8.metaDescription: ComfyUI tutorial: Outpaint and enlarge videos with Wan 2.1 VACE. Learn setup, masks, prompts, and constraints to create extended, coherent video frames.
3427fd6e0fa8.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow teaches you how to outpaint a video—expanding its canvas while keeping the original content intact—using Wan 2.1 VACE. It loads your source clip with LoadVideo and extracts dimensions and frame count via GetVideoComponents and PreviewImage. You then define where to expand using ImagePadForOutpaint and a mask built from ImageToMask/MaskToImage, replicated across time with RepeatImageBatch. Prompts are encoded with CLIPTextEncode, and generation runs through KSampler with ModelSamplingSD3 scheduling on a Wan 2.1 VACE UNet/Decoder stack (UNETLoader, VAELoader), with VAEDecode converting latents to frames. WanVaceToVideo handles video-specific conditioning, and TrimVideoLatent ensures temporal shapes align. The result is assembled with CreateVideo and saved via SaveVideo.

Technically, two alignment rules matter for stable inference: the spatial size you set for outpainting must be divisible by 16 (a constraint of WanVaceToVideo and the VAE), and the sequence length must satisfy the temporal constraint (Length - 1 divisible by 4), which TrimVideoLatent addresses. Because core Comfy nodes don’t yet expose video size/frame-count utilities, this template uses PreviewImage as a practical workaround; you can swap in custom utility nodes if available. The workflow includes model groups for Wan2.1-VACE-1.3B (lighter, recommended for 480p) and Wan2.1-VACE-14B (higher quality, suitable for higher resolutions like 720p if resources allow). Default generation settings are steps: 20 and cfg: 6.0, with optional CausVid LoRA tuning at steps: 2–4 and cfg: 1.0.
howToUse: Load the workflow and select your model: in the "Load models here" group, choose either the 1.3B or 14B path. Point UNETLoader and VAELoader to the Wan2.1 VACE checkpoints that match your choice.

Import your source clip with LoadVideo. Use GetVideoComponents and PreviewImage to read the current width/height and total frames. In the "Video size - Must be divisible by 16" group, set your target outpainted width/height to multiples of 16.

Define the outpaint region: configure ImagePadForOutpaint to add pixels on the sides you want to expand. Build a binary mask with ImageToMask/MaskToImage to protect the original content area, then RepeatImageBatch so the mask length matches all frames.

Write prompts in the "Prompt" group using CLIPTextEncode (positive) and a negative like "bad quality, blurry, messy, chaotic" if desired. In KSampler, start with steps=20 and cfg=6.0 (or for CausVid LoRA: steps=2–4, cfg=1.0). Choose your sampler/scheduler via ModelSamplingSD3 and set a seed.

Ensure temporal alignment: use the "Length - 1 should be divisible by 4" group and TrimVideoLatent so the sequence length conforms to VAE/VACE expectations. Then run WanVaceToVideo -> VAEDecode to generate the outpainted frames.
Assemble and save: feed frames into CreateVideo, set fps from GetVideoComponents, and export with SaveVideo (MP4). If edges look off, adjust the mask or padding, tweak CFG/steps, and re-run.
suggestedUseCases: Reformatting horizontal videos to vertical (or vice versa) by outpainting additional background for social platforms.
Adding safe headroom or side-space for titles, lower thirds, and UI overlays without cropping the subject.
Extending establishing shots by widening the scene for a more cinematic composition.
Repairing tight framing: add background context around the subject to avoid cutoffs.
Creating gentle push-in/pull-back storytelling space while preserving the original action area.

faqItems.question: Why must width/height be divisible by 16 and length-1 be divisible by 4?
faqItems.answer: WanVaceToVideo and the VAE downsample spatially by powers of two, so dimensions must align to 16 for clean latent shapes. The temporal pathway expects sequence lengths that satisfy (frames - 1) % 4 == 0. TrimVideoLatent enforces the temporal rule; set your target resolution to multiples of 16 for the spatial rule.

faqItems.question: Which model should I use: Wan2.1-VACE-1.3B or 14B?
faqItems.answer: Use 1.3B for faster runs and 480p outputs on modest GPUs. Choose 14B for higher quality and, if your VRAM allows, higher resolutions such as 720p. The 14B model produces better detail but is slower and more memory-intensive.

faqItems.question: How do I control where outpainting happens?
faqItems.answer: Use ImagePadForOutpaint to add canvas on chosen sides (top/bottom/left/right). Then create a mask that protects the original video region (ImageToMask/MaskToImage) and replicate it across frames with RepeatImageBatch. The model synthesizes only in the unmasked, newly padded areas.

faqItems.question: My output is black/misaligned. What should I check?
faqItems.answer: Verify three points: 1) Output width/height are divisible by 16, 2) TrimVideoLatent is applied so (frames - 1) is divisible by 4, 3) VAEDecode is connected before CreateVideo/SaveVideo. Also confirm fps and frame count from GetVideoComponents, and that your mask batch length matches the video length.

346ccc5e1b8d.title: Pose Detection: SDPose Multi-Person (Video)
346ccc5e1b8d.description: Upload a video to detect human poses. Supports detection for both single individuals and multiple people within the same scene
346ccc5e1b8d.metaDescription: Multi-person pose detection in video with SDPose-OOD. Overlay pose maps and bounding boxes, then export a processed clip in ComfyUI.
346ccc5e1b8d.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow performs multi-person human pose detection on video using the SDPose-OOD model and the sdpose_wholebody_fp16.safetensors checkpoint. It starts by loading your clip with LoadVideo, then GetVideoComponents extracts frames and the original FPS. Each frame is optionally resized with ResizeImageMaskNode for speed/quality control before being fed into the SDPose detection node (01b6a731-fb78-4070-9a38-c87146da9604). The detector estimates body keypoints for one or more people per frame and can also return person bounding boxes.

For visualization, the workflow overlays the generated pose map on top of the original frames using ImageBlend and can draw per-person rectangles with DrawBBoxes. PreviewImage lets you check a few frames before committing to a full run. Finally, CreateVideo reassembles the processed frames (preserving the original FPS from GetVideoComponents unless you override it) and SaveVideo writes the finished clip. A PrimitiveInt node exposes max_detections so you can easily switch between single-person and multi-person analysis. This makes the workflow useful for motion studies, choreography review, or preparing pose maps as guides for downstream generation tasks.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and ensure the SDPose checkpoint (e.g., sdpose_wholebody_fp16.safetensors) is downloaded from the linked model hub and selected in the SDPose node.
Open LoadVideo and choose your source video. GetVideoComponents will extract frames and FPS automatically.
Set max_detections via the PrimitiveInt node to match the number of people you expect (e.g., 1 for solo, 3–6 for groups).
Optionally adjust ResizeImageMaskNode to control processing resolution (higher = better detail, slower; lower = faster).
Tune visualization: enable/disable DrawBBoxes and set ImageBlend’s alpha to control how strongly the pose map overlays the original frames. Use PreviewImage to verify a few frames.
Queue the graph. CreateVideo will rebuild the sequence (using the original FPS from GetVideoComponents unless changed), and SaveVideo will write the output file.
suggestedUseCases: Choreography and dance rehearsal review with clear multi-person pose overlays.
Team sports practice analysis to compare player positioning and movement.
Fitness class or classroom recording with visual pose feedback for multiple participants.
Precomputing pose maps for pose-guided video generation or motion transfer pipelines.
Rapid visual QA for crowd scenes to verify coverage and detect occlusion issues.

faqItems.question: How do I switch between single-person and multi-person detection?
faqItems.answer: Use the PrimitiveInt node wired to the SDPose node’s max_detections input. Set it to 1 for single-person, or increase it to cover the expected number of people in the scene.

faqItems.question: Do I need a GPU for this workflow?
faqItems.answer: A CUDA-capable GPU is strongly recommended for practical speeds. CPU-only inference will be significantly slower, especially for higher resolutions or longer videos.

faqItems.question: Does the workflow track identities across frames?
faqItems.answer: No. The SDPose node performs per-frame detection. It outputs pose maps and bounding boxes each frame but does not assign persistent person IDs over time.

faqItems.question: How can I improve pose quality when people are small or occluded?
faqItems.answer: Increase the processing resolution in ResizeImageMaskNode, raise max_detections to avoid missing people, and ensure good lighting and contrast in the source video. Higher resolution improves keypoint detail but will be slower.

34cc3b9ecbe1.title: Luma Ray 3.2: Image to Video
34cc3b9ecbe1.description: Generate cinematic-quality videos from text prompts using Luma Ray 3.2, with support for extending previous generations by providing a generation ID. The workflow accepts 1 input image and produces 1 video output, enabling seamless iterative refinement. Ideal for creating short film sequences, marketing content, and professional video production.
34cc3b9ecbe1.metaDescription: ComfyUI tutorial: Turn an image into a cinematic video with Luma Ray 3.2 and extend it via generation_id. Includes preview and export steps.
34cc3b9ecbe1.extendedDescription:
This workflow turns a single image into a cinematic video using the Luma Ray 3.2 model, with an optional extension pass to continue the shot across multiple generations. The pipeline starts with LoadImage to supply your reference frame, then feeds that into LumaRay32ImageToVideoNode, which sends the request to Luma’s API and returns a generated clip. PreviewAny lets you quickly inspect results and exposes the generation_id as text, while SaveVideo writes the final video to disk. A MarkdownNote node embedded in the graph provides in-workflow tips on how to wire and reuse IDs.

What makes this setup especially useful is the dedicated LumaRay32ExtendVideoNode. By default, it inherits source_generation_id from the initial run, enabling seamless continuation for longer sequences or iterative refinements. If you want to extend from a prior session, you can disconnect the automatic wire and paste any valid generation_id captured in PreviewAny. This keeps motion, look, and continuity consistent across segments while you experiment with prompts or timing—all within a minimal, reliable node chain.
howToUse: Open the workflow in ComfyUI, select the grouped nodes, and press Ctrl+B to enable the group if it’s disabled.
Load your starting frame with the LoadImage node (use an image that matches your desired framing/aspect for best results).
Configure LumaRay32ImageToVideoNode with your prompt and any node-specific settings required by your Luma Ray 3.2 setup (ensure your Luma API access is configured if needed). Run the graph.
Inspect the output with PreviewAny. Note the generation_id shown in the Preview as Text (generation_id) output. Save the initial clip via SaveVideo.

To continue the same shot, use LumaRay32ExtendVideoNode. By default, it uses the wired source_generation_id from the previous node. If you want to extend a past run, disconnect that input and paste the generation_id you saved from PreviewAny.
Run again to generate the extended segment and export with SaveVideo. Repeat the extend step as needed to build longer sequences while maintaining visual continuity.
suggestedUseCases: Pre-visualization for short films or commercials starting from a keyframe or concept art
Marketing clips that evolve from a single product image into dynamic hero shots
Storyboard animatics that need motion continuity across multiple beats
Social media teasers and loopable micro-videos built from a branded still
Continuing or refining a previous generation to reach a final, polished sequence

faqItems.question: Where do I find the generation_id to extend a video?
faqItems.answer: After your first run, open the PreviewAny outputs. Look for the Preview as Text (generation_id) field—it displays the generation_id. Copy that ID to reuse or extend the shot later.

faqItems.question: How do I extend a previous session’s video instead of the current run?
faqItems.answer: In LumaRay32ExtendVideoNode, disconnect the automatically wired source_generation_id input. Then paste the saved generation_id (from PreviewAny) directly into the node’s generation_id field and run the graph.

faqItems.question: Do I need an internet connection or API key?
faqItems.answer: Yes. The LumaRay32ImageToVideoNode and LumaRay32ExtendVideoNode call Luma’s API. Ensure you have network access and configure any required Luma credentials per your node installation.

faqItems.question: What format does SaveVideo export, and where is it saved?
faqItems.answer: SaveVideo lets you choose the file name and output path. The container/codec options depend on your ComfyUI setup and the node’s settings (commonly MP4 or WEBM). Set your desired folder and format in SaveVideo before running.

3515c5083027.title: Image to Video
3515c5083027.description: This app generates a high quality video with sound. All you need is to upload an input image and write prompt.
3515c5083027.metaDescription: Turn a single image into a video with prompt-guided motion in ComfyUI. LoadImage + Image-to-Video node + SaveVideo for fast, controllable results.
3515c5083027.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow turns a single still image into a short video guided by a text prompt. It uses LoadImage to bring in your source frame, passes it to a dedicated Image-to-Video generator node (ID: 770dde0e-f342-49aa-ad1e-184724671c5d), and then encodes the resulting frame sequence with SaveVideo. The generator node conditions on both the input image (as a visual anchor) and your prompt (to suggest motion, style, or scene changes), producing a coherent set of frames that evolve over time.

Technically, the generator node synthesizes a batch of images (frames) from the static input by sampling with a controllable seed and typical parameters such as number of frames, motion/denoise strength, guidance, and resolution. SaveVideo then assembles those frames into a playable clip at your chosen FPS and output format (e.g., MP4 or WebM). You control duration via frame count and playback feel via FPS, while the seed lets you repeat or iterate on results consistently. This makes the workflow useful for quick motion studies, cinemagraph-like clips, and social-ready animations without needing full video capture.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and confirm the three key nodes are present: LoadImage, the Image-to-Video generator (ID: 770dde0e-f342-49aa-ad1e-184724671c5d), and SaveVideo.
Open LoadImage and select your source image. Use a reasonably sized input (e.g., 512–1024 on the long side) to balance quality and VRAM usage.
In the Image-to-Video generator node, enter a clear prompt describing desired motion and mood (e.g., “gentle camera push-in, soft breeze moving hair, golden-hour lighting”).

Adjust core parameters in the generator node: set number of frames (clip length), FPS (playback speed), resolution, motion/denoise strength (how much it departs from the source), guidance scale, and seed for reproducibility.
Configure SaveVideo: choose FPS to match the generator output and your preferred output format/quality. Set an output file name/path.

Click Queue Prompt to run. When finished, open the saved video to review. If you see artifacts or over-strong motion, lower motion/denoise strength, reduce resolution or frame count, and re-run with the same or a new seed.
suggestedUseCases: Cinemagraph-style loops from product or portrait photos (subtle motion like hair, fabric, or light shifts).
Quick animated previews for concept art or storyboards to explore camera moves and atmosphere.
Social media posts that add motion to key visuals for higher engagement without full video shoots.
Product hero animations for e-commerce banners and landing pages.
Ambient motion backgrounds derived from brand imagery for intros or titles.

faqItems.question: How long can the generated video be?
faqItems.answer: Length is determined by the number of frames and FPS. For example, 48 frames at 12 FPS ≈ 4 seconds. Longer clips require more VRAM and time; increase frames gradually and consider lowering resolution or FPS if you hit memory limits.

faqItems.question: How do I keep the video faithful to the original image?
faqItems.answer: Use a conservative prompt and reduce the node’s motion/denoise strength so it deviates less from the source. Also try increasing guidance strength and using a fixed seed. If available, choose a sampler or setting that favors stronger conditioning.

faqItems.question: My output has jitter or artifacts. What should I change?
faqItems.answer: Lower motion/denoise strength, reduce resolution, and try a different seed. You can also decrease the number of frames or use a slightly higher guidance value. Subtle, specific prompts often produce more stable motion than broad or conflicting ones.

faqItems.question: Which formats can I save to?
faqItems.answer: SaveVideo can assemble the frames into a video container like MP4 or WebM (options depend on your node’s settings and installed encoders). Match FPS between the generator and SaveVideo to avoid timing issues.

This capability not only enhances the user experience but also broadens the potential applications of the workflow. By integrating advanced AI techniques with intuitive user input, Kling 3.0 sets a new standard in video generation, offering unprecedented flexibility and creativity for content creators, filmmakers, and digital artists.

Input multilingual prompts if needed to guide the video generation process.
Execute the workflow to generate the video sequence.

36794f399aa0.title: Z-Image-Turbo_Oldschool-Hud-Graphics
36794f399aa0.description: Create Oldschool Hud Graphics with a LoRA and Z-Image Turbo. Use a LoRA to create unique styles, characters or looks.
36794f399aa0.metaDescription: ComfyUI tutorial: Generate old-school HUD graphics fast with a style LoRA and Z-Image Turbo. Batch variants, then export images or animated clips.
36794f399aa0.extendedDescription:
This workflow generates retro, old‑school HUD graphics from text prompts by combining a style LoRA with a turbo sampler for rapid iteration. The "Oldschool Hud Graphics" LoRA steers the base checkpoint toward geometric UI motifs—reticles, gridlines, rings, readouts—while the Z‑Image Turbo node accelerates sampling for fast previews and quick style exploration. BatchImagesNode lets you spin up variations in one pass, and SaveImage captures your chosen frames. When you’re ready to animate, CreateVideo and SaveVideo assemble your batch into a short motion clip.

Under the hood, your prompt is encoded and fed to the base model with the LoRA applied at a user‑set weight, biasing attention layers toward the HUD aesthetic. Z‑Image Turbo then samples with low step counts for speed, which you can tune for crisper lines or more detail. Keep the LoRA weight moderate to strong to emphasize the graphic look, and pair it with concise prompts (e.g., "retro heads‑up display, concentric circles, grid overlay, monochrome green") plus a negative prompt to suppress photoreal clutter. The included MarkdownNote contains in‑graph tips, while the custom nodes (listed by UUID) handle the LoRA/Turbo plumbing so you can focus on prompts, batch size (BatchImagesNode), and output (SaveImage/SaveVideo).
howToUse: Load the workflow JSON in ComfyUI. Place your base checkpoint in models/checkpoints and the "Oldschool Hud Graphics" LoRA in models/loras, then select them in the corresponding model/LoRA nodes in the graph.

Open the prompt nodes feeding Z-Image Turbo and write a concise positive prompt (e.g., "old-school HUD, reticle, wireframe circles, grid overlay, monochrome green"). Add a negative prompt to suppress unwanted elements (e.g., "photoreal, face, background scene, text artifacts").
Set the LoRA weight to control style intensity (start around 0.7–1.0). Use BatchImagesNode to choose how many variants to generate per run (e.g., 4–8) for quick exploration.

Configure Z-Image Turbo for speed and clarity: begin with low steps for previews (e.g., 4–8), moderate guidance (CFG) to avoid clutter, and a layout-friendly resolution/aspect ratio suited to your design (e.g., square for icons, portrait for posters).
Run the graph. Review the batch outputs, then fine-tune the prompt, LoRA weight, steps, and CFG until the HUD elements are crisp and legible. Use SaveImage to export final stills.
Optional: To create an animated clip from your batch, connect the images to CreateVideo, set frame rate and order, then finalize with SaveVideo.
suggestedUseCases: Editorial and poster layouts needing retro HUD accents, frames, and readouts.
Branding moodboards and styleframes exploring techy, wireframe visual language.
Game UI concepts and overlays for prototypes or pitch decks.
YouTube/TikTok bumpers and lower‑thirds using animated HUD elements.
Icon sets and badges with minimal, high‑contrast instrumentation motifs.

faqItems.question: Which base model should I use with the Oldschool Hud Graphics LoRA?
faqItems.answer: Use a checkpoint that matches the LoRA’s architecture (e.g., SD 1.5 LoRA with an SD 1.5 checkpoint, SDXL LoRA with an SDXL checkpoint). Check the LoRA’s model card or filename for its target version. Mixing versions will reduce quality or fail to load.

faqItems.question: How do I control how strong the HUD style appears?
faqItems.answer: Adjust the LoRA weight (lower for subtle, higher for strong). Refine prompts to emphasize geometry (reticle, grid, ring, UI readouts) and use a negative prompt to suppress photoreal features. If outputs feel busy, slightly lower CFG or reduce steps to simplify shapes.

faqItems.question: My lines look soft or messy—how can I sharpen them?
faqItems.answer: Increase sampling steps modestly in Z‑Image Turbo, keep CFG moderate, and try a resolution that matches your final layout (avoid extreme upscales in one pass). Tighten the prompt to fewer, clearer elements (e.g., one reticle + one grid) and avoid conflicting style terms.

faqItems.question: How do I turn a batch of images into a video?
faqItems.answer: After generating a batch with BatchImagesNode, connect the sequence to CreateVideo, set your frame rate and ordering, then export with SaveVideo. This compiles your HUD variants into a short motion clip for previews or social posts.

howToUse: Load the ComfyUI workflow and ensure the CheckpointLoaderSimple node is set to your local SDXL model.

38a5302d2c2d.title: LTX-2.3 Style Transition
38a5302d2c2d.description: Apply the ltx2.3-transition LoRA to create smooth style and scene transitions. This workflow uses a specialized model to blend visual elements.
38a5302d2c2d.metaDescription: Create smooth style and scene transitions in LTX-2.3 video using the ltx2.3-transition LoRA. Text-guide the change, add references, and export with SaveVideo.
38a5302d2c2d.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow builds a guided style and scene transition on top of the LTX-2.3 text-to-video model by applying the ltx2.3-transition LoRA. The core generation happens inside a custom LTX-2.3 pipeline node (beb19732-5803-4af6-b2d2-289692ce780b), which takes your prompt, applies the LoRA at a user-defined weight, and renders a sequence of frames that smoothly evolve from one style or scene description to another. If you provide a reference image with LoadImage, the pipeline can also pull color palettes or subject cues into the transition; if you skip it, the transition is guided purely by text.

Practical controls are surfaced where you need them: prompt fields (with support for the trigger word "zhuanchang"), frame count and FPS for timing, and LoRA strength to dial how assertively the transition behaves. MarkdownNote is embedded to keep prompting tips visible as you iterate, and SaveVideo encodes the final frames into a video file at your chosen frame rate and quality. The result is a reliable, loop-friendly way to blend visual elements—style, lighting, subject emphasis, or even scene composition—without hand-animating or post-processing crossfades.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and read the embedded MarkdownNote for LTX-2.3 prompting tips and the trigger word guidance.
Open the custom LTX-2.3 pipeline node (beb19732-5803-4af6-b2d2-289692ce780b) and confirm LTX-2.3 is selected as the base model and the ltx2.3-transition LoRA is enabled.

Write your prompt to describe the transition over time (e.g., "A city street at dusk slowly becomes a neon cyberpunk alley, camera dolly forward, soft fog"), then add the trigger word "zhuanchang" near the end. Keep subject, scene, camera movement, and transformation behavior clearly stated.

Optionally use LoadImage to bring in a style or subject reference and connect it to the pipeline’s reference input. Start with a moderate LoRA strength (e.g., 0.6–0.8) and keep other defaults as-is for a first pass.
Set frame count and FPS to control transition duration (more frames = slower, smoother change). Fix a seed for reproducibility if you plan to iterate. Then run the graph.

Preview the output and, if needed, adjust LoRA strength (lower for subtler transitions, higher for stronger shifts), refine the prompt timing language, and re-run. Use SaveVideo to export at your chosen FPS and quality.
suggestedUseCases: Scene-to-scene bridges in short films: evolve from one location or time-of-day to another without a hard cut.
Style morphs for product reels: smoothly change materials, finishes, or lighting styles around a single subject.
Title and logo reveals: transition from abstract textures to clean branding assets.
Mood shifts in music videos: gradually shift color grade and atmosphere to match track sections.
Concept art explorations: iterate across art styles while maintaining core composition and subject.

faqItems.question: What does the "zhuanchang" trigger word do, and where should I put it?
faqItems.answer: It activates the ltx2.3-transition behavior in the model+LoRA combo. Place it near the end of your prompt so your core subject, scene, camera, and transformation details remain dominant. This helps the base description stay clear while the transition logic is applied.

faqItems.question: How do I control how fast the transition happens?
faqItems.answer: Use frame count and FPS. More frames at the same FPS produce a longer, slower transition; fewer frames produce a faster one. You can also phrase timing cues in your prompt (e.g., "first half… then…"), but duration is primarily governed by total frames and playback speed.

faqItems.question: When should I use a reference image with LoadImage?
faqItems.answer: Use a reference if you want to anchor color palette, texture, or a specific subject look. Connect it to the pipeline’s reference input. If you aim for a purely text-driven transition, skip the reference and rely on descriptive prompts.

faqItems.question: The transition feels too strong or inconsistent. How can I improve stability?
faqItems.answer: Lower the LoRA strength to 0.4–0.6 for subtler shifts, fix the seed for repeatability, and simplify the prompt to fewer, clearer visual goals. Avoid conflicting descriptors; keep subject and camera consistent while describing how the scene or style evolves.

38fa33effd1e.title: Flux Video Edit
38fa33effd1e.description: Edit and transform images with FLUX using simple text prompts. Change characters, objects, backgrounds, styles, or entire scenes while preserving the key details and overall consistency of the original image.
38fa33effd1e.metaDescription: Text-guided video editing in ComfyUI with Flux. Load a clip, describe changes, and export a coherent, structure-preserving edit.
38fa33effd1e.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow performs text-guided video-to-video editing with Flux. It uses a simple three-node path: LoadVideo reads your source clip, FluxVideoEditNode applies your prompt-driven edits while preserving core scene structure and motion, and SaveVideo encodes the edited frames back to an MP4. A MarkdownNote in the canvas provides quick reminders and links. The included sample, subway_musician.mp4, is a great starting point to learn the technique.

Technically, FluxVideoEditNode conditions the Flux model on each incoming frame plus your prompt to steer appearance, style, and scene elements while maintaining temporal consistency so motion remains coherent across frames. This is ideal for restyling characters, swapping backgrounds, or changing objects without breaking the original composition. Depending on your setup, the node can run with locally prepared Flux model weights or call a compatible API; ensure ComfyUI and required models are up to date before running.
howToUse: Open the workflow in ComfyUI and update ComfyUI and models as needed. If your FluxVideoEditNode uses an API, configure credentials; if it runs locally, ensure Flux weights are installed.
In LoadVideo, select your input clip (try the provided subway_musician.mp4) and confirm it previews correctly.

Open FluxVideoEditNode and enter a clear prompt describing the desired transformation (e.g., "convert the scene to a rainy night with neon reflections; keep the musician and composition"). If the node exposes options like negative text or edit strength, adjust them to favor preservation vs. stronger changes.
Set the output path and format in SaveVideo so you know where the result will be written.
Click Queue Prompt (or Run). Monitor the console for progress and VRAM usage. When complete, open the exported video to review temporal consistency and detail.
Iterate: refine your prompt for specificity (subjects, style cues, what to keep) and, if available, nudge any preservation/strength settings to balance identity and stylization.
suggestedUseCases: Background and environment swaps (e.g., move a scene from day to night or add weather) while keeping the original performance.
Character or wardrobe restyling for social content and concept previews without reshooting.
Product/prop replacement and quick continuity fixes where layout and timing must remain intact.
Localized variants of the same clip (signage, color grading, ambience) for different markets.
Storyboarding and previsualization: rapidly test alternate looks on the same footage.

faqItems.question: How do I preserve the subject and layout while still changing style?
faqItems.answer: Be explicit in your prompt about what must remain: name the subject ("same person/musician"), call out "keep composition and camera motion," and describe changes narrowly (e.g., "replace background with a tiled subway wall" rather than "change the whole scene"). If your node exposes an edit strength or preservation control, reduce strength to favor identity and structure retention.

faqItems.question: Can it handle long or high-resolution videos?
faqItems.answer: Processing time and VRAM grow with resolution, frame count, and prompt strength. For longer clips, work in shorter segments, reduce resolution, or downscale before editing and upscale afterward if needed. Close other GPU apps to free VRAM, and monitor the ComfyUI console for out-of-memory messages.

faqItems.question: Will the output keep the original audio?
faqItems.answer: By default, SaveVideo exports a silent MP4. If you need audio, export the edited video and then reattach the original track with a tool like ffmpeg (e.g., map the input audio onto the edited video) or perform the merge in your NLE.

faqItems.question: Do I need an API key or special models?
faqItems.answer: It depends on your FluxVideoEditNode variant. Some setups run locally with downloaded Flux model weights; others call a remote API and require credentials. Check the node’s documentation and ensure ComfyUI and the required Flux models or API settings are prepared before running.

3ab5e4d51129.title: Image Upscale: WaveSpeed SeedVR2
3ab5e4d51129.description: Upload an AI-generated image to restore details and upscale. The workflow preserves colors and sharpness while minimizing artifacts. Output is a high-quality, enlarged version of your input.
3ab5e4d51129.metaDescription: ComfyUI tutorial: upscale images with WaveSpeed + SeedVR2. Restore detail, preserve color, compare before/after, and export high-res results.
3ab5e4d51129.extendedDescription:
This tutorial workflow upscales an existing image while restoring fine details and keeping colors true to the source. It’s centered on the WavespeedImageUpscaleNode configured with the WaveSpeed upscaler and the SeedVR2 model, which together prioritize edge clarity and color fidelity. You bring your source image in with LoadImage, preview the transformation with ImageCompare (under Nodes 2.0), and export the high-resolution result via SaveImage. A MarkdownNote in the graph provides inline guidance and tips.

Technically, the WavespeedImageUpscaleNode takes the input image tensor and applies learned super-resolution using the WaveSpeed/SeedVR2 weights to reconstruct high-frequency content while suppressing common upscale artifacts like ringing and over-sharpened halos. The node’s scale setting (e.g., 2x or 4x) determines the final size, and its quality/fidelity controls help you balance crisp detail against noise suppression. ImageCompare places the original and upscaled outputs side by side for quick quality control before you commit the result with SaveImage. The result is a clean, enlarged image that preserves the original palette and contrast, well-suited for print, portfolios, and production handoffs.
howToUse: Open ComfyUI and load the workflow JSON titled “Image Upscale: WaveSpeed SeedVR2.” If you don’t see ImageCompare, switch to Nodes 2.0 (Menu -> Nodes 2.0).
Load your source image with the LoadImage node (drag-and-drop or file picker). Use a clean, uncompressed input when possible.
Open the WavespeedImageUpscaleNode and set your scale (e.g., 2x or 4x). Ensure the node is using the WaveSpeed/SeedVR2 configuration. Leave the default quality settings for a balanced start.
Queue/Run the workflow. When it finishes, use the ImageCompare node to view a side-by-side before/after and check edges, skin tones, and gradients for unwanted halos or shifts.
If needed, adjust the upscale scale or quality/fidelity controls in the WavespeedImageUpscaleNode to reduce artifacts or enhance fine detail, then re-run.
Export the final image with SaveImage. Confirm your output folder and naming pattern to keep versions organized.
suggestedUseCases: Upscaling AI-generated portraits and character art to print-ready resolutions while preserving skin tones and textures.
Enhancing concept art, matte paintings, and environment renders for client review decks or portfolio sites.
Preparing product mockups, UI elements, and icons for high-DPI displays with minimal ringing or color shift.
Cleaning and enlarging game textures or sprites for remasters and asset libraries.
Sharpening and resizing social media visuals to platform-specific dimensions without overshooting contrast.

faqItems.question: Do I need Nodes 2.0 for this workflow?
faqItems.answer: Only for ImageCompare. If ImageCompare doesn’t appear, switch to Nodes 2.0 (Menu -> Nodes 2.0). The rest of the nodes (LoadImage, WavespeedImageUpscaleNode, SaveImage) work as usual.

faqItems.question: What input resolution and scale should I use?
faqItems.answer: For best quality, start with a reasonably clean image (e.g., 512–2048 px on the short side) and upscale 2x. If you need more, evaluate the 2x result with ImageCompare, then try 4x. Avoid stacking multiple aggressive upscales in one pass if you see halos.

faqItems.question: How can I reduce halos or oversharpened edges?
faqItems.answer: Lower the detail/fidelity emphasis in the WavespeedImageUpscaleNode if available, or try a smaller scale (2x instead of 4x). Ensure your source isn’t already heavily sharpened or compressed, and re-check with ImageCompare before exporting.

faqItems.question: Can I run this via the ComfyUI API or batch multiple images?
faqItems.answer: Yes. You can invoke the same graph through the ComfyUI API by supplying your image to the LoadImage input and reading the SaveImage outputs. For batches, iterate over your input list and set unique output names so each result is saved separately.

3b435b0ca944.title: Pose Map: SDPose-OOD (Video to Pose Map)
3b435b0ca944.description: Upload a video to extract pose keypoints and generate a pose map. The workflow supports multiple person detection and uses an enhanced SDPose model for accurate whole-body feature extraction.
3b435b0ca944.metaDescription: Extract multi-person whole-body pose maps from video with SDPose-OOD in ComfyUI. Load video, detect body/hands/face, and export a pose-map video.
3b435b0ca944.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI tutorial workflow converts any input video into a clean pose-map video using the SDPose-OOD whole-body model. It detects multiple people per frame and extracts body, hands, and face keypoints, then renders them as a skeletal pose map—ideal as a control signal for pose-conditioned image/video generation or for motion analysis without exposing identities. The provided checkpoint (sdpose_wholebody_fp16.safetensors) runs in FP16 for faster, memory-efficient inference while maintaining robust keypoint coverage.

Technically, the pipeline is straightforward and reproducible: LoadVideo reads your clip and emits frames; the SDPose-OOD inference node (01b6a731-fb78-4070-9a38-c87146da9604) estimates whole-body keypoints for each frame and draws a standardized pose map; CreateVideo stitches the pose-map frames back into a video; and SaveVideo writes the result to disk. A MarkdownNote node is included to document in-graph instructions and links to model resources. The combination of multi-person support and whole-body detection makes this workflow reliable across action, dance, fitness, and crowded scenes where hands and face landmarks matter.
howToUse: Open the workflow in ComfyUI and review the MarkdownNote for quick tips and model links. Ensure your GPU is available for inference.
Download the sdpose_wholebody_fp16.safetensors checkpoint from the SDPose repo (Hugging Face or ModelScope) and place it where your SDPose-OOD node expects model files.
In LoadVideo, select your source video. Optionally choose a target resolution/FPS if the node exposes those settings; lower resolution can speed up inference.

On the SDPose-OOD whole-body node (01b6a731-fb78-4070-9a38-c87146da9604), select the sdpose_wholebody_fp16.safetensors checkpoint. Keep default detection settings to start; the model supports multiple persons automatically.

Connect the pose-map frames to CreateVideo and verify its FPS matches your input (or your desired output). Point SaveVideo to an output path, then run the queue to generate and save the pose-map video.
suggestedUseCases: Prepare pose-control inputs for pose-to-image/video generation (e.g., conditioning Stable Diffusion or similar pipelines with clean skeleton maps).
Sports or dance analysis where limb trajectories and timing matter while preserving participant privacy.
Fitness and ergonomics feedback systems that track form using full-body plus hands/face landmarks.
Crowd or multi-person activity visualization in research or prototyping without exposing identities.
Pre-annotation for downstream motion processing or keypoint-based analytics.

faqItems.question: What does SDPose-OOD detect, and does it handle multiple people?
faqItems.answer: It estimates whole-body keypoints—body, hands, and face—and renders them into a pose map. The workflow supports multi-person detection per frame, so multiple people are drawn simultaneously.

faqItems.question: Do I need a GPU, and how can I speed up processing?
faqItems.answer: A GPU is strongly recommended for reasonable throughput. For faster runs, use the FP16 checkpoint (sdpose_wholebody_fp16.safetensors), lower the input resolution or FPS in LoadVideo, and avoid extremely long clips. Good lighting and reduced motion blur improve accuracy.

faqItems.question: Will the pose tracker keep the same person IDs across frames?
faqItems.answer: This workflow performs frame-by-frame detection and pose rendering; it does not provide temporal identity tracking. If you need persistent IDs, add a dedicated tracking step downstream.

faqItems.question: How do I keep output settings consistent with the source video?
faqItems.answer: Match CreateVideo’s FPS (and resolution, if exposed) to the input video. SaveVideo will write the assembled pose-map video to your chosen path. Note that audio is not included by default in this pipeline.

3b73b8146375.title: Image Outpainting: Flux.1
3b73b8146375.description: Upload an image to expand its canvas using Flux.1. Generate an outpainted image with extended content.
3b73b8146375.metaDescription: Outpaint images with Flux.1 in ComfyUI. Expand canvas in any direction with prompt control and save clean, on‑style results for banners, prints, and reframing.
3b73b8146375.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow demonstrates fast, high‑quality outpainting with Flux.1. You upload a source image, then use Flux.1 to extend the canvas in one or more directions while keeping content, lighting, and style consistent. The core path is simple and transparent: LoadImage feeds your reference into FluxProExpandNode (which performs the outpainting using the Flux/Flux.1 model), and SaveImage writes the final result to disk.

Technically, FluxProExpandNode conditions the Flux.1 generator on your input image and prompt, synthesizing new pixels only in the added border region while preserving the original content. You control which sides to expand, how far to extend, and the textual guidance (prompt and, optionally, negative prompt) that steers what appears in the new area. Guidance strength, steps, and seed influence fidelity and variation. This makes the workflow ideal for reframing shots, adapting aspect ratios for different platforms, and adding breathable whitespace around subjects—without manual cloning or painting.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and ensure the Flux/Flux.1 model is installed and selectable in FluxProExpandNode.
Open the LoadImage node and choose the source image you want to extend. Use a clean, well‑exposed image for best results.

In FluxProExpandNode, select Flux.1 as the model, choose which sides to expand (left/right/top/bottom) and how much to extend. Add a concise prompt that describes the subject and surrounding environment; optionally add a negative prompt to avoid unwanted elements.

Adjust generation settings in FluxProExpandNode as needed (e.g., guidance strength, steps, and seed). Use a moderate guidance strength and enough steps to maintain style consistency without overbaking details.

Queue/Run the workflow. Review the preview. If the new area drifts off‑style or adds artifacts, refine the prompt to match the original image’s scene, reduce or increase guidance slightly, or try a different seed.
When satisfied, SaveImage will write the final outpainted image to your configured output directory. Iterate by changing expansion sides/amount and seed to produce alternate crops and aspect ratios.
suggestedUseCases: Social banners and thumbnails: Extend edges to fit platform‑specific aspect ratios without cropping the subject.
Product photos: Add clean space for text, pricing, or callouts while preserving the original scene and lighting.
Portraits and editorials: Reframe tight shots for magazine layouts or prints by expanding background context.
Panorama completion: Continue scenery at the borders to fill wide canvases or repair clipped edges.
UI and print layouts: Add breathing room around key visuals for headlines and branding without manual retouching.

faqItems.question: How do I control what appears in the expanded area?
faqItems.answer: Describe the desired surroundings in the prompt (materials, setting, time of day, style). Keep it consistent with the source image—e.g., mention the same environment and lighting. Use a negative prompt to exclude elements you don’t want (e.g., extra people, text, logos).

faqItems.question: Will the original part of the image change?
faqItems.answer: FluxProExpandNode focuses generation on the added canvas area and aims to keep the original region intact. Minor adjustments at the boundary can occur to blend seams. If you notice unwanted changes, reduce guidance strength slightly, add clarifying prompt text, or expand in smaller increments.

faqItems.question: What image size works best?
faqItems.answer: Use reasonably detailed inputs (e.g., standard photo or higher). Very small images may lack texture for convincing continuation. If you need large final outputs, consider expanding in stages and upscaling after outpainting.

faqItems.question: Can I automate this via the ComfyUI API?
faqItems.answer: Yes. This graph (LoadImage → FluxProExpandNode → SaveImage) can be executed via ComfyUI’s /prompt API by posting the serialized workflow JSON with your parameters (image path, prompt, expansion sides/amount, steps, seed).

3b8274edb58c.title: Tripo H3.1: Image to Model
3b8274edb58c.description: Upload a reference image of your object. Generate a high-detail 3D model with dense geometry and PBR-ready materials.
3b8274edb58c.metaDescription: Turn a single image into a dense, PBR-textured 3D model with Tripo H3.1 in ComfyUI. Optional auto-rig and retarget, then export GLB/FBX/OBJ.
3b8274edb58c.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI tutorial workflow turns a single reference photo into a high-detail, PBR-textured 3D asset using the Tripo H3.1 pipeline. It starts with LoadImage, passes the image into TripoImageToModelNodeV2 to reconstruct dense geometry, then refines materials with TripoTextureNodeV2 to produce physically based texture maps (albedo/base color, normal, roughness, metallic, and optional ambient occlusion when available). TripoConversionNode prepares the mesh and materials for your target format, and Save3DAdvanced writes the final GLB/FBX/OBJ to disk with embedded or external textures.

For character or prop animation, the workflow includes TripoRigNode to auto-rig supported shapes and TripoRetargetNode to map that skeleton to a target rig. This makes it practical to go from a single product or character photo to an engine-ready 3D asset in minutes. The nodes are organized under the Tripo Toolset group—select the group and press Ctrl+B to enable it—so you can toggle the full pipeline on/off and focus on generation, texturing, conversion, and export as separate stages.
howToUse: Open the workflow in ComfyUI, locate the Tripo Toolset group, select it, and press Ctrl+B to enable the group. If nodes are missing, install the Tripo Toolset/extension and reload.
Configure Tripo credentials: open TripoImageToModelNodeV2 (and related Tripo nodes) and enter your API key or set credentials in the extension settings as required.
Load your reference photo in LoadImage. Use a sharp, well-lit image with a clear silhouette and minimal background clutter; center the object and avoid heavy occlusions.

In TripoImageToModelNodeV2, set generation options such as detail density and output scale (use Higher/High detail where available for dense geometry). Run the node or execute the workflow to generate the initial mesh.

Open TripoTextureNodeV2 to refine materials. Choose texture resolution (e.g., 2K–4K) and enable available PBR maps (albedo/base color, normal, roughness, metallic, AO if offered). Preview and re-run if you adjust settings.

Set your export in TripoConversionNode and Save3DAdvanced: pick format (GLB, FBX, OBJ), embed or externalize textures, adjust units/scale if needed. Then run Save3DAdvanced to write the final asset. Optionally enable TripoRigNode and TripoRetargetNode before export if you need a rigged, retargeted model.
suggestedUseCases: E-commerce and marketing: generate PBR-ready product models for turntables and interactive viewers from a single catalog image.
Game and realtime prototyping: quickly convert references into dense placeholder or hero assets for engine testing.
AR/VR previews: produce textured GLB assets for rapid AR try-ons or scene layout.
Concept design: iterate on 3D forms derived from sketches or reference photos to validate proportion and material direction.
Digital twins: build quick 3D stand-ins for physical objects for visualization and training demos.

faqItems.question: What image quality works best for reconstruction?
faqItems.answer: Use a high-resolution, sharp image with neutral lighting and a clean background. Keep the object fully visible with minimal occlusion and motion blur. Strong silhouettes and mid-to-high contrast surfaces improve geometry and texture fidelity.

faqItems.question: Which outputs and textures can I export?
faqItems.answer: With TripoTextureNodeV2 and Save3DAdvanced you can export GLB, FBX, or OBJ. Textures typically include base color (albedo), normal, roughness, and metallic; ambient occlusion may be available depending on settings. You can embed textures in GLB/FBX or save them as external image files.

faqItems.question: Can I animate the result?
faqItems.answer: Yes—use TripoRigNode to auto-rig supported meshes (e.g., humanoid-like forms), then TripoRetargetNode to map the skeleton to your target rig before export. If your object isn’t suitable for rigging, you can still export a static PBR asset.

faqItems.question: Does this require an internet connection or an API key?
faqItems.answer: The Tripo nodes call the Tripo service, so you need a valid API key and internet access. Configure credentials in TripoImageToModelNodeV2 or the extension settings. Without a key or connectivity, generation will fail.

faqItems.question: How do I control polygon count or scale?
faqItems.answer: Use TripoImageToModelNodeV2 and TripoConversionNode settings to set output scale/units and target format. If a target face count or decimation option is exposed, adjust it there; otherwise, export with Save3DAdvanced and decimate or remesh in your DCC or engine as needed.

3b9e9f29c1dc.title: LTX-2: Image to Video
3b9e9f29c1dc.description: Transform static images into dynamic videos with LTX-2 Pro. Generate cinematic video sequences with natural motion, synchronized audio, and support for up to 4K resolution at 50fps.
3b9e9f29c1dc.metaDescription: Convert static images to dynamic videos with synchronized audio using LTX-2 for expressive lip sync and natural motion.
3b9e9f29c1dc.extendedDescription: The LTX-2: Image to Video workflow is designed to transform static images into dynamic videos, seamlessly integrating audio and video generation. This workflow utilizes the LTX-2 model from Lightricks, known for its ability to produce expressive lip synchronization and natural motion, ensuring that the generated videos appear realistic and engaging. The workflow leverages several nodes, including SaveVideo for output, LoadImage for importing static images, and ResizeImageMaskNode for adjusting image dimensions to fit video requirements. The b7c2d337-c38d-4c04-922b-2d638449d13e node is crucial for processing and synchronizing audio with video, enhancing the overall multimedia experience. By using this workflow, users can efficiently create high-quality videos from images, making it a powerful tool for content creators looking to add dynamic elements to their projects.
howToUse: Load the LTX-2: Image to Video workflow in ComfyUI.
Import your static image using the LoadImage node.
Adjust the image dimensions with the ResizeImageMaskNode to ensure compatibility with video settings.
Configure the LTX-2 model parameters, ensuring width and height are divisible by 64, and frame count by 8 + 1.
Run the workflow to generate the video, and use the SaveVideo node to export your final output.
suggestedUseCases: Creating dynamic video content from static marketing images.
Enhancing educational materials with animated visuals.
Developing engaging social media posts with synchronized audio-visual elements.
Producing video presentations with realistic lip-sync and motion.
Transforming traditional photo albums into interactive video stories.

faqItems.question: What image dimensions should I use for the best results?
faqItems.answer: Ensure your image dimensions are divisible by 64 for optimal video compatibility.

faqItems.question: How do I ensure the video has synchronized audio?
faqItems.answer: The b7c2d337-c38d-4c04-922b-2d638449d13e node handles audio synchronization, so ensure it's correctly configured in your workflow.

faqItems.question: Can I use this workflow for high-resolution videos?
faqItems.answer: Yes, you can use 1920x1088 resolution if your hardware supports it, but ensure all parameters meet the divisibility requirements.

faqItems.question: What happens if I use invalid parameters?
faqItems.answer: The workflow will silently adjust to the nearest valid parameters without causing errors, ensuring smooth operation.

3c8a442fcc25.title: Bria: FIBO 2.0 Image Edit
3c8a442fcc25.description: Edit an image with Bria FIBO 2.0 by describing the change in plain language, with an optional mask to confine it to one region. FIBO 2.0 is one model for both editing and generation, trained on structured VGL captions, so it holds everything you did not ask to change, and it returns that structured prompt so the edit can be rebuilt or refined from JSON.
3c8a442fcc25.metaDescription: Edit images with Bria FIBO 2.0 in ComfyUI using plain text and optional masks, with structured VGL JSON for reproducible, refinable edits.
3c8a442fcc25.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI tutorial shows how to make precise, natural-language edits to a photo using Bria FIBO 2.0. The core of the graph is the BriaImageEditNode, which takes an input image, an optional mask to localize the change, and a plain-language instruction like "replace the cloudy sky with a clear blue sky" or "change the roof tiles to terracotta." FIBO 2.0 is a single model for both generation and editing, trained on structured VGL captions. That training helps it preserve everything you don’t mention while transforming only what you do, so backgrounds, lighting, and composition remain stable unless requested otherwise.

Technically, the workflow wires LoadImage to bring in your source (for example, sunlit_rooftop_capture.png), BriaImageEditNode to apply the instruction (and optional mask), ImageCompare to preview before/after, and SaveImage to write the result. A key advantage of FIBO 2.0 here is that it also returns a structured VGL prompt (JSON-like) that captures the edit. You can keep that JSON to reproduce or refine the result later, making your edits traceable and iterative rather than one-off guesses. MarkdownNote is included for in-graph guidance, and ImageCompare (available under Nodes 2.0) gives a quick visual A/B check so you can dial in changes confidently.
howToUse: Open the workflow in ComfyUI and update ComfyUI if needed. If you want the before/after view, enable Nodes 2.0 (Menu -> Nodes 2.0) so ImageCompare appears.
Load your source image with LoadImage (e.g., sunlit_rooftop_capture.png). Optionally load a black/white mask image with another LoadImage if you want to confine edits to a region.

Open BriaImageEditNode and enter a clear instruction describing only what should change (e.g., “replace the sky with a clear blue sky” or “make the roof tiles terracotta”). Leave out elements you want to remain unchanged.

Connect the source image to BriaImageEditNode’s image input. If using a mask, connect it to the node’s mask input. Wire the edited output to ImageCompare (alongside the original) for preview, and to SaveImage to export.
Queue the graph. Inspect the before/after in ImageCompare. If available from BriaImageEditNode, copy the returned structured VGL JSON so you can rebuild or refine the edit later.
Adjust your instruction or mask as needed and re-run. When satisfied, use SaveImage to write the final image to disk.
suggestedUseCases: Product photography cleanup: replace backgrounds, fix minor defects, or recolor packaging while preserving lighting and perspective.
Architecture and real estate: swap skies, adjust exterior materials, or tidy landscaping with masked, localized edits.
Fashion and portrait tweaks: change garment colors or accessories without altering skin tones or the overall scene.
Marketing variations: generate multiple on-brand edits from the same base image using the saved VGL JSON to ensure consistency.
Social media content: quick, targeted enhancements (e.g., brighten the sky, remove a sign) without full retouching pipelines.

faqItems.question: How do I keep the rest of the image unchanged?
faqItems.answer: FIBO 2.0 is trained on structured VGL captions and preserves everything you don’t mention. Keep your instruction focused on only the desired change, and use a mask to restrict edits to a specific area if needed.

faqItems.question: Where do I find the structured VGL JSON for my edit?
faqItems.answer: BriaImageEditNode surfaces the model’s structured VGL prompt alongside the edited image. After running, check the node’s outputs or logs for the JSON and save it for reproducibility or iterative refinement.

faqItems.question: Do I need to configure an API key for Bria?
faqItems.answer: Some Bria integrations use an API. If your node requires credentials, set them in the node’s settings or your ComfyUI environment as documented by the Bria extension. If everything runs locally for your setup, no API key is needed.

faqItems.question: Why don’t I see ImageCompare?
faqItems.answer: ImageCompare is available under Nodes 2.0. Enable it via Menu -> Nodes 2.0, then reload the node list. You can also skip it and view results in the image preview or saved output.

3c9ffca52a5e.title: HY 3D: Image to Model
3c9ffca52a5e.description: Upload an image to generate a 3D model with geometry and PBR textures.
3c9ffca52a5e.metaDescription: Convert 2D images into 3D models with geometry and PBR textures using the HY 3D workflow in ComfyUI. Efficient and accurate image-to-model conversion.
3c9ffca52a5e.extendedDescription:
The 'HY 3D: Image to Model' workflow in ComfyUI is a powerful tool designed to convert 2D images into detailed 3D models, complete with geometry and PBR (Physically Based Rendering) textures. This workflow leverages the Hunyuan3D model, known for its advanced capabilities in interpreting image data and generating accurate 3D representations. The process begins with the LoadImage node, which allows users to upload their desired image. The core transformation is handled by the TencentImageToModelNode, which processes the image data and constructs a 3D model. This node utilizes sophisticated algorithms to ensure that the resulting model maintains high fidelity to the original image's features.

Once the model is generated, the SaveGLB node is used to export the model in the GLB format, which is widely supported for 3D assets and ensures easy integration into various applications. Additionally, the Preview3D node provides a real-time visualization of the model, allowing users to inspect the geometry and textures before finalizing the output. This workflow is particularly useful for artists and developers looking to quickly prototype 3D assets from existing 2D designs, offering a seamless transition from concept to 3D model.
howToUse: Start by loading the 'HY 3D: Image to Model' workflow in ComfyUI.
Use the LoadImage node to upload your 2D image.
Connect the image to the TencentImageToModelNode to process and generate the 3D model.
Preview the generated model using the Preview3D node to ensure it meets your expectations.
Export the final 3D model using the SaveGLB node to save it in GLB format.
Integrate the exported model into your preferred 3D application or platform.
suggestedUseCases: Creating 3D assets for video games from concept art.
Prototyping product designs by converting sketches into 3D models.
Generating 3D models for virtual reality environments from real-world images.
Developing educational tools by transforming historical images into interactive 3D models.
Enhancing architectural visualizations by converting floor plans into 3D models.

faqItems.question: What type of images work best with this workflow?
faqItems.answer: High-resolution images with clear details and distinct features yield the best results, as they provide more data for the model to interpret.

faqItems.question: Can I edit the 3D model after it's generated?
faqItems.answer: Yes, once exported in GLB format, the model can be imported into most 3D editing software for further refinement and customization.

faqItems.question: Is the generated 3D model suitable for animation?
faqItems.answer: The model includes geometry and PBR textures, making it suitable for static scenes. For animation, additional rigging and adjustments may be required.

faqItems.question: How long does it take to generate a 3D model?
faqItems.answer: The processing time depends on the complexity of the image and your system's capabilities, but it typically takes a few minutes.

3ca102a6e582.title: Bria: Product Holding
3ca102a6e582.description: Place a product into the hands of the person in a photo with Bria. One person photo plus one to three product shots is enough for a lifestyle image in which the face, pose and background stay untouched and the product is held naturally. Ideal for e-commerce and social content that would otherwise need a shoot.
3ca102a6e582.metaDescription: ComfyUI tutorial: Use BRIA to place a product into a person’s hands while preserving the face, pose, and background. Ideal for fast lifestyle images.
3ca102a6e582.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow uses BRIA’s product holding model to place a chosen product naturally into the hands of a person in a photo, while preserving the subject’s face, pose, and background. Supply one portrait (with a clearly visible hand) and one to three product images, and the BriaProductHolding node returns a realistic composite at roughly one megapixel. It’s a fast way to generate convincing lifestyle visuals without organizing a photo shoot.

Technically, the pipeline is simple and robust: LoadImage nodes bring in the person photo and product shots, which feed into the BriaProductHolding node that calls the BRIA model via API. The node handles the placement and compositing automatically and outputs a single edited image that you save with SaveImage. A MarkdownNote in the graph provides quick inline guidance.

For best results, use a person photo where at least one hand is clearly visible and unobstructed, and choose product shots with a clean view of the item. If your initial result needs refinement, try swapping in an alternate product angle or cropping the person image to emphasize the intended hand and grip area before re-running.
howToUse: Open the Bria: Product Holding workflow in ComfyUI and read the MarkdownNote for quick tips.
Use LoadImage to add your person photo (one person, hand clearly visible). Connect it to the BriaProductHolding person input.
Use one to three additional LoadImage nodes to import your product shots. Connect these to the BriaProductHolding product inputs.
Verify your BRIA API configuration so the BriaProductHolding node can run (API access is required).
Queue/Execute the workflow. Inspect the preview result; if needed, try alternate product angles or adjust your crop for a clearer hand.
When satisfied, connect the output to SaveImage (or confirm it’s already connected) and run to save the final composite.
suggestedUseCases: E-commerce lifestyle visuals showing a product in-hand without scheduling a photoshoot
Social media posts and ads featuring natural, human-scale product presentation
Marketplace listing variations (e.g., multiple colors or accessories held by the same model)
Rapid concept mockups for packaging or handheld device ergonomics
A/B testing different product angles or versions in the same scene

faqItems.question: What kinds of images work best for the person photo?
faqItems.answer: Use a single-person photo with at least one hand clearly visible and not heavily occluded. Neutral lighting and minimal motion blur help the model place the product naturally while preserving the face, pose, and background.

faqItems.question: How many product images can I provide?
faqItems.answer: You can connect one to three product shots to the BriaProductHolding node. If the first result isn’t ideal, try alternate angles or cleaner product views to improve realism.

faqItems.question: What resolution should I expect, and how do I get higher resolution?
faqItems.answer: The BriaProductHolding output returns at roughly one megapixel. If you need larger images, pass the result to an upscaling workflow or model after SaveImage.

faqItems.question: Does this run locally or use an external service?
faqItems.answer: The BriaProductHolding node uses the BRIA API (external service). Your images are sent to BRIA for processing. Review your BRIA account settings and data policy for details on privacy and retention.

3cb47a67b81a.title: LTX 2.3 - Cozy Felt
3cb47a67b81a.description: Stylized text-to-video generation using VRGameDevGirl84's LTX 2.3 LoRAs + Workflow, adapted to run on Comfy Cloud. Creates adorable felt worlds and characters.
3cb47a67b81a.metaDescription: Create adorable felt-style text-to-video clips with LTX 2.3 LoRAs in ComfyUI. Pick a LoRA, add its trigger word, and export with VHS_VideoCombine.
3cb47a67b81a.extendedDescription:
LTX 2.3 - Cozy Felt is a stylized text-to-video workflow that wraps VRGameDevGirl84’s LTX 2.3 LoRAs around the LTX-2.3-22B-DISTILLED-1.1 model to generate short, adorable "felt" animations from a prompt. The core generation is driven by a custom LTX node (ID 45d6b185-beee-4467-b4c2-debdf835cb35) configured to load the LTX2 video VAE (LTX2_video_vae_bf16.safetensors) for latent-space video sampling. You pick a LoRA from a dropdown, include its trigger word in your prompt (for example, F3ltCut0u7 for the cozy felt look), and the node produces a sequence of stylized frames. The MarkdownNote node embedded in the canvas provides quick instructions and lists the LoRA trigger words so you don’t have to leave the workspace.

After diffusion, frames are assembled into a playable clip with VHS_VideoCombine, where you set the frame rate and output format. This separation (generate frames first, then encode) makes iteration fast and predictable: you can tweak prompts, LoRA strength, seed, frame count, or resolution on the generation node, then re-run only the combine step to change FPS or container. The result is a reliable, beginner-friendly pipeline for creating soft, craft-like animations—great for cozy title cards, character snippets, or looping social posts. Note: the audio VAE (LTX2_audio_vae_bf16.safetensors) is listed in the assets but is not wired into this canvas by default.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI (or Comfy Cloud) and confirm the required files are available: LTX-2.3-22B-DISTILLED-1.1-GGUF and LTX2_video_vae_bf16.safetensors. If a node reports a missing model, update the file path in the core LTX node.

Open the core LTX generation node (ID 45d6b185-beee-4467-b4c2-debdf835cb35). Choose a LoRA from the lora_name dropdown and include its trigger word in your positive prompt (e.g., “F3ltCut0u7” for the cozy felt style). Add a concise subject and simple motion cues.

Set key parameters on the generation node: seed (fixed for repeatability), steps (increase for cleaner detail), guidance/CFG (moderate values for style adherence), resolution (keep the short side ~512–768 for speed), frames and FPS (e.g., 24–48 frames at 8–12 FPS). Adjust LoRA strength if exposed.

Optionally add a negative prompt to reduce unwanted textures or artifacts (e.g., “text, watermark, logo, blurry, noisy”). Keep camera motion and scene complexity simple for the most consistent felt look.
Run the generation to produce frames. Inspect a few frames to confirm the style and subject match your intent; if needed, refine the prompt, LoRA strength, or steps and re-run.
Open VHS_VideoCombine, set the desired FPS and container (e.g., MP4), then execute it to assemble the frames into a video. Download the result from the file browser or Comfy Cloud output panel.
suggestedUseCases: Cozy title cards or intros for craft, DIY, or children’s content
Short character loops for social posts or stickers with a handmade aesthetic
Whimsical product stingers for toy or stationery brands
Educational snippets for kids’ apps with soft, friendly visuals
Seasonal greeting animations with felt cutout themes

faqItems.question: Do I have to use the LoRA trigger word?
faqItems.answer: Yes. Each LTX 2.3 LoRA has a trigger keyword (e.g., F3ltCut0u7) that activates its style. Include it in the positive prompt along with your subject for consistent results.

faqItems.question: What controls improve temporal consistency?
faqItems.answer: Keep prompts simple, use a fixed seed, avoid rapid camera moves, and limit clip length (e.g., 24–48 frames). Increasing steps can help detail, while moderate guidance/CFG avoids jittery overcorrection.

faqItems.question: Where do I put the models and VAE files?
faqItems.answer: Place the base model (LTX-2.3-22B-DISTILLED-1.1-GGUF) and LTX2_video_vae_bf16.safetensors in the paths expected by the core LTX node. If the node reports a missing file, update its model and VAE fields to your actual paths. The audio VAE is not used by default.

faqItems.question: How do I change the playback speed without re-generating frames?
faqItems.answer: Use VHS_VideoCombine. Re-run only that node and change the FPS or format; it will re-encode the existing frames into a new video without redoing diffusion.

3cf3c6a082ed.title: LTX-2 Pose to Video
3cf3c6a082ed.description: Generate high-quality videos from pose guidance with synchronized audio-video generation using LTX-2. Features precise pose control, expressive motion, and efficient performance.
3cf3c6a082ed.metaDescription: Transform pose guidance into high-quality videos with LTX-2, featuring precise pose control and synchronized audio-video generation.
3cf3c6a082ed.extendedDescription:
The LTX-2 Pose to Video workflow is designed to transform pose guidance into high-quality video content with synchronized audio and video generation. Utilizing the LTX-2 model from Lightricks, this workflow offers precise control over pose and expressive motion, making it ideal for creating dynamic video content. The workflow integrates various nodes such as GetVideoComponents, PreviewImage, and SaveVideo, which help in breaking down the video into components, previewing frames, and saving the final output, respectively. A key feature of this workflow is its use of the comfyui_controlnet_aux custom nodes, which enhance the precision of pose control and motion expression.

Technically, the workflow begins with video and image preprocessing using nodes like LoadVideo and ResizeImageMaskNode. It then employs the DWPreprocessor for refining video settings, ensuring optimal frame count and resolution. The workflow is designed to handle resolutions up to 1920x1088, though it defaults to 720p for efficiency. The frame count must be divisible by 8 plus 1, ensuring smooth transitions and synchronization. This workflow is particularly useful for creators seeking to produce videos with detailed motion and synchronized audio, leveraging the power of the LTX-2 model to achieve professional-grade results.
howToUse: Load the LTX-2 Pose to Video workflow in ComfyUI.
Import your pose guidance data using the LoadVideo node.
Adjust video settings such as resolution and frame count, ensuring they meet the required divisibility conditions.
Use the PreviewImage node to review frames and make necessary adjustments.
Process the video with the LTX-2 model to generate the final output.
Save the generated video using the SaveVideo node.
suggestedUseCases: Creating animated videos from motion capture data for entertainment or educational purposes.
Developing promotional content with synchronized audio and expressive motion.
Producing training videos where precise motion control is essential.
Enhancing video game development by generating realistic character animations.
Designing virtual reality experiences with detailed motion and pose accuracy.

faqItems.question: What are the resolution requirements for this workflow?
faqItems.answer: The resolution must be divisible by 64. The default is 720p, but you can use up to 1920x1088 if your system supports it.

faqItems.question: Why must the frame count be divisible by 8 plus 1?
faqItems.answer: This ensures smooth transitions and synchronization in the video, preventing any potential artifacts or glitches.

faqItems.question: Can I use this workflow for real-time video generation?
faqItems.answer: While the workflow is efficient, real-time generation depends on your system's capabilities and the complexity of the video content.

faqItems.question: How do I ensure the best results from the LTX-2 model?
faqItems.answer: Focus on detailed pose guidance and ensure your video settings, such as resolution and frame count, adhere to the workflow's requirements.

3ddb7afa1aa4.title: Seedance 2.5: FLF2V
3ddb7afa1aa4.description: Generate a smooth video transition between a user-provided start frame and end frame with Seedance 2.5, which automatically interpolates the motion, camera movement, and visual evolution while locking both endpoints. Ideal for shot transitions, storyboard previz, and before-and-after scene showcases like empty-to-packed or day-to-night shifts.
3ddb7afa1aa4.metaDescription: Create smooth, locked-endpoint video transitions from two images using Seedance 2.5. Load start/end frames, auto-interpolate motion, and export with SaveVideo.
3ddb7afa1aa4.extendedDescription:
Seedance 2.5: FLF2V is a first–last frame to video workflow that generates a smooth, locked-endpoint transition between two user-provided images. It uses two LoadImage nodes to bring in your start and end frames, then passes them to ByteDance2FirstLastFrameNode, which calls the Seedance 2.5 model to synthesize the in-between motion and appearance changes while preserving both endpoints. Finally, SaveVideo encodes the returned frame sequence into a playable video file.

Technically, the ByteDance2FirstLastFrameNode estimates a coherent motion path and visual evolution between the first and last frames so the video “lands” exactly on your inputs. This makes it ideal for creating believable camera moves, time-of-day shifts, or scene population changes without re-shooting. Because endpoints are locked, the output is especially stable for shot bridges, storyboard previz, and before–after showcases. SaveVideo then packages the generated frames at your chosen playback rate for quick review or handoff.
howToUse: Load the Seedance 2.5: FLF2V workflow in ComfyUI and confirm the three nodes are present: two LoadImage nodes, ByteDance2FirstLastFrameNode, and SaveVideo.
Import your start and end images with the LoadImage nodes. For best results, use matching resolution and aspect ratio; crop or pad so both images are the same size.
Connect the start image output to the First/Start input on ByteDance2FirstLastFrameNode and the end image output to the Last/End input. Verify the node shows both images are received.

Open ByteDance2FirstLastFrameNode and set its available generation controls (e.g., number of in-between frames or duration if exposed, any seed/reproducibility options, and interpolation quality settings). If the node uses an API, make sure your credentials are configured.
Configure SaveVideo (e.g., filename/prefix and playback FPS) so the final timing matches your target duration. Higher FPS yields smoother playback at the same frame count.
Queue and run the workflow. Review the saved video output; if you see warping or pacing issues, adjust the input alignment or interpolation settings, then re-run.
suggestedUseCases: Shot transitions: bridge two adjacent storyboards or plates with a believable move that lands precisely on the next shot.
Before–after reveals: transform empty-to-crowded spaces, clean-to-stylized looks, or day-to-night progressions while keeping endpoints fixed.
Previsualization: quickly iterate camera paths and scene evolution between two keyframes for pitch decks or animatics.
Product makeovers: show refurbish or colorway changes from baseline to final without retraining a model.
Environmental changes: simulate seasonal or lighting shifts between two photographic keyframes.

faqItems.question: Do my start and end images need the same size?
faqItems.answer: Yes—use matching resolution and aspect ratio for stable interpolation. Crop or pad one image to match the other before sending both into ByteDance2FirstLastFrameNode.

faqItems.question: How do I control the speed of the transition?
faqItems.answer: Adjust the total frames generated (if exposed by ByteDance2FirstLastFrameNode) and/or the FPS in SaveVideo. More frames or lower FPS lengthens the clip; fewer frames or higher FPS shortens it.

faqItems.question: How can I reduce flicker or warping in the middle frames?
faqItems.answer: Use clean, minimally compressed inputs with consistent framing. Align subjects similarly across both images, avoid drastic composition jumps, and, if available, tweak the node’s interpolation/quality settings or try a different seed.

faqItems.question: Does the workflow export audio?
faqItems.answer: No. SaveVideo writes a silent video. Add music or sound effects later in a video editor.

3ddf4a6144a7.title: Runway: Gen4 Turbo Image to Video
3ddf4a6144a7.description: Generate dynamic videos from images using Runway Gen4 Turbo.
3ddf4a6144a7.metaDescription: ComfyUI tutorial: convert a still image into a short video using Runway Gen4 Turbo with LoadImage, RunwayImageToVideoNodeGen4, and SaveVideo.
3ddf4a6144a7.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow turns a single still image into a short, dynamic video using Runway’s Gen4 Turbo image-to-video model. It wires together four nodes: LoadImage to bring your source image into the graph, RunwayImageToVideoNodeGen4 to call the hosted Gen4 Turbo API and synthesize motion over time, SaveVideo to encode the result to a standard video file, and a MarkdownNote with links and setup guidance. Because the heavy lifting runs through the Runway partner node, the workflow stays lightweight and fast on your local machine.

Technically, the LoadImage node supplies the pixel data to RunwayImageToVideoNodeGen4, which sends the image (and your chosen settings like duration and frame rate) to the Runway API. The API returns a generated video stream compatible with ComfyUI’s SaveVideo node, which encodes the final clip (e.g., MP4) at your selected FPS. The partner node uses HTTPS and requires a secure network setup as noted in the Author Notes (see "About API Node"): run from localhost/127.0.0.1 and ensure outbound HTTPS is allowed.
