64abde72a70b.title: Remove Background: Bria Solid Color
64abde72a70b.description: Upload a video to remove its background and replace it with your chosen color. Generate a video with the subject isolated and a new solid background.
64abde72a70b.metaDescription: Remove a video background in ComfyUI with BRIA and replace it with a solid color using BriaRemoveVideoBackground. Load, process, and save clean cutouts.
64abde72a70b.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI tutorial walks you through a simple, reliable workflow for removing a video’s background and replacing it with a solid color. The pipeline uses three nodes: LoadVideo to ingest your clip, BriaRemoveVideoBackground to segment and cut out the subject with the BRIA model, and SaveVideo to encode the final composite. Under the hood, BriaRemoveVideoBackground performs per‑frame foreground/background segmentation and composites the subject over a constant color fill, producing a clean, uniform backdrop without green-screen footage.

Technically, the workflow keeps your video’s frame timing from LoadVideo, passes frames to the BRIA segmentation model inside BriaRemoveVideoBackground, and outputs frames with the original subject isolated against your chosen color. SaveVideo then assembles these frames back into a video file. This approach is useful for social content, product showcases, and corporate assets where consistency matters—solid backgrounds are easy to brand-match, caption, and compress.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI, then open the LoadVideo node and choose your source clip (use a short test clip first to validate results).
Open the BriaRemoveVideoBackground node and pick your solid background color using the node’s color input. Choose a color that contrasts with your subject for cleaner edges.
Optionally lower resolution or shorten your test clip externally to preview faster. Good lighting and steady footage improve the segmentation quality.
Click Queue Prompt to run. The video frames flow from LoadVideo through BriaRemoveVideoBackground, where the BRIA model isolates the subject and composites the solid color.
When processing completes, check the SaveVideo node output path in the ComfyUI UI. Play the result to confirm subject edges (hair, hands) look clean.
If needed, adjust your background color or try a higher-quality source (less motion blur, better contrast), then re-run until you’re satisfied.
suggestedUseCases: Product demos on brand-colored backdrops for e-commerce or ads
Talking-head clips for corporate videos with a consistent, on-brand background
Short-form social media posts that need fast background cleanup
Training or onboarding videos where a neutral background reduces distractions
Compositing prep for motion graphics by standardizing the background color

faqItems.question: How does BriaRemoveVideoBackground work in this workflow?
faqItems.answer: It uses the BRIA model to segment the foreground subject in each frame and composites it over a constant color. LoadVideo supplies frames and timing; SaveVideo assembles the processed frames into a final video.

faqItems.question: What video settings affect the quality of the cutout?
faqItems.answer: Sharp, well-lit footage with minimal motion blur and clear subject–background contrast produces cleaner edges. Higher-resolution sources help, but also increase processing time and memory use.

faqItems.question: Can I export with a transparent background instead of a solid color?
faqItems.answer: This workflow is designed for a solid-color replacement. If you need transparency (alpha), use a workflow or node setup that outputs an alpha channel or an alpha mask and then export to a format that supports it.

faqItems.question: Will the output include audio?
faqItems.answer: Depending on your ComfyUI environment and SaveVideo configuration, audio may not be muxed. If the output lacks audio, export the video here and then merge the original audio track in a video editor.

64f4db9e3e33.title: Seedance 2.0: Reference to Video
64f4db9e3e33.description: Generate cinematic videos from reference images and text prompts. Preserve subject identity and composition while adding expressive motion with synchronized audio. Control camera movement and lighting through detailed prompts.
64f4db9e3e33.metaDescription: Create cinematic videos from a reference image in ComfyUI with Seedance 2.0. Preserve identity, direct camera and lighting via prompts, and export MP4 with SaveVideo.
64f4db9e3e33.extendedDescription:
Seedance 2.0: Reference to Video turns a single reference image into a short cinematic video by combining a strong identity lock with prompt-driven motion and lighting. The LoadImage node supplies a clean, high-resolution reference frame, while ByteDance2ReferenceNode runs the Seedance 2.0 model to synthesize a sequence of frames that preserve the subject’s look and composition. You guide the scene using natural language—add camera cues (dolly-in, slow pan left), lighting notes (soft rim light, golden hour), and style hints (35mm, shallow depth of field) directly in the prompt.

Technically, ByteDance2ReferenceNode conditions Seedance 2.0 on both the reference image and your text prompt, then generates a video at the duration, resolution, and frame rate you specify. Key controls typically include reference adherence versus motion intensity (to balance identity preservation with expressiveness), guidance strength, negative prompts for artifact control, seed for reproducibility, and output timing (fps, seconds). The SaveVideo node then encodes the generated frames into a compact MP4 at your chosen fps and quality. This minimalist graph—LoadImage → ByteDance2ReferenceNode → SaveVideo—makes iteration fast: tweak a prompt or slider, queue again, and compare results side by side to quickly dial in the look you need.

While the workflow is optimized for visuals, you can time your motion to external audio by setting duration and beats per section to match your soundtrack. SaveVideo produces a silent video, so plan to add or replace audio in your editor after export. The result is a reliable identity-preserving image-to-video pipeline that responds well to clear prompts and produces cinematic movement without complex node graphs.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and open the LoadImage node. Choose a clean, high‑resolution reference image with the subject centered and the intended aspect ratio (keep dimensions divisible by 8 or 16 for stable video encoding).

Open ByteDance2ReferenceNode and enter your prompt (camera moves, lighting, style) and optional negative prompt (e.g., deformed, flicker, warped hands). If the node exposes API settings for Seedance 2.0, add your endpoint/key.

Set output specs in ByteDance2ReferenceNode: duration (e.g., 2–6 seconds), fps (e.g., 16–24), and resolution. Adjust reference adherence vs. motion strength to balance identity lock with expressive movement. Set a seed for repeatable results.

Refine creative controls: describe camera motion explicitly (dolly-in, slow pan right, tilt up), lighting (soft rim light, cinematic contrast), and lens cues (35mm, shallow depth of field). If identity drifts, increase reference adherence or shorten the duration.
Configure SaveVideo to match the chosen fps. Set filename and quality (CRF/bitrate options, if exposed). Ensure SaveVideo’s fps matches the generation fps so playback speed is correct.
Click Queue/Execute. After the run completes, find the MP4 in ComfyUI’s output folder. Review and iterate—tweak prompt wording, motion strength, or seed to converge on your desired look.
suggestedUseCases: Portrait motion shots that preserve a subject’s face while adding subtle dolly or pan moves for reels and intros.
Product hero clips with controlled parallax, soft studio lighting, and smooth camera arcs for ads or landing pages.
Fashion and lookbook snippets using stylized lighting cues and lens language while keeping outfit details intact.
Storyboard and previsualization of scenes where quick prompt edits explore alternate camera moves and moods.
Music or teaser visuals timed to a track by matching video duration and beat emphasis, then adding audio in post.

faqItems.question: What reference images work best?
faqItems.answer: Use a clean, high‑resolution image with the subject centered, minimal motion blur, and a background that matches your intended scene. Keep the aspect ratio close to your target output and avoid heavy filters that may conflict with the prompt.

faqItems.question: How do I keep the subject’s identity stable?
faqItems.answer: Increase the reference adherence (or similar control) in ByteDance2ReferenceNode, reduce duration, and use a consistent aspect ratio. Keep prompts descriptive but not contradictory, and add a negative prompt to discourage unwanted style drift.

faqItems.question: How can I control camera movement and lighting?
faqItems.answer: Use explicit language in the prompt: “slow dolly‑in,” “subtle pan left,” “tilt up,” “soft rim light,” “cinematic contrast,” “35mm, shallow depth of field.” If motion overwhelms identity, lower motion strength or raise reference adherence.

faqItems.question: Does the workflow generate audio or sync to music?
faqItems.answer: This workflow focuses on visuals. SaveVideo exports a silent MP4. To pair with music, set duration to match your track and add audio later in an editor. If your Seedance 2.0 endpoint exposes audio‑driven options, configure them in ByteDance2ReferenceNode (if available), but audio isn’t embedded by default.

65380ddc148a.title: Ideogram Vector 1: Image to SVG
65380ddc148a.description: Trace a bitmap into a fully editable SVG with Ideogram Vector 1 and save it as one vector file. Ideal for turning logos, flat illustration, patterns and line art into clean paths that stay crisp at any size, with a detail mode that either keeps large flat color blocks or finer color regions. Photographs also work, but convert into many small paths, so clean sources with large areas of flat color and transparent backgrounds vectorize best.
65380ddc148a.metaDescription: ComfyUI workflow that traces bitmaps to clean, editable SVGs via Ideogram Vector 1. Ideal for logos, flat art, patterns, and line drawings.
65380ddc148a.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow converts a bitmap image into a clean, fully editable SVG using Ideogram Vector 1. It chains a simple, reliable path: LoadImage imports your source bitmap, IdeogramVectorImageToSVGApi sends it to Ideogram’s vectorization service to segment the image into paths, and SaveSVGNode writes a single .svg file to disk. The MarkdownNote in the canvas provides inline tips, but the core logic is intentionally minimal so you can drop in an image and get a vector out quickly.

Technically, the IdeogramVectorImageToSVGApi node analyzes color regions and edges to produce paths with solid fills, preserving flat areas as fewer shapes or breaking them into smaller regions depending on the chosen detail mode. For logos, icons, flat illustrations, patterns, and line art, this yields crisp, scalable vectors that edit cleanly in any vector editor. Photographs also work, but expect many small paths and larger files. For best results, start with a clean source (ideally with a transparent background), choose the appropriate detail level, and inspect the output in your vector editor to tweak stroke/fill as needed.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and confirm all nodes are present: LoadImage → IdeogramVectorImageToSVGApi → SaveSVGNode (plus a MarkdownNote with tips). Add your Ideogram API key in the IdeogramVectorImageToSVGApi node if required.
Open LoadImage and select a high-contrast source bitmap (PNG/JPG). Transparent backgrounds vectorize best; if possible, remove white or noisy backgrounds before loading.

In IdeogramVectorImageToSVGApi, choose the detail mode: use a setting that favors large flat color blocks for logos and icons, or a finer-region setting for illustrations that need more internal detail.
Set SaveSVGNode’s output path and filename, ensuring the .svg extension. Use a unique name to avoid overwriting previous results.
Click Queue Prompt (or Execute) to run the graph. The image is sent to Ideogram’s service for vectorization and the resulting SVG is saved by SaveSVGNode.
Open the saved SVG in a vector editor (e.g., Illustrator, Inkscape, Figma). If you see too many tiny paths, re-run with a simpler detail mode or a cleaner source image.
suggestedUseCases: Logo cleanup: Convert raster logos to sharp vectors for print, web, and signage.
Flat illustration and icon packs: Turn PNG exports into scalable, easily recolorable SVGs.
Pattern and surface design: Vectorize repeating tiles so they scale cleanly across products.
Line art and scans: Convert ink drawings into editable paths for editing and coloring.
UI assets: Produce lightweight, resolution-independent SVGs for apps and websites.

faqItems.question: What makes this better for logos and flat art than for photos?
faqItems.answer: Ideogram Vector 1 segments color regions into paths. Flat graphics have large uniform areas that become a small number of clean shapes. Photos contain continuous tone and texture, which produce thousands of tiny paths and heavier SVGs.

faqItems.question: Do I need an Ideogram account or API key?
faqItems.answer: Yes. The IdeogramVectorImageToSVGApi node calls Ideogram’s service. Provide a valid API key where the node requests it (or in your ComfyUI environment if configured). Without it, the request will fail.

faqItems.question: How can I reduce SVG complexity or file size?
faqItems.answer: Use the simpler detail mode (favoring large flat blocks), start from a cleaner source (remove noise, gradients, and backgrounds), and consider slightly downscaling oversized inputs. Re-run until you balance detail and editability.

faqItems.question: Will colors be preserved exactly?
faqItems.answer: Colors are approximated by filled vector shapes. With a simpler detail mode, large areas may be merged, slightly simplifying color boundaries. For precise brand colors, you can adjust fills afterward in your vector editor.

655893ad7990.title: SD3.5 Large Blur
655893ad7990.description: Generate images guided by blurred reference images using SD 3.5.
655893ad7990.metaDescription: Generate stunning images using blurred references with SD3.5 Large Blur workflow in ComfyUI. Perfect for artists and designers.
655893ad7990.extendedDescription:
The SD3.5 Large Blur workflow is designed to generate high-quality images by leveraging blurred reference images as a guide. This technique utilizes the Stable Diffusion 3.5 (SD3.5) model, which is known for its ability to create detailed and visually appealing images. The workflow incorporates several key nodes, including the KSampler, CheckpointLoaderSimple, and ControlNetLoader, to efficiently manage the image generation process. By using a blurred image as a reference, the workflow can focus on capturing the essence of the image while allowing for creative interpretation in the finer details. This approach is particularly useful for artists and designers looking to create unique and imaginative visuals based on existing images.

The workflow begins by loading the necessary models and checkpoints, such as the 'sd3.5_large_fp8_scaled.safetensors' and the 'sd3.5_large_controlnet_blur.safetensors'. These models are essential for the ControlNetApplyAdvanced node, which applies advanced control techniques to the image generation process. Users are encouraged to preprocess their images using the 'comfyui_controlnet_aux' tool to ensure optimal results. The CLIPTextEncode node allows for the integration of text prompts that guide the image generation, enabling users to specify desired characteristics, such as color and style. The final output is decoded using the VAEDecode node and saved with the SaveImage node, providing users with a ready-to-use image that meets their creative needs.
howToUse: Load the SD3.5 Large Blur workflow in ComfyUI.
Ensure the necessary models, 'sd3.5_large_fp8_scaled.safetensors' and 'sd3.5_large_controlnet_blur.safetensors', are loaded using CheckpointLoaderSimple.
Upload a preprocessed blurred reference image or preprocess your image using 'comfyui_controlnet_aux'.
Set the desired image size and enter a text prompt using the CLIPTextEncode node to guide the image generation.
Run the workflow to generate the image, and use the VAEDecode node to decode the final output.
Save the generated image using the SaveImage node.
suggestedUseCases: Creating artistic interpretations of existing photographs.
Generating concept art for films or video games.
Designing unique visual content for marketing materials.
Exploring creative variations of a single image theme.
Developing personalized digital artwork for clients.

faqItems.question: Do I need to preprocess my images before using this workflow?
faqItems.answer: Yes, it is recommended to preprocess your images using 'comfyui_controlnet_aux' for the best results.

faqItems.question: Can I use any text prompt with this workflow?
faqItems.answer: Yes, you can use any descriptive text prompt to guide the image generation process, allowing for creative flexibility.

faqItems.question: What image formats are supported for the reference images?
faqItems.answer: The workflow supports common image formats such as JPEG and PNG for the reference images.

faqItems.question: How can I improve the quality of the generated images?
faqItems.answer: Ensure that your reference images are well-preprocessed and that you use detailed and specific text prompts to guide the generation.

Enter your desired text prompt into the ByteDanceSeedreamNode.
Adjust any available settings to refine the style and layout of the output image.

faqItems.question: What type of text prompts work best with this workflow?
faqItems.answer: Detailed and descriptive prompts yield the best results, as the model can better interpret and visualize complex ideas.

faqItems.question: Can I modify the style of the generated image?

faqItems.question: How do I save the generated images?

faqItems.question: Is this workflow suitable for commercial projects?

6645006a0cb7.title: Seedance2.0 4K: Reference to Video
6645006a0cb7.description: Generate a reference-based video from a single input image using Seedance 2.0, producing native 4K output with 10-bit color depth and clean fine detail retention. The workflow takes 1 image and outputs 1 video. Ideal for high-resolution motion graphics, cinematic VFX shots requiring downstream grading, and professional video production where 4K finishing is essential.
6645006a0cb7.metaDescription: Turn a single image into a native 4K, 10-bit video using Seedance 2.0 in ComfyUI. Reference-preserving motion with ByteDance2ReferenceNode and SaveVideo.
6645006a0cb7.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI tutorial shows how to turn a single still image into a native 4K video using Seedance 2.0’s reference-to-video method. The workflow is intentionally minimal: LoadImage brings in your reference frame, ByteDance2ReferenceNode (the Seedance 2.0 reference model) synthesizes temporally consistent motion while preserving the look of the source, and SaveVideo encodes the generated frames into a 4K file. The result is a reference-faithful clip with clean, fine detail that’s suitable for editorial finishing and downstream color work.

Technically, the ByteDance2ReferenceNode conditions its generative video on the appearance of the input image and drives motion from learned priors, with user-adjustable parameters like output resolution, frame count, frame rate, seed, and motion/strength controls (names may vary by build). Set the node to 3840x2160 to produce true UHD frames, choose a frame count and FPS for duration, and keep a fixed seed for repeatability. SaveVideo then assembles the frames; when configured with a 10‑bit-capable encoder and pixel format, it exports in 10‑bit color, which helps maintain subtle gradients and grading latitude. If a 10‑bit encoder or pixel format isn’t available, the node will export in standard 8‑bit.
howToUse: Load the Seedance2.0 4K: Reference to Video workflow in ComfyUI. Ensure ByteDance2ReferenceNode is installed and its Seedance 2.0 model files are available. Confirm FFmpeg is set up for video export.
Open the LoadImage node and select your reference image. For best results, start with a sharp, high-resolution image composed for 16:9 framing to match 3840x2160 output.

Configure ByteDance2ReferenceNode: set resolution to 3840x2160, pick an FPS (e.g., 24 or 30), and set the frame count (e.g., 96 frames ≈ 4 seconds at 24 fps). Adjust seed for reproducibility and tune motion/strength controls to balance movement with detail retention.

Set up SaveVideo for your deliverable. To target 10-bit, choose a 10‑bit‑capable codec/pixel format (e.g., HEVC Main10 with yuv420p10le or ProRes via prores_ks) if available in your build. Specify output path and filename.

Run the graph. Review the render for motion quality and fine detail. If you see over-smearing or loss of texture, lower motion strength or try a different seed; if motion is too subtle, increase strength or frames.
Iterate: adjust FPS/frame count for different durations, tweak motion parameters to emphasize camera or subject movement, and re‑export. Keep a log of seed and settings to reproduce favored looks.
suggestedUseCases: Cinematic VFX shots: create graded, reference-faithful 4K plates from concept art for previs or background elements.
Product hero clips: generate smooth parallax or reveal motions from a single packshot while retaining branding details.
Title and logo motion: add subtle, high-fidelity motion to static designs for 4K broadcast packages.
Environment fly‑throughs: turn keyframe paintings into short exploratory camera moves for pitch decks or animatics.

faqItems.question: How do I ensure the output is truly 4K and 10-bit?
faqItems.answer: In ByteDance2ReferenceNode, set resolution to 3840x2160. In SaveVideo, select a 10‑bit-capable encoder and pixel format (e.g., HEVC Main10 with yuv420p10le or ProRes via prores_ks) and verify your FFmpeg build supports them. If 10‑bit isn’t available, the node will export 8‑bit.

faqItems.question: How can I preserve more fine detail from the reference image?
faqItems.answer: Use a sharp, high-resolution source image, keep motion/strength settings moderate, and reduce any aggressive denoising if exposed. Lock a seed for consistency and try a few nearby seeds to find a motion field that keeps textures stable.

faqItems.question: How do I change the video duration and frame rate?
faqItems.answer: Duration is frame_count ÷ FPS. Increase frame_count for longer clips, adjust FPS for smoother or more cinematic motion (e.g., 24 or 30). Make sure SaveVideo matches your intended FPS.

faqItems.question: What if I run out of GPU memory at 4K?
faqItems.answer: Try lowering the frame batch size (if exposed by your build), reducing motion complexity, or temporarily testing at a lower resolution. Once settings are dialed in, switch back to 3840x2160 for the final pass.

67981edb9ad4.title: AI on the Lot 2026 - LTX-2.3 - i2v
67981edb9ad4.description: The fifth workflow released for AI on the Lot 2026, made available for ComfyUI 101 workshop attendees to open and follow along if they choose. An image-to-video workflow built on the LTX 2.3 model, turning a still image into a generated video clip.
67981edb9ad4.metaDescription: Animate a still image into a video in ComfyUI with LTX‑2.3. Load an image, prompt motion, tune frames/FPS, and export your clip with SaveVideo.
67981edb9ad4.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow turns a single still image into a short, animated video using Lightricks’ LTX‑2.3 image‑to‑video model. The pipeline is straightforward: LoadImage brings your source frame into the graph, a custom LTX‑2.3 node (2454ad83-157c-40dd-9f19-5daaf4041ce0) synthesizes motion conditioned on that image and a text prompt, and SaveVideo assembles the generated frames into a playable clip. MarkdownNote nodes inside the graph provide in‑context guidance and prompt tips so you can follow along during the AI on the Lot 2026 ComfyUI 101 workshop.

Technically, the LTX‑2.3 node encodes your input image into the model’s latent space and generates a temporally coherent sequence guided by your prompt. You control the character and pace of motion by describing events over time ("Core Actions") and specifying concrete "Visual Details" you want to preserve, as recommended in the LTX‑2.3 prompting tips. Typical controls exposed by the node include the text prompt, seed for reproducibility, and clip characteristics such as number of frames and/or FPS (exact parameters depend on the node build). SaveVideo then writes the frames to disk at your chosen frame rate. For model weights, use Lightricks/LTX‑2.3 from Hugging Face (see the links provided), and follow the node’s loader field to point to the correct files.
howToUse: Load the workflow file (AI on the Lot 2026 - LTX-2.3 - i2v) in ComfyUI. Ensure the LTX‑2.3 model weights are available (Hugging Face: Lightricks/LTX-2.3) and that the LTX node points to them.
Open the LoadImage node and select your source image. Keep a clean, reasonably high‑resolution image and maintain the aspect ratio you intend to output.

Configure the LTX‑2.3 node (2454ad83-157c-40dd-9f19-5daaf4041ce0): write a prompt that describes the Core Actions over time and the Visual Details to preserve. If available, set seed, number of frames, motion strength, and/or guidance as needed. Refer to the MarkdownNote tips in the graph.
Set the SaveVideo node’s output path and FPS. The video’s resolution follows the generated frames; FPS controls playback smoothness and duration when combined with the frame count.
Run the graph once with conservative settings (shorter clip or lower FPS) to validate everything works. Inspect the preview/output and note how the prompt affected motion and fidelity.
Iterate: refine the prompt, adjust motion strength or frame count (if exposed), and re‑run. Use a fixed seed for repeatable results or change it to explore variations.
suggestedUseCases: Cinemagraph‑style animations from product or lifestyle photos for social posts and ads
Animating key art or storyboards for fast previz and mood exploration in film/video
Subtle portrait or environmental motion for profile headers, hero banners, or teasers
Turning static marketing stills into short looping video assets
Creating dynamic B‑roll from brand images when live footage is unavailable

faqItems.question: How should I prompt LTX‑2.3 for the best motion?
faqItems.answer: Describe Core Actions as they unfold over time (e.g., “the camera slowly dolly‑zooms in as leaves drift across the foreground”) and list concrete Visual Details you want to preserve (composition, lighting, color, subject attributes). Keep directives concise and unambiguous.

faqItems.question: What image inputs work best?
faqItems.answer: Clean, well‑lit images with clear subject separation tend to animate more coherently. Use a resolution that matches your VRAM and the workflow’s defaults, and keep the aspect ratio consistent across input and output to avoid stretching.

faqItems.question: How do I control clip length and smoothness?
faqItems.answer: Clip length is a function of the number of generated frames and the SaveVideo FPS. Increase frames for longer clips and adjust FPS for playback feel. If the LTX‑2.3 node exposes frame count or duration, change it there; then set the desired FPS in SaveVideo.

faqItems.question: My results change between runs. How can I make them repeatable?
faqItems.answer: Set and reuse a fixed seed in the LTX‑2.3 node (if available), keep the prompt identical, and avoid changing other generation parameters. Changing the seed is useful when you want controlled variations.

67a816af8a73.title: Wan 2.2 14B Fun Control
67a816af8a73.description: Generate videos guided by pose, depth, and edge controls using Wan 2.2 Fun Control.
67a816af8a73.metaDescription: Tutorial: Generate controllable videos with Wan2.2 Fun Control using pose, depth, and edges. Learn setup, prompts, sampling, and export in ComfyUI.
67a816af8a73.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI tutorial workflow demonstrates how to generate controllable videos with Wan2.2 Fun Control (14B), guided by pose, depth, and edge inputs. At its core, the Wan22FunControlToVideo node fuses your text prompt from CLIPTextEncode with one or more control streams derived from a reference video. The model stack loads via UNETLoader and VAELoader, while CLIPLoader and CLIPTextEncode provide multilingual text conditioning. Sampling runs through ModelSamplingSD3 with KSamplerAdvanced to balance quality, speed, and control strength. Finally, VAEDecode reconstructs frames and SaveVideo exports the result.

You can preprocess control videos directly in the graph: LoadVideo and GetVideoComponents ingest your footage, Canny extracts edges, and optional custom nodes (comfyui_controlnet_aux and ComfyUI-DepthAnythingV2) add pose/depth maps. CreateVideo sets resolution, frame count, and FPS to match Wan2.2’s training regime (multi-resolution 512/768/1024, 81 frames at 16 FPS). The Start_image group lets you anchor the first frame with LoadImage for a consistent subject/look. An optional LoraLoaderModelOnly applies the Wan2.2 Lighting LoRA for faster renders at the cost of reduced motion dynamics. This gives you a flexible, reproducible pipeline for video-to-video generation with reliable structure preservation and style control.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and install required models and custom nodes. Download wan2.2_fun_control_high_noise_14B_fp8_scaled.safetensors for UNETLoader and your VAE. For depth/pose controls, add comfyui_controlnet_aux and ComfyUI-DepthAnythingV2.

Step 1 – Load models: Set CLIPLoader and VAELoader, then point UNETLoader to the Wan2.2 Fun Control checkpoint. If you want speed over motion fidelity, enable the Wan2.2 Lighting LoRA via LoraLoaderModelOnly (or switch to the fp8+4-steps LoRA group).

Step 3 – Control video and preprocessing: Load your reference video with LoadVideo. Use GetVideoComponents to read fps and frame count. Connect Canny to extract edge maps. Optionally add depth (DepthAnythingV2) and pose (OpenPose from controlnet_aux) nodes to generate additional control streams.
Step 2 – Start_image (optional): If you need a consistent subject or style anchor, load an initial image with LoadImage and wire it into the Start_image inputs provided by the workflow.

Step 4 – Prompt and sampling: Enter your positive/negative prompts in CLIPTextEncode. In ModelSamplingSD3 + KSamplerAdvanced, start with 8 steps for the base model (CFG 3–6), or 4 steps if using the Lighting LoRA. Keep seed locked for reproducible results.

Step 5 – Video size & length: In CreateVideo, pick 512, 768, or 1024 resolution and set FPS to 16 with up to 81 frames for best alignment with Wan2.2. Run the graph. Inspect frames in PreviewImage, then decode with VAEDecode and export using SaveVideo (e.g., MP4).
suggestedUseCases: Edge-accurate stylization: Preserve scene geometry with Canny while reimagining the look via prompts (e.g., cinematic, anime, or painterly styles).
Pose-driven character motion: Use pose controls to transfer choreography or gestures to a new character while keeping consistent identity via Start_image.
Depth-aware relighting and parallax: Combine depth maps with prompts to emphasize 3D structure, depth-of-field, or subtle camera movement cues.
Design and product demos: Maintain object contours and motion while generating polished, on-brand video variations from rough captures.
Previsualization and animatics: Lock in motion beats with pose/trajectory guidance and iterate on style quickly before full production.

faqItems.question: Do I need all three controls (edge, depth, pose) to get good results?
faqItems.answer: No. Wan2.2 Fun Control works with any single control stream (e.g., just Canny) or combinations. More controls generally increase structural faithfulness but can limit stylistic freedom. Start with edges, then add depth or pose if you need stronger guidance.

faqItems.question: How should I match video length and FPS?
faqItems.answer: Use GetVideoComponents to read your source video’s FPS and frame count, then set CreateVideo to 16 FPS and up to 81 frames for best alignment with Wan2.2’s training. If your source differs, you can still run it—just expect slightly different motion timing.

faqItems.question: What does the Wan2.2 Lighting LoRA do?
faqItems.answer: The Lighting LoRA reduces generation time and can improve lighting consistency, but it tends to reduce video dynamics. The workflow includes a dedicated fp8 + 4 steps LoRA group for speed. If you prioritize richer motion, disable the LoRA and increase steps modestly.

faqItems.question: How can I improve temporal coherence and reduce flicker?
faqItems.answer: Use stronger controls (edges + depth), keep CFG moderate (around 3–6), fix the seed, and match resolution/FPS to 512/768/1024 at 16 FPS. Ensure prompts are stable across the whole run and avoid overly aggressive negative prompts that can destabilize details.

683bf6af0c9f.title: Anima Lllite: Any Control to Image
683bf6af0c9f.description: Apply lightweight, LoRA-like conditional control to Anima-Base v1.0 anime-style images using ControlNet-LLLite, accepting one conditioning input and one optional mask for inpainting to produce a single generated output. Ideal for anime inpainting with dynamic masking, style transfer from lineart or grayscale sketches, and controlled character generation in multi-scene compositions.
683bf6af0c9f.metaDescription: Guide: Use Anima-LLLite to add lightweight ControlNet-style conditioning and inpainting to Anima-Base v1.0 for precise, anime-style image generation.
683bf6af0c9f.extendedDescription:
Anima LLLite: Any Control to Image is a compact ComfyUI workflow that adds lightweight, LoRA-like conditional control to Anima-Base v1.0 for clean, anime-style image generation and inpainting. It accepts one conditioning input (for example, an edge map or sketch) and an optional mask to restrict edits, then produces a single, guided output. A ControlNet-LLLite controller (encapsulated as a custom node, UUID: 147b517e-5ea6-4fba-84f7-46851be6e4ce) injects the structural cue into the diffusion process so you can steer composition, pose, or line fidelity without the overhead of a full ControlNet.

The workflow’s Image Preprocessing group includes common utilities to prepare inputs: LoadImage to bring in a reference or sketch; Canny to create an edge-based conditioner; ImageInvert to flip mask semantics when needed; GetImageSize and ResizeImageMaskNode to keep masks aligned to the generation canvas; and PreviewImage to quickly inspect intermediate results. ImageCompare helps you verify how closely the output follows the control input, and SaveImage captures the final render. You can swap Canny for other native preprocessors (Node Library -> Comfy Blueprints -> Conditioning & Preprocessors) to change the conditioning type while keeping the rest of the pipeline intact. Model weights are provided via Anima-LLLite, designed to pair with the Anima base model for consistent anime aesthetics.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI, then open the Image Preprocessing group. Use LoadImage to bring in your conditioning source (e.g., a sketch, lineart, or reference image).

Generate a control signal: connect your source to the Canny node to detect edges. PreviewImage to confirm you’re getting clear, useful contours. Adjust Canny thresholds if edges are too sparse or noisy.

Optional inpainting: Load a mask image with LoadImage. Use GetImageSize from your target canvas and connect it to ResizeImageMaskNode so the mask matches the generation size. If edits occur in the wrong area, run the mask through ImageInvert and preview again.

Feed the processed control (from Canny or your chosen preprocessor) and the optional mask into the Anima-LLLite control node (UUID: 147b517e-5ea6-4fba-84f7-46851be6e4ce). Set conditioning strength and related parameters in that node to balance faithfulness versus creativity.

Run the graph. Use PreviewImage to inspect the result and ImageCompare to evaluate how well the output follows your control. If needed, refine Canny thresholds, mask edges (softer or sharper), or lower/raise conditioning strength.
When satisfied, save your final image with SaveImage. Keep the same seed and conditioning for consistent results across variations or multi-scene compositions.
suggestedUseCases: Anime inpainting with dynamic masks to fix faces, clothing details, or backgrounds while preserving the rest of the image.
Lineart-to-anime rendering: turn clean edges or sketches into fully rendered anime frames with controlled structure.
Controlled character generation across scenes by reusing the same conditioning edges and seed for consistency.
Grayscale or rough concept refinement: use a tonal or edge map to guide pose and silhouette while letting style emerge from the model.
Panel or storyboard cleanup: constrain edits to specific regions using a mask for quick iterative polish.

faqItems.question: What kinds of conditioning inputs work besides Canny edges?
faqItems.answer: You can replace Canny with other native preprocessors (Node Library -> Comfy Blueprints -> Conditioning & Preprocessors), such as lineart or depth-style detectors. Swap the node feeding the Anima-LLLite controller while keeping the rest of the graph the same.

faqItems.question: My inpainted region is the opposite of what I expect. How do I fix mask direction?
faqItems.answer: Mask conventions can differ. If edits happen outside the intended area, pass the mask through ImageInvert and preview again. ResizeImageMaskNode ensures your mask matches the canvas size to avoid offset artifacts.

faqItems.question: How do I balance structure adherence versus creativity?
faqItems.answer: Use the conditioning strength controls in the Anima-LLLite node: higher values increase faithfulness to the control (edges/sketch), while lower values allow more stylization. You can also tune Canny thresholds—cleaner edges typically yield tighter adherence.

faqItems.question: How can I keep results consistent across multiple images or scenes?
faqItems.answer: Re-use the same seed, prompt, and conditioning input. Keep resolution and preprocessor settings constant. For inpainting, use the same mask (or consistent mask shapes) and similar conditioning strength.

68c39b4c6a6f.title: Seedance 2.0 Cinematic Prompt Studio
68c39b4c6a6f.description: Create production-ready cinematic shots with concise, director-style Seedance 2.0 prompts built around intentional camera motion, visual storytelling, and strong final frames.
68c39b4c6a6f.metaDescription: Tutorial: Generate cinematic Seedance 2.0 videos in ComfyUI using concise, director-style prompts with optional image references and Gemini-assisted prompt crafting.
68c39b4c6a6f.extendedDescription:
Seedance 2.0 Cinematic Prompt Studio is a ComfyUI workflow for turning concise, director-style prompts into production-ready cinematic shots. It pairs optional image references with a structured Seedance 2.0 prompt that emphasizes intentional camera motion, visual storytelling beats, and a strong final frame. The workflow is organized into three groups: Load Images, Generate Seedance 2.0 Prompt, and Generate Video.

Technically, LoadImage supplies one or more visual references, while GeminiNode converts a short shot brief into a Seedance 2.0–formatted prompt (camera verbs, lens/composition cues, lighting, pacing, and a closing frame directive). These are fed into ByteDance2ReferenceNode, which performs image-conditioned or text-only video generation via the Seedance 2.0 backend. PreviewAny lets you inspect intermediate outputs and play back results in-canvas, and SaveVideo writes the final render to disk. A MarkdownNote in the graph provides on-canvas guidance and a prompt template so you can iterate quickly and keep prompts concise and cinematic.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and review the three groups: Load Images, Generate Seedance 2.0 Prompt, and Generate Video. Check the MarkdownNote for on-canvas tips.
Add optional references in the Load Images group using the LoadImage node (e.g., a character sheet, product packshot, or location still). Leave it empty for text-only shots.

In the Generate Seedance 2.0 Prompt group, enter a brief shot description (subject, setting, mood) and desired camera motion. Run the GeminiNode to transform this into a Seedance 2.0–style prompt. Inspect the output and edit if needed to keep it concise and directive.

Route the generated prompt and any reference image outputs into the ByteDance2ReferenceNode. Configure its exposed parameters (e.g., aspect ratio, duration, guidance) as available in your installation. Ensure your API credentials are set for any external services used by GeminiNode and ByteDance2ReferenceNode.

Execute the Generate Video group. Use PreviewAny to review the result. If the motion feels vague or the ending is weak, refine the prompt with explicit camera verbs (e.g., steady dolly-in, slow tilt-up, lock-off ending) and a clear final-frame instruction, then re-run.
When satisfied, save the output using SaveVideo. Name your file and choose the desired container/codec based on what the node exposes.
suggestedUseCases: Previsualization for narrative or commercial shoots: block camera moves and tone before production.
Character or product hero shots with controlled reveals and strong end frames.
Establishing shots and mood pieces to define location, lighting, and pacing.
Social media motion posters and short teasers with clear, readable camera motion.
Look development for brand style guides: consistent framing, motion, and lighting across variants.

faqItems.question: Do I need a reference image, or can I generate from text only?
faqItems.answer: References are optional. LoadImage provides identity and style cues (faces, products, environments) for image-conditioned results. If you omit references, ByteDance2ReferenceNode will generate from the prompt alone.

faqItems.question: How do I make the camera motion feel intentional instead of random?
faqItems.answer: Write concise, directive prompts. Use specific camera verbs (dolly-in, push, crane down, handheld sway, static lock-off), define beats (start, middle, end), and explicitly instruct the final frame (e.g., end on a locked close-up). GeminiNode helps structure this into Seedance 2.0 format, but clarity in your brief matters most.

faqItems.question: What settings control duration, resolution, or aspect ratio?
faqItems.answer: These are configured on ByteDance2ReferenceNode, subject to what your node version exposes and what the backend supports. Set aspect ratio and duration there if available. Keep durations short for crisper motion and stronger final frames.

faqItems.question: How do I get consistent subjects across multiple shots?
faqItems.answer: Reuse the same reference images and keep your key identity cues and framing language consistent across prompts. Avoid over-describing style changes between shots, and maintain similar camera and composition cues for continuity.

68dcfc02a679.title: ACE-Step 1.5XL SFT： Text to Music
68dcfc02a679.description: Generate high-quality music from text prompts using a 4B parameter SFT model. Control output with CFG for precise prompt adherence.
68dcfc02a679.metaDescription: Generate music from text with ACE-Step 1.5XL SFT in ComfyUI. Control duration, CFG, and sampling for precise, high-quality audio. Exports directly to MP3.
68dcfc02a679.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow turns text prompts into finished music using the ACE-Step 1.5XL SFT (4B) model. It follows a familiar diffusion pipeline adapted for audio: DualCLIPLoader and TextEncodeAceStepAudio1.5 convert your prompt (and optional negative prompt) into conditioning; EmptyAceStep1.5LatentAudio creates a latent audio canvas for your chosen duration; UNETLoader brings in the ACE-Step 1.5XL SFT model; and KSampler performs iterative denoising guided by CFG. ModelSamplingAuraFlow configures the sampler strategy tuned for ACE-Step audio, while VAELoader + VAEDecodeAudio convert the final latent back into a waveform that SaveAudioMP3 writes to disk.

Technically, CFG (classifier-free guidance) lets you balance creativity and prompt adherence: lower CFG values explore broadly, higher values follow your text more strictly. ConditioningZeroOut provides a clean unconditional branch if you don’t specify a negative prompt, ensuring stable guidance. Workflow groups (Model, Duration, Prompt) make it easy to swap checkpoints, set seconds, and iterate on prompts. The result is a practical, reproducible text-to-music pipeline that can quickly iterate across genres, moods, instruments, and structure—ideal for ideation, temp scoring, and background tracks.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and ensure required nodes are installed. Place the ACE-Step 1.5XL SFT UNet, the matching audio VAE, and ACE-Step text encoders where your ComfyUI installation expects model files.

Open the Model group: set UNETLoader to the ACE-Step 1.5XL SFT checkpoint, VAELoader to the corresponding audio VAE, and DualCLIPLoader to the ACE-Step text encoder weights. Leave ModelSamplingAuraFlow at its defaults unless you need a different sampler configuration.

Open the Duration group: use EmptyAceStep1.5LatentAudio (and the connected PrimitiveInt/PrimitiveNode controls) to choose the length of the clip. Adjust duration or frame count as exposed by the node. Longer durations increase VRAM/time.

Open the Prompt group: write a descriptive text prompt in TextEncodeAceStepAudio1.5 (e.g., "uplifting orchestral score, strings and brass, cinematic, fast tempo, no vocals"). Optionally provide a negative prompt or use ConditioningZeroOut for a clean unconditional branch.

Configure KSampler: set steps, CFG, and seed via the attached Primitive nodes. As a starting point, try 30–60 steps and CFG 2.5–5.0. Keep the seed fixed for reproducibility or randomize to explore variations.

Run the workflow. Inspect the output after VAEDecodeAudio, then SaveAudioMP3 will export your clip. If results drift from your intent, refine the prompt, tweak CFG, adjust steps, or change the seed and run again.
suggestedUseCases: Rapid background music generation for social videos, reels, or shorts.
Ideation of genre, mood, and instrumentation for temp scores or briefs.
Ambient and lo-fi loops for streams, focus sessions, or prototypes.
Exploring multiple stylistic variations quickly by seeding and CFG sweeps.
Game jams and prototyping level themes without a full composing pass.

faqItems.question: What do KSampler and ModelSamplingAuraFlow each control?
faqItems.answer: KSampler performs the denoising process using your steps, CFG, and seed. ModelSamplingAuraFlow configures the sampler strategy/schedule tailored for ACE-Step audio, so you get stable, high-quality convergence without manual scheduler tuning.

faqItems.question: How do I change the length of the generated music?
faqItems.answer: Use EmptyAceStep1.5LatentAudio in the Duration group. Adjust its duration or frame parameters (often driven by connected PrimitiveInt/PrimitiveNode controls). Longer clips require more compute and memory.

faqItems.question: My output sounds off-topic or noisy. How can I improve it?
faqItems.answer: Refine the prompt with clearer descriptors (genre, instruments, mood, tempo, mix notes) and add a negative prompt (e.g., "distortion, artifacts, vocals"). Try lowering CFG slightly if the audio is harsh, or increasing steps moderately if it lacks detail. Changing the seed can also help.

faqItems.question: Can I export WAV instead of MP3?
faqItems.answer: This workflow saves with SaveAudioMP3. If you prefer WAV, add or swap in a SaveAudioWAV node (if available in your setup) after VAEDecodeAudio and select the desired format and path.

69850664cf89.title: Restore Old Photos
69850664cf89.description: This app enhances your old photos. You can simply upload your image to fix faded or damaged photos in seconds.
69850664cf89.metaDescription: ComfyUI workflow to restore old photos with a custom restoration node, A/B comparison, and easy export using LoadImage, ImageCompare, and SaveImage.
69850664cf89.extendedDescription:
Restore Old Photos is a focused ComfyUI workflow for bringing faded, scratched, or low-contrast images back to life without guesswork. It combines essential utility nodes with a dedicated restoration stage to let you preview, compare, and export confidently. The flow begins with LoadImage, passes through a custom restoration operator (node ID 4c000cf8-4ec4-49a6-853c-e78dd316edc6), and gives you non-destructive control via ComfySwitchNode so you can instantly flip between the untouched input and the restored result.

Technically, the original and processed images are routed into ImageCompare for side-by-side evaluation, while PreviewAny provides quick on-canvas checks as you iterate. PrimitiveStringMultiline is included to keep multi-line notes (e.g., session settings or change logs) directly in the graph, and SaveImage writes your final selection to disk. This layout emphasizes A/B validation and repeatability: adjust the restoration node’s settings (as exposed by the custom node), use the switch to judge impact, verify with ImageCompare, and export only when the result meets your standards.
howToUse: Open the Restore Old Photos workflow in ComfyUI. If you see a missing-node warning for 4c000cf8-4ec4-49a6-853c-e78dd316edc6, install the corresponding custom node/extension and restart ComfyUI.
Select LoadImage and choose your old or damaged photo. The image will feed both the restoration branch and the baseline (original) branch for comparison.

Open the custom restoration node (ID 4c000cf8-4ec4-49a6-853c-e78dd316edc6) and adjust its available controls (e.g., overall repair/enhancement strength, color/contrast options if provided). Click Queue Prompt to process.
Use ComfySwitchNode to toggle between Original and Restored outputs. Watch updates in PreviewAny for quick checks.
Open ImageCompare to view the original and restored images side by side. Zoom in to inspect faces, edges, and textures. Tweak the restoration node settings and re-queue until you are satisfied.
Before exporting, ensure ComfySwitchNode is routed to the restored branch that you prefer. Then use SaveImage to write the final image to disk (set your filename/prefix and output folder as needed).
suggestedUseCases: Digitizing and refreshing family photo albums with minimal manual retouching.
Preparing heritage or archival images for exhibits, newsletters, or websites.
Improving scans of old newspapers, yearbooks, or magazines for readability and presentation.
Reviving vintage portraits for genealogy projects or memorial books.
Quick cleanups of auction or catalog photos where clarity and contrast matter.

faqItems.question: What does the custom node 4c000cf8-4ec4-49a6-853c-e78dd316edc6 do exactly?
faqItems.answer: It’s the dedicated restoration stage in this workflow. Depending on its implementation and exposed parameters, it typically performs operations like denoising, contrast and color restoration, and artifact reduction. Open the node to see which controls are available in your install.

faqItems.question: Do I need a GPU to run this workflow?

faqItems.question: Can I export both the original and the restored image?
faqItems.answer: Yes. Run once with ComfySwitchNode set to the restored branch and SaveImage enabled, then toggle the switch to the original branch and run again to save that version as well. ImageCompare is for evaluation; SaveImage handles the actual file export.

faqItems.question: Does this workflow include upscaling?

6991493996fd.title: HappyHorse 1.1: Image to Video
6991493996fd.description: Animate a static first frame into a short video with synchronized audio using HappyHorse 1.1, taking 1 input image and producing 1 video output. Ideal for e-commerce product demos, brand marketing content, and short episodic series.
6991493996fd.metaDescription: Animate a single image into a short video with synced audio using HappyHorse 1.1 in ComfyUI. Simple LoadImage → API → SaveVideo pipeline.
6991493996fd.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow turns a single still image into a short, shareable video with synchronized audio using the HappyHorse 1.1 service. The pipeline is intentionally simple: LoadImage feeds your first frame, HappyHorseImageToVideoApi sends it to the HappyHorse 1.1 API for motion synthesis and audio alignment, and SaveVideo writes the returned clip to disk as a single video file. Because generation happens through the API node, you don’t need local GPU compute for the heavy lifting.

Technically, the HappyHorseImageToVideoApi node packages your image and the node’s settings (such as duration, resolution, and other options exposed by the node) into a request. The HappyHorse 1.1 backend generates a sequence of coherent frames from the static first frame and returns a video container that includes both the visual track and synchronized audio. SaveVideo then preserves the container and filename you specify. This setup is ideal for rapid creation of product demos, branded motion posters, or short episodic content where you want quick iteration and consistent, audio-backed motion from a single frame.
howToUse: Open the workflow in ComfyUI and confirm the HappyHorseImageToVideoApi node is installed and visible. If it’s missing, install the required custom node/extension and restart ComfyUI.
Load your source still using the LoadImage node. Choose a clear, well-lit image with your subject centered for best motion inference.

Open the HappyHorseImageToVideoApi node and enter any required credentials or endpoint settings. Configure the available options (e.g., duration, resolution/aspect ratio, and audio handling) as exposed by the node.
Verify the connections: LoadImage output should feed the HappyHorseImageToVideoApi image input. Set a filename and output directory on the SaveVideo node.

Queue and run the workflow. When the API call completes, SaveVideo will write the resulting video (with audio if returned by the API) to your output folder. Review, adjust settings if needed, and re-run for refinements.
suggestedUseCases: E-commerce product loops and quick demo reels generated from a single product photo
Brand marketing motion posters or social teasers with synchronized music or sound
Short episodic intro shots and character idle animations created from key art
Event or campaign title cards animated from a static graphic for reels and stories
Album or podcast cover animations for promotional posts

faqItems.question: Do I need a GPU to use this workflow?
faqItems.answer: No. The heavy processing runs on the HappyHorse 1.1 service via the HappyHorseImageToVideoApi node. ComfyUI handles the request and saving the result locally.

faqItems.question: Can I control duration, resolution, or aspect ratio?
faqItems.answer: Yes, to the extent exposed by the HappyHorseImageToVideoApi node. Open the node and adjust available fields such as clip length and output size. If a setting is not exposed, the API will use its defaults.

faqItems.question: Will the output always include audio?
faqItems.answer: The API can return a video with synchronized audio. If audio is enabled by the node or API defaults, SaveVideo will preserve the audio track in the final file. If disabled, you’ll get a silent video.

faqItems.question: How do I get the best motion from a single image?
faqItems.answer: Use a clean, high-quality image with a clear subject and minimal clutter. Center important elements, avoid heavy motion blur, and match your target aspect ratio to reduce unwanted cropping or padding.

69a3789c4840.title: Wan 2.1 FLF2V 720p F16
69a3789c4840.description: Generate videos by controlling first and last frames using Wan 2.1 FLF2V.
69a3789c4840.metaDescription: ComfyUI Wan 2.1 FLF2V: create 720p, 16‑frame videos guided by start and end images plus text prompts. Precise transitions with CLIPVision and KSampler.
69a3789c4840.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI tutorial shows you how to generate smooth, guided video clips by explicitly controlling the first and last frames using Wan 2.1 FLF2V. The core of the workflow is the WanFirstLastFrameToVideo node, which fuses three condition sources: your prompt embeddings from CLIPTextEncode, visual guidance from CLIPVisionEncode of the start/end images, and the Wan 2.1 UNet loaded by UNETLoader. The workflow is configured for 720p output and 16 frames (F16), giving you a compact, visually coherent clip that cleanly transitions from the first frame to the last.

Under the hood, the model components are loaded in the "Load Models Here" group: VAELoader and VAEDecode handle latent-to-RGB decoding of frames; CLIPLoader and CLIPTextEncode create text and (optionally) negative prompt embeddings; CLIPVisionLoader with CLIPVisionEncode extract visual features from your start and end images. ModelSamplingSD3 defines the timestep/schedule used by KSampler to drive diffusion steps for the Wan 2.1 UNet. Finally, CreateVideo assembles the decoded frames and SaveVideo writes the MP4 to disk. This setup is ideal when you want precise control over motion and composition—e.g., matching storyboard keyframes—while still benefiting from text-driven styling.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI. In the "Load Models Here" group, point UNETLoader to the Wan 2.1 FLF2V diffusion weights, CLIPLoader to the Wan text encoder, CLIPVisionLoader to the vision encoder, and VAELoader to the Wan VAE. If using the Wan_2.1_ComfyUI_repackaged split files, place them in ComfyUI/models (clip → models/clip, clip_vision → models/clip_vision, vae → models/vae, diffusion/unet → models/checkpoints or models/unet as instructed in the repo).

In the "Start & End frames" group, use two LoadImage nodes to import your first and last frame images. Feed each image to its own CLIPVisionEncode so the WanFirstLastFrameToVideo node receives both vision embeddings. Match your images to 1280×720 (or the workflow’s resolution) to avoid unwanted cropping or padding.

Open the "Prompt" group. Enter your positive prompt in a CLIPTextEncode node (e.g., "glass flower blossom"). If you use a negative prompt, add it to a second CLIPTextEncode (the provided Chinese string is a strong artifact-suppression example). Ensure both text encodes are connected to WanFirstLastFrameToVideo.

In "Sampling & Video Generation", set KSampler parameters: steps (e.g., 20–30), CFG scale (e.g., 3–6), and seed for reproducibility. Leave ModelSamplingSD3 on its default preset unless you know the schedule you want to use for Wan 2.1.

Verify the frame count and resolution are set as intended (this preset is 720p, F16). Run the graph. VAEDecode will convert latents to frames, then CreateVideo will assemble the sequence. Adjust fps and quality settings in CreateVideo to control playback speed and bitrate.

Use SaveVideo to write the final MP4 to disk. If the transition feels too abrupt or too loose, iterate: refine your start/end images, tighten the prompt and negative prompt, tweak CFG/steps, or adjust the motion-related controls inside WanFirstLastFrameToVideo if exposed.
suggestedUseCases: Storyboard-to-shot: lock in a first and last composition to visualize a planned camera move or subject motion between two keyframes.
Product spins and reveals: start with a clean hero angle and end on a detail close-up, while prompting for specific lighting or material style.
Logo and brand stingers: guide the animation between two layout frames while enforcing style via prompt and negative prompt.
Environment transitions: morph from daytime to dusk or from empty to populated scenes using paired keyframes and descriptive prompts.
Before/after concept previews: demonstrate a designed change (e.g., interior remodel) by transitioning between two reference frames.

faqItems.question: Do I have to provide both a start and an end frame?
faqItems.answer: Yes—this FLF2V workflow is designed to use both. If you only have one image, duplicate it into both inputs to produce subtle motion without a large scene change.

faqItems.question: How can I change the duration or resolution?
faqItems.answer: Increase the frame count parameter (e.g., F24 or F32) to lengthen the clip, and adjust the resolution fields to your target size. Keep aspect ratios consistent with your start/end images to avoid padding or distortions. Higher frame counts and resolutions require more VRAM.

faqItems.question: Which settings most affect motion smoothness?
faqItems.answer: Your start/end images and prompt coherence matter most. Technically, KSampler steps and CFG scale influence stability: slightly higher steps and moderate CFG (3–6) often improve consistency. If exposed, motion or guidance weights in WanFirstLastFrameToVideo can also tighten the match to the keyframes.

faqItems.question: I see artifacts or flicker—how do I reduce them?
faqItems.answer: Use a strong negative prompt (the provided Chinese example helps), lower CFG slightly, ensure both images share exposure/composition, and raise steps moderately. Also verify models (UNet/CLIP/CLIPVision/VAE) match the Wan 2.1 repackaged set and that resolution aligns with your inputs.

69f55d5c8cec.title: SDXL1.0: Text to Image (Simple)
69f55d5c8cec.description: Generate high-quality images from text prompts using the SDXL 1.0 model, offering a straightforward text-to-image generation workflow. Ideal for quick concept visualization, creative brainstorming, and rapid prototyping of visual ideas.
69f55d5c8cec.metaDescription: Showcase SDXL 1.0 text-to-image in ComfyUI: simple nodes, prompt + negative control, and sampler/size tweaks for fast, polished visuals.
69f55d5c8cec.extendedDescription:
SDXL1.0: Text to Image (Simple) is a clean, minimal ComfyUI graph that spotlights what SDXL 1.0 can do with just the essentials. Using CheckpointLoaderSimple to load sd_xl_base_1.0.safetensors, prompts are encoded with CLIPTextEncode, denoised with KSampler, and brought to life via VAEDecode before SaveImage writes final outputs. This streamlined path delivers impressive compositions and detail without extra overhead—perfect for quick concept passes that still look gallery‑ready.

Despite its simplicity, the workflow offers meaningful creative control. EmptyLatentImage sets your canvas size and batch, while a pair of CLIPTextEncode nodes let you balance a vivid prompt with a tight negative prompt (e.g., "lowres, blurry, watermark, text, logo, signature") to guide style and cleanliness. KSampler puts the finishing touch on mood and fidelity through steps, sampler/scheduler choice, CFG, and seed control—so you can jump from minimalist fine art (like the marble statue in a white void) to moody, cinematic frames or stylized concept art with just a few prompt edits.
howToUse: Load the model: Point CheckpointLoaderSimple to sd_xl_base_1.0.safetensors (the node also provides the CLIP and VAE used downstream).

Write your prompts: In the Prompt group, enter a descriptive positive prompt in one CLIPTextEncode. Optionally add a negative prompt in the second CLIPTextEncode (e.g., "lowres, blurry, watermark, text, logo, signature").
Set image size and batch: Use EmptyLatentImage to choose width, height, and batch size. Keep dimensions near 1024 on the long edge for best SDXL detail and stable composition.

Tune the sampler: In KSampler, adjust steps (quality/time), CFG (prompt strength), sampler/scheduler (e.g., Euler/DPM++ variants), and seed. Use a fixed seed for reproducibility or -1 for fresh variations.
Generate and save: Run the graph. SaveImage will write your results; set a filename prefix to keep series organized.
Iterate creatively: Refine wording, swap stylistic terms, or nudge CFG/steps. For rapid exploration, increase batch or vary the seed to fan out multiple looks.
suggestedUseCases: Minimalist fine‑art studies (e.g., statues, objects, and still lifes in clean lighting and negative space).
Cinematic style frames for previsualization and mood boards.
Stylized product ideation and packaging mockups without photography.
Poster and cover concept directions to explore composition quickly.
Worldbuilding thumbnails for environments, props, and keyframes.

faqItems.question: How do I get sharper, cleaner results without adding extra nodes?
faqItems.answer: Increase steps moderately (e.g., 30–50), keep dimensions near 1024 on the long side, and refine your negative prompt (e.g., "lowres, blurry, watermark, text, logo, signature"). Try a different sampler/scheduler and nudge CFG toward 6–8 for a balanced prompt influence.

faqItems.question: What image sizes work best with SDXL in this simple setup?
faqItems.answer: SDXL is strongest around 1024 resolution. Use square 1024×1024 or near‑native aspect pairs like 896×1152 or 1152×896. Larger sizes can work but may demand more VRAM and careful sampling to maintain detail.

faqItems.question: How can I explore multiple styles or variations quickly?
faqItems.answer: Increase batch in EmptyLatentImage, set seed to -1 for fresh randomness, or keep a fixed seed and iterate on your prompt. Small changes to style terms (lighting, lens, medium) plus CFG/sampler tweaks can yield diverse looks fast.

faqItems.question: Can I add the SDXL Refiner to this workflow?
faqItems.answer: This graph showcases the SDXL base model only. To use a refiner, extend the workflow by adding a second pass with a refiner checkpoint and KSampler at a low denoise on the generated latents. That modification is outside this simple template but is a common enhancement.

faqItems.question: Can I use any image as a profile picture?

faqItems.question: What themes can I use for the variations?

faqItems.question: How long does it take to generate the variations?

6a2b37d44146.title: Step 1: Contact Sheet Workflow
6a2b37d44146.description: Upload your character, scene and product. Integrates all images into a fashion editorial style photograph.
6a2b37d44146.metaDescription: ComfyUI contact sheet: merge character, scene, and product into editorial-style images using Nano Banana Pro, then batch into a reviewable grid.
6a2b37d44146.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow builds a fast, repeatable contact sheet for fashion editorial concepts by compositing three inputs—your character, a scene/background, and a product—into cohesive images. Three LoadImage nodes bring in your assets, a PrimitiveStringMultiline node holds your creative brief, and a GeminiImage2Node uses the "Nano Banana Pro" model to integrate the images according to your instructions (lighting, mood, styling, composition). Because the model conditions on all three sources plus text, it can harmonize color and lighting while preserving key identity and product details.

Once the GeminiImage2Node produces one or more variations, a BatchImagesNode assembles them into a multi-tile contact sheet for quick side-by-side review. Finally, SaveImage writes the resulting grid (and/or individual frames, depending on how the graph is wired) to your output folder. The result is a practical, iteration-friendly tool: feed it new characters, scenes, or products and quickly compare editorial directions without rebuilding the pipeline.
howToUse: Load the "Step 1: Contact Sheet Workflow" JSON into ComfyUI and confirm all nodes are green. If GeminiImage2Node or BatchImagesNode are missing, install their custom-node packages and reload.

Open each LoadImage node and select your assets: a clean character image, a suitable scene/background, and a product cutout (PNG with transparency is ideal when available). Prefer high-quality, well-exposed sources.

In the PrimitiveStringMultiline node, write your creative brief: e.g., "fashion editorial, studio key light with soft rim, glossy magazine color grade, 3/4 camera angle, product prominently featured, refined shadows."

In GeminiImage2Node, select the "Nano Banana Pro" model. If the node exposes controls like output size or variation count, set them to your needs (e.g., square or portrait frames, multiple variations). Keep defaults for other parameters on your first run.
Optionally adjust BatchImagesNode to define your contact sheet layout (columns/rows, padding, order) so multiple variations are tiled in a single grid for review.
Set a filename prefix in SaveImage, then run/queue the workflow. Review the tiled contact sheet in the ComfyUI viewer and find the saved files in your ComfyUI output directory.
suggestedUseCases: Fashion lookbook exploration: quickly compare lighting and styling directions across multiple compositions.
E-commerce hero and lifestyle testing: place a product with consistent character presence across different scenes to evaluate visual impact.
Social campaign planning: generate a grid of on-brand editorial variations to shortlist the strongest creatives.
Client pitch decks: produce polished contact sheets that communicate multiple concepts in one deliverable.
Moodboard development: harmonize disparate references (character, set, product) into unified editorial frames.

faqItems.question: What image sizes work best for the character, scene, and product?
faqItems.answer: Use clean, high-resolution sources (e.g., 1024–2048 px on the long side). Keep similar scales across inputs so the model can align them more naturally. Transparent PNGs for products help with clean placement.

faqItems.question: How do I keep brand details (logos, patterns) accurate in the composite?
faqItems.answer: Start with a clear, front-facing product image and call out constraints in the brief (e.g., “preserve logo and pattern”). If the GeminiImage2Node exposes style/strength controls, reduce the style strength to favor fidelity.

faqItems.question: How can I generate multiple looks on the same setup?
faqItems.answer: Create several brief variants in PrimitiveStringMultiline or, if available, increase the variation/batch setting in GeminiImage2Node. BatchImagesNode will tile the resulting frames into a single contact sheet for fast comparison.

faqItems.question: Where are the outputs saved and in what format?
faqItems.answer: SaveImage controls filename prefix and format (PNG/JPG). Files are written to your ComfyUI output directory. Set a unique prefix per run to keep iterations organized.

6afbca6e9d22.title: Sora 2: Text & Image to Video
6afbca6e9d22.description: OpenAI's Sora-2 and Sora-2 Pro video generation with synchronized audio.
6afbca6e9d22.metaDescription: Tutorial: Generate Sora-2/Sora-2 Pro text- or image-to-video in ComfyUI with proper pad/crop sizing, preview, and SaveVideo output (audio supported).
6afbca6e9d22.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow demonstrates end-to-end text- and image-to-video generation using the OpenAIVideoSora2 node, with optional synchronized audio. You can start from a text prompt alone or condition the video with a reference image loaded via LoadImage. Because Sora-2 and Sora-2 Pro expect fixed input sizes, the workflow offers two branches to make your image fit: Option 1 uses ResizeAndPadImage to letterbox without cropping, and Option 2 crops to fill the frame. PreviewImage lets you confirm framing before you trigger the API call, and SaveVideo writes the returned video to disk.

Technically, the OpenAIVideoSora2 node is the core of the graph, exposing model selection (Sora-2 or Sora-2 Pro), resolution, and prompt fields. The supported sizes are: Sora-2 (720x1280, 1280x720) and Sora-2 Pro (720x1280, 1280x720, 1024x1792, 1792x1024). The workflow groups keep things organized: Upload image, Option1 - Pad image, and Option 2 - Crop image. MarkdownNote and Note nodes include usage and pricing links for the partner API. ImageScale and ResizeAndPadImage align your image to the chosen video size so the API accepts it, while SaveVideo captures the API’s output, including audio when available. This design helps you iterate quickly—preview the conditioned frame, adjust your prompt, then render.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and read the MarkdownNote/Note nodes for API details and pricing. Ensure you’re running in a secure environment (localhost/127.0.0.1) per the partner node requirements.

Open the OpenAIVideoSora2 node: choose the model (Sora-2 or Sora-2 Pro), set one of the supported resolutions, and enter your text prompt. Configure credentials/endpoint as required by the partner docs.

If conditioning with an image, add it via the LoadImage node in the Upload image group. Then choose either Option1 - Pad image (ResizeAndPadImage to fit without cropping) or Option 2 - Crop image (configure the resize/crop path to fill the frame). Use PreviewImage to verify composition.
Important: the input image must exactly match the selected video size. If it doesn’t, adjust with the pad or crop branch until PreviewImage shows the correct resolution and framing.
For text-to-video only, bypass the image branch (select those nodes and press Ctrl-B in ComfyUI) so OpenAIVideoSora2 runs from the text prompt alone.
Set an output path in SaveVideo, then queue and run. When the job completes, check the saved file. If the API returned audio, it will be included in the video; otherwise you’ll get a silent clip.
suggestedUseCases: Prompt-to-video concept sketches for storyboards using 1280x720 for fast iteration.
Image-anchored product spins or hero shots by padding a brand image to 720x1280 portrait.
Social content (Reels/Shorts) with portrait 1024x1792 via Sora-2 Pro to keep subjects large in frame.
Cinematic openings or camera moves guided by a style reference image to lock look and palette.
Education or explainer clips where a diagram image is preserved with letterboxing to avoid cropping labels.

faqItems.question: Which model and resolution should I choose: Sora-2 or Sora-2 Pro?
faqItems.answer: Use Sora-2 for 720x1280 or 1280x720 when you want faster, standard aspect results. Choose Sora-2 Pro if you need the additional sizes (1024x1792, 1792x1024) or higher fidelity. Always match your input image to the exact resolution you select.

faqItems.question: How do I make my image match the required video size?
faqItems.answer: Use Option1 - Pad image (ResizeAndPadImage) to letterbox and preserve the entire image, or use Option 2 - Crop image to fill the frame edge-to-edge. Check the result with PreviewImage before running the API. The API will reject mismatched sizes.

faqItems.question: Can I run text-to-video without providing an image?
faqItems.answer: Yes. Bypass the image branch (select those nodes and press Ctrl-B) so OpenAIVideoSora2 receives only your text prompt. You can re-enable the image path later to switch back to image-to-video.

faqItems.question: How is audio handled?
faqItems.answer: When available, the OpenAIVideoSora2 API returns a video that includes synchronized audio. SaveVideo writes the received video file to disk. If the API response is silent, your output will not contain audio.

faqItems.question: I’m getting network or authorization errors. What should I check?
faqItems.answer: Confirm you’re running in a secure environment that allows localhost/127.0.0.1, your API credentials are set in the OpenAIVideoSora2 node, and your firewall/proxy isn’t blocking the request. See the partner node overview and pricing links in the MarkdownNote.

6b04e55bf06b.title: Luma Photon: Image to Image

Provide a textual prompt to guide the image generation process.
