b8c030205d86.title: Fast GAN Video Upscaler
b8c030205d86.description: Upload a video to upscale it using a fast GAN model. The output resolution is determined by your chosen model (e.g., 2x or 4x). For best results, upscale first, then resize to your target resolution.
b8c030205d86.metaDescription: Efficiently upscale videos using GAN models with ComfyUI's Fast GAN Video Upscaler workflow for high-quality video enhancement.
b8c030205d86.extendedDescription:
The Fast GAN Video Upscaler workflow is designed to efficiently upscale videos using a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) model, specifically Real-ESRGAN. This workflow is ideal for enhancing video resolution, making it suitable for applications where higher quality is desired without the need for creating new details, as diffusion models might. The workflow utilizes several key nodes, including the UpscaleModelLoader and ImageUpscaleWithModel, to apply the upscaling model to each frame of the video. It begins by loading your video with the LoadVideo node, breaking it down into frames with GetVideoComponents, and then applying the upscaling process.

Technically, the workflow leverages the Real-ESRGAN model to upscale each frame by a factor determined by the model (e.g., 2x or 4x). This is achieved through the ImageUpscaleWithModel node, which processes each frame individually before the frames are reassembled into a video using the CreateVideo node. Finally, the SaveVideo node outputs the upscaled video. This process is notably faster than diffusion-based methods, making it a practical solution for quick enhancements. For optimal results, it is recommended to first upscale the video to the highest desired resolution and then resize it to the target resolution if needed.
howToUse: Load the Fast GAN Video Upscaler workflow in ComfyUI.
Use the LoadVideo node to upload your video file.
Select the desired upscale model (e.g., 2x or 4x) in the UpscaleModelLoader node.
Run the workflow to process the video frames with ImageUpscaleWithModel.
Reassemble the upscaled frames into a video using the CreateVideo node.
Save the final upscaled video using the SaveVideo node.
suggestedUseCases: Enhancing low-resolution videos for better viewing on high-definition displays.
Preparing video content for platforms that require higher resolution uploads.
Improving the quality of archived videos for digital restoration projects.
Upscaling video game footage for content creators and streamers.

b95499a55c9f.title: InfiniteTalk: Audio-Driven Full-Body Video Dubbing
b95499a55c9f.description: Upload a source Image and target audio. Generate a full-body dubbed video with synchronized motion while preserving the original identity, background, and camera movement.
b95499a55c9f.metaDescription: Create full-body dubbed videos from a single image and audio with Wan2.1 InfiniteTalk. Multi-speaker, lip-synced, camera-aware results in ComfyUI.
b95499a55c9f.extendedDescription: InfiniteTalk: Audio-Driven Full-Body Video Dubbing turns a single image and one or more audio tracks into a lip‑synced, full‑body video while preserving the original identity, background, and camera motion. The core of the pipeline is WanInfiniteTalkToVideo, which fuses features from the loaded Wan2.1 I2V model with an audio embedding to drive body and facial motion. Step1 - Load Models prepares the UNet and VAE (UNETLoader, VAELoader) for image‑to‑video synthesis, and loads text and audio backbones (CLIPLoader with CLIPTextEncode for camera/stage prompts, and AudioEncoderLoader with AudioEncoderEncode for voice features). You import the starting frame via LoadImage, then draw masks per character in the MaskEditor to localize motion to each speaker.
howToUse: Load the workflow and models. In Step1 - Load Models, point UNETLoader to Wan2_1-I2V-14B-480p_fp8 (diffusion model), load the matching VAELoader and CLIPLoader, and set AudioEncoderLoader to the provided InfiniteTalk audio encoder. Optional: apply LoraLoaderModelOnly or ModelPatchLoader if you need a style/character LoRA or an InfiniteTalk patch.

Import the start frame and create masks. Upload your image in LoadImage, then right‑click it and choose Open in MaskEditor. Brush a clean mask for Character 1 (include mouth, jaw, upper torso for natural motion). Repeat in the Step2/Step3 Character Audio and Mask groups for additional speakers, each with its own mask.

Add audio and arrange dialogue. Use LoadAudio for each speaker line. If you have multiple clips or alternating speakers, connect them with AudioConcat to build the final timeline. Keep one speaker per track when possible for cleaner lip sync.

Set prompt and conditioning. In Step3 - Prompt, describe camera behavior and scene (e.g., “The camera zooms in. Two characters are talking.”). If you want to minimize text bias and preserve the original look, use ConditioningZeroOut to dampen or remove CLIP conditioning.

Choose size and duration. In Video Size, set width/height (default 480p for the Wan2.1 I2V weights). To match longer audio, duplicate the Video Extend group: each copy adds 81 frames at 25 fps (~3.24 s). As a rule of thumb, number_of_extends = ceil(audio_length_seconds / 3.24). Select the Video Extend group box, press Ctrl‑C then Ctrl‑Shift‑V to duplicate until the total duration covers your audio.

Generate and export. Run the graph. VAEDecode, ImageBatch, and ImageFromBatch will assemble frames; CreateVideo compiles them at your chosen fps (typically 25), and SaveVideo writes the final file. Review the result; if you see drift or over‑motion, refine masks, simplify the prompt, or reduce/add LoRA influence.
suggestedUseCases: Localizing short commercial clips: keep the scene and actor identity while dubbing into a new language.
Animating character posters or key art into short talking segments with natural camera moves.
Previsualization and animatics: block dialogue timing and staging before full production.
Social content and explainers: turn a still host image into a voiced full‑body presenter.
Dialogue mock‑ups with two speakers using separate audio tracks and masks.

faqItems.question: What models and nodes are essential for this to work?
faqItems.answer: At minimum: UNETLoader with Wan2.1 I2V 14B 480p weights, VAELoader, CLIPLoader + CLIPTextEncode (for camera/scene prompts), AudioEncoderLoader + AudioEncoderEncode (for voice features), LoadImage for the start frame, WanInfiniteTalkToVideo to drive motion, VAEDecode to get frames, and CreateVideo/SaveVideo to export. LoraLoaderModelOnly and ModelPatchLoader are optional for style or InfiniteTalk patches.

faqItems.question: How do I match the video length to my audio?
faqItems.answer: Use the Video Extend group. Each copy adds 81 frames at 25 fps (~3.24 s). Compute ceil(audio_seconds / 3.24) and duplicate the group that many times (box‑select, Ctrl‑C, then Ctrl‑Shift‑V). If you have multiple audio clips, assemble them with AudioConcat first so the total duration is clear.

faqItems.question: Why does the background or identity drift?
faqItems.answer: Over‑strong text or style conditioning can push the look away from the source. Reduce CLIP influence using ConditioningZeroOut, avoid heavy style LoRAs (or lower their weight in LoraLoaderModelOnly), and keep prompts descriptive (camera, staging) rather than stylistic. Also ensure masks are tight around speaking characters so motion doesn’t bleed into the background.

faqItems.question: What audio format works best and how do I improve lip sync?
faqItems.answer: Use clean, single‑speaker audio per track where possible. Common WAV/MP3 files load via LoadAudio; if a file fails, convert to a standard WAV (e.g., 16–48 kHz, mono). Better lip sync comes from clear diction and minimal background noise. For multi‑speaker scenes, keep separate audio files and masks per character and arrange them with AudioConcat.

baa06a413558.title: Seedance 2.0 Image to Video
baa06a413558.description: This workflow is an easy start for generating 4-15 second videos from a single image, using Seedance 2.0
baa06a413558.metaDescription: Turn a single image into a 4–15s video in ComfyUI with Seedance 2.0. LoadImage → ByteDance2FirstLastFrameNode → SaveVideo. Simple setup, adjustable motion.
baa06a413558.extendedDescription:
Seedance 2.0 Image to Video turns a single still image into a short, natural-looking video. The workflow is intentionally minimal: LoadImage brings your source photo or artwork into the graph, ByteDance2FirstLastFrameNode (powered by Seedance 2.0) synthesizes motion and generates a sequence of frames, and SaveVideo encodes the result as a playable clip. It’s a fast, focused way to create 4–15 second motion from a static image without extra conditioning or complex control nodes.

Technically, ByteDance2FirstLastFrameNode uses Seedance 2.0 to infer a coherent motion arc anchored by consistent first and last frames, then interpolates the in-betweens to preserve subject structure and style. You control core parameters such as clip length (seconds or frames), frames-per-second, motion intensity, and (if exposed by your version) a seed for repeatability. The node outputs a frame sequence that SaveVideo compiles into a video at the chosen fps. For best results, start with a clean, well-lit image where the main subject is centered, keep motion strength moderate, and target 6–10 seconds for the most natural movement.
howToUse: Load the workflow JSON in ComfyUI and confirm the ByteDance2FirstLastFrameNode (Seedance 2.0) model files are installed and detected. If the node shows missing weights, install them per the node’s repository instructions.
Open LoadImage and select your source image. Use a clean, subject-focused photo or artwork; 720–1080 px on the longer side is a good starting point for speed and quality.

Select ByteDance2FirstLastFrameNode and set the clip duration (e.g., 4–15 seconds) and frames-per-second. Start with moderate motion strength; if your node version exposes a seed, set one to make results reproducible.
Queue the workflow. If you run out of VRAM or it’s slow, reduce input resolution, shorten duration, or lower fps, then re-run.
In SaveVideo, choose the output path, filename, and ensure fps matches the generation. Queue again to encode and save the video file.
Review the result and iterate: adjust motion strength, try different seeds, or fine-tune duration/fps. For smoother motion, keep durations modest and avoid extreme motion on busy backgrounds.
suggestedUseCases: Create subtle product spins or portrait cinemagraphs for social posts from a single still.
Add animated hero banners or background loops to websites using brand imagery.
Generate quick B-roll from stock photos to fill gaps in edits or mood films.
Animate concept art and storyboards to explore motion and pacing early in production.
Produce eye-catching motion thumbnails or interstitials from static key art.

faqItems.question: What image size and aspect ratio should I use?
faqItems.answer: Use clean, well-lit images around 768–1080 px on the long edge for a good quality/speed balance. Keep your desired aspect ratio; the node will resize if needed, but larger inputs require more VRAM and time.

faqItems.question: My video looks jittery or warps the subject. How can I improve it?
faqItems.answer: Lower the motion strength, shorten the duration, and increase fps if possible. Start with simpler, subject-centered images and try a different seed for stability. Reducing background clutter also helps.

faqItems.question: How do I control clip length precisely?
faqItems.answer: Set duration (in seconds or frames) in ByteDance2FirstLastFrameNode and match that fps in SaveVideo. Duration = frames ÷ fps, so verify both to get the exact length you expect.

faqItems.question: Can I make a seamless loop?
faqItems.answer: Seamless loops aren’t guaranteed, but the node’s first/last frame consistency can help. Keep motion subtle and cyclical, aim for similar start/end framing, and if needed, trim or crossfade the ends in an external editor.

badeb885763a.title: HiDream I1 Fast
badeb885763a.description: Generate images quickly with HiDream I1 Fast - Lightweight version with 16 inference steps, ideal for rapid previews on lower-end hardware.
badeb885763a.metaDescription: Generate fast text-to-image previews with HiDream I1 Fast in ComfyUI. SD3-style sampling, 16 steps, and FP8 UNet for low VRAM and quick iterations.
badeb885763a.extendedDescription:
HiDream I1 Fast is a lightweight text-to-image workflow tuned for rapid previews and low-VRAM GPUs. It pairs the HiDream I1 Fast FP8 UNet (loaded with UNETLoader) with SD3-style sampling (ModelSamplingSD3) and runs just 16 inference steps in KSampler. Prompts are handled through QuadrupleCLIPLoader and CLIPTextEncode, while EmptySD3LatentImage creates the starting latent at your chosen resolution. The result is a fast, responsive pipeline that’s ideal for exploring ideas and iterating on compositions without long waits.

Technically, the workflow loads a matching VAE via VAELoader and decodes samples with VAEDecode, then writes outputs using SaveImage. ModelSamplingSD3 exposes the HiDream/SD3 “shift” parameter (commonly around 3.0 per official guidance) to balance prompt conditioning across multiple text encoders. Because the UNet is FP8 and the step count is low, VRAM use stays modest, making this a practical option for laptops or older GPUs while still producing coherent, stylized results.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI, then install/place models: put hidream_i1_fast_fp8.safetensors in ComfyUI/models/diffusion_models and the HiDream text encoders (e.g., clip_l_hidream) in ComfyUI/models/text_encoders. Ensure a compatible VAE is available in ComfyUI/models/vae.
Step 1 – Load Models: In UNETLoader, select hidream_i1_fast_fp8.safetensors. In QuadrupleCLIPLoader, choose the HiDream-compatible text encoders. In VAELoader, pick the VAE that matches HiDream/SD3.
Step 2 – Image size: Set your target resolution and batch size in EmptySD3LatentImage. Start with 768×768 (or 1024×576 for wides) to keep VRAM low; larger sizes cost more memory.
Step 3 – Prompt: Enter your positive and negative prompts using CLIPTextEncode. For negatives, try phrases like “bad, ugly, jpeg artifacts” to suppress common defects.

Sampling and quality: In ModelSamplingSD3, keep shift around 3.0 as a starting point (from official HiDream guidance). In KSampler, use 16 steps for speed; you can raise steps for cleaner details. Sampler/scheduler are user-selectable—uni_pc with a simple scheduler is a solid default per HiDream’s notes.

Generate: Execute the workflow. Inspect the output from VAEDecode and SaveImage. If results look soft or off-prompt, adjust shift slightly, raise steps to 20–24, refine negatives, or try a different sampler, then re-run.
suggestedUseCases: Rapid concept exploration for illustrations and environment studies
Style and composition iteration when art-directing a scene
Quick thumbnails and moodboards on lower-end or mobile GPUs
Batching lightweight previews before committing to high-quality renders
Fast negative-prompt testing to diagnose and reduce artifacts

faqItems.question: How do I reduce VRAM usage further?
faqItems.answer: Keep steps at 16, lower resolution in EmptySD3LatentImage, reduce batch size to 1, and ensure you’re using the FP8 model (hidream_i1_fast_fp8.safetensors). Larger images and higher steps raise memory use.

faqItems.question: What does the SD3 shift parameter do?
faqItems.answer: The ModelSamplingSD3 shift balances conditioning across the multiple text encoders used by HiDream/SD3-style models. Start near 3.0 (official guidance) and adjust slightly if prompts feel over/under-strong.

faqItems.question: Which sampler should I use?
faqItems.answer: The workflow is sampler-agnostic. Per HiDream’s notes, uni_pc with a simple scheduler is a reliable default. If you need different behavior, try Euler or DPM++ variants and compare results at the same step count.

faqItems.question: How can I improve quality if images look blurry or off-prompt?
faqItems.answer: Increase steps moderately (e.g., 20–24), refine your positive/negative prompts, tweak shift (±0.5), and consider a slightly higher resolution. Also set a fixed seed in KSampler for reproducible tuning.

bb33cc433026.title: LTX-2.3: FLF2V
bb33cc433026.description: Upload a starting image to generate a video sequence. The workflow creates a short video with consistent style and motion, beginning with your provided frame.
bb33cc433026.metaDescription: Turn a single image into a short, coherent video with LTX-2.3. Guide motion via prompts, keep style consistent, and export ready-to-share video.
bb33cc433026.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow, built around the LTX-2.3 video model, turns a single reference image into a short, coherent video clip with controllable motion and style. It uses your uploaded first frame (LoadImage in the First Frame group) as a strong visual anchor, optionally blends in an ending reference from the Last Frame group, and lets you steer the scene with natural language prompts. Text conditioning is handled by CLIPTextEncode and LTXAVTextEncoderLoader in the Conditioning group, while LTXVAddGuide fuses your reference frame(s) into the model’s conditioning stream.

Under the hood, EmptyLTXVLatentVideo creates the video latent with your chosen resolution, frame count, and FPS. RandomNoise seeds the generation, and sampling is performed with SamplerEulerAncestral guided by CFGGuider and a ManualSigmas schedule for stable, consistent motion. LTXVConcatAVLatent pairs the video latent with an audio latent (LTXVEmptyLatentAudio by default, resulting in silence) so your output is a proper A/V container. Final frames are decoded efficiently with VAEDecodeTiled and written to disk via SaveVideo. Utility nodes like GetImageSize and LTXVCropGuides help you frame the subject reliably, and LTXVPreprocess normalizes your input image to the model’s expected space. The result is a fast, practical pipeline for turning a single image into a smooth, on-style video clip.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and ensure the LTX nodes are installed. In the Model group (LTXVConditioning), set the model to LTX-2.3.
In the First Frame group, connect your starting image to LoadImage. Use LTXVCropGuides and GetImageSize to check framing, and let LTXVPreprocess normalize the image.
Optionally, add an ending reference image in the Last Frame group. Adjust LTXVAddGuide so the first/last frames guide strength matches how tightly you want to preserve look and layout.

In the Prompt group, enter your positive and negative text prompts via CLIPTextEncode. Describe motion over time (e.g., camera moves), visual specifics, and optional audio cues (these condition visuals; the default audio track is silent).

Open the Settings and Sampling groups: set frames/FPS/resolution in EmptyLTXVLatentVideo, pick a seed in RandomNoise, then tune CFGGuider (guidance scale) and SamplerEulerAncestral steps. Leave ManualSigmas at defaults unless you need a custom schedule.

Run the graph. Inspect the decoded frames from VAEDecodeTiled, then export with SaveVideo. If results drift from your subject, increase guide strength or reduce steps/CFG slightly and re-run with the same seed.
suggestedUseCases: Turning a character portrait or product shot into a simple camera move (dolly, tilt, or orbit) for social posts.
Storyboarding: create short motion beats from a single keyframe to communicate camera direction and pacing.
Style-lock reels: maintain a consistent aesthetic across multiple clips by reusing the same first frame and prompt.
Before/after transitions: guide toward a last-frame reference to visualize a transformation over a few seconds.
Silent hero loops for websites and UI backgrounds, rendered at lightweight resolutions and FPS.

faqItems.question: How do I control duration, FPS, and resolution?
faqItems.answer: Use EmptyLTXVLatentVideo in the Settings group. Set frame count for duration, FPS for playback speed, and width/height for resolution. VAEDecodeTiled helps decode higher resolutions on limited VRAM.

faqItems.question: Why does the video drift from my reference image?
faqItems.answer: Increase the guide weight in LTXVAddGuide, reduce CFG in CFGGuider, or lower sampling steps in SamplerEulerAncestral. Using a stable seed (RandomNoise) and keeping ManualSigmas at defaults often improves consistency.

faqItems.question: Can I add or generate audio?
faqItems.answer: This template wires LTXVEmptyLatentAudio, so the output is silent by default. You can keep it silent or replace that node with real audio latents. Text like “Music: …” conditions the visuals but does not synthesize audio in this setup.

faqItems.question: Do I need a last-frame image?
faqItems.answer: No. The workflow works with just the first frame. Supplying a last frame and tuning LTXVAddGuide can help target a specific end look or facilitate smooth start–end transitions.

bb7e03924a5c.title: Qwen Image 2.1: Text to Image
bb7e03924a5c.description: Generate images from text prompts with Qwen Image 2.1, the latest open-weight Qwen-Image model, producing a single 1024×1024 image over 25 sampling steps. Generation and instruction-based editing share one model with native 2K output, professional typography, and alpha-channel support. Ideal for poster and layout design, transparent asset creation, and rapid concept visualization.
bb7e03924a5c.metaDescription: ComfyUI tutorial: Generate text-to-image with Qwen Image 2.1, 1024–2048 px, 25 steps, alpha support. Includes ResolutionSelector and advanced PNG saving.
bb7e03924a5c.extendedDescription:
This workflow generates high-quality images from text prompts using Qwen Image 2.1, an open-weight diffusion model known for strong layout and typography rendering and native 2K (2048×2048) output. At its core is a custom Qwen generator node (UUID: c291ceec-b98f-4751-9d0b-7bc288f27b30) that loads either qwen_image_2.1_bf16.safetensors or the memory-saving qwen_image_2.1_int8_convrot.safetensors. By default, it produces a single 1024×1024 image in about 25 sampling steps, with support for transparent (alpha) backgrounds when saved as PNG. ResolutionSelector sets the canvas size, and SaveImageAdvanced handles file output and metadata.

Technically, the subgraph encapsulates prompt conditioning and a built-in sampler inside the Qwen node, so you don’t need separate sampler nodes. You provide a prompt (and optionally a negative prompt if exposed), choose a resolution, and the node performs the full diffusion pass. The workflow’s MarkdownNote/Note nodes document on-canvas instructions, while SaveImageAdvanced ensures your output is written with correct color and alpha handling. This makes it ideal for fast concept visualizations, posters, and assets that benefit from clean text and layout—without leaving the ComfyUI canvas.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and ensure the subgraph is visible. Install the model by placing qwen_image_2.1_bf16.safetensors or qwen_image_2.1_int8_convrot.safetensors into ComfyUI/models/diffusion_models/.
In the Qwen Image 2.1 node (UUID: c291ceec-b98f-4751-9d0b-7bc288f27b30), select the desired model file. Use bf16 for best fidelity on higher-VRAM GPUs; use int8_convrot to reduce memory usage.
Enter your text prompt in the node’s prompt field. If the node exposes a negative prompt or guidance options, set them as needed. Keep the default 25 steps for a fast first pass.
Set your image size with ResolutionSelector. Start at 1024×1024 for speed and stability; switch to 2048×2048 to leverage Qwen’s native 2K output if your GPU can handle it.

Run the workflow. The generator node performs the diffusion pass and outputs an image (RGBA when transparency is produced). SaveImageAdvanced will write the result to your configured output folder (use PNG to preserve alpha).
Iterate: adjust the prompt for clearer typography and layout (e.g., specify headline placement, style, alignment), tweak steps (e.g., 30–40 for more detail), or change the seed for new variations.
suggestedUseCases: Poster and flyer mockups with legible headlines and balanced layout.
Social media cards and banners where text rendering quality matters.
Transparent UI or icon assets (export as PNG to keep alpha).
Presentation thumbnails and concept boards at 2K for crisp detail.
Quick brand moodboards with consistent composition and type cues.

faqItems.question: Which model file should I choose: bf16 or int8_convrot?
faqItems.answer: Use qwen_image_2.1_bf16.safetensors for the best image fidelity if your GPU has ample VRAM. Use qwen_image_2.1_int8_convrot.safetensors to reduce memory requirements at a small quality trade-off. If you encounter out-of-memory errors—especially at 2K—switch to int8 or lower the resolution.

faqItems.question: How do I get sharper text and cleaner layout?
faqItems.answer: Be explicit in your prompt about hierarchy and placement (e.g., “bold sans-serif headline, centered title, small subheading, clean margins”). Use 1024–2048 px resolution, try 30–40 steps for more refinement, and keep the seed fixed while iterating so you can make controlled adjustments.

faqItems.question: Can this workflow do instruction-based editing?
faqItems.answer: Qwen Image 2.1 supports instruction-based editing with the same underlying model, but this specific workflow is set up for text-to-image generation. To do edits, add or switch to a compatible Qwen editing node/subgraph that accepts an input image and edit instructions.

faqItems.question: How do I preserve transparency in the output?
faqItems.answer: Ensure you save as PNG in SaveImageAdvanced. If the model outputs an alpha channel (transparent background), PNG will keep it; JPG will discard transparency. You can verify by opening the saved image in an editor that shows the checkerboard background.

bcc5d7da614c.title: HiDream O1 Full: Image generation
bcc5d7da614c.description: Input a text prompt and optionally upload reference images. Generate a high-resolution image up to 2048x2048 with text-to-image, editing, or subject-driven personalization.
bcc5d7da614c.metaDescription: Generate high-res images with HiDream O1 from text or references. Supports up to 10 reference images, size presets, and flexible samplers for 2048x2048 output.
bcc5d7da614c.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow uses the HiDream O1 Image model to generate high-resolution images from text prompts, with optional reference images for subject-driven personalization or style guidance. At its core, CheckpointLoaderSimple loads the HiDream-O1-Image checkpoint and VAE, CLIPTextEncode embeds your prompt, and a sampling chain built from BasicScheduler plus either KSamplerSelect or SamplerCustom synthesizes a latent image. VAEDecode turns that latent into a final RGB image, while PreviewAny and SaveImage handle live previews and exports.

Two pathways are provided: pure text-to-image and image-guided editing. A ComfySwitchNode toggles between these modes. For text-to-image, EmptyHiDreamO1LatentImage initializes a latent at your chosen size (in the Size: Text to Image group). For image edit/personalization, you can LoadImage inputs and optionally pass up to 10 of them into HiDreamO1ReferenceImages to inject subject/style cues, with GetImageSize and the Size: Image Edit group ensuring dimensions line up. ImageScaleToTotalPixels, together with ComfyMathExpression, can downscale large inputs to a safe pixel budget; enable it (Select + Ctrl-B) when your sources are too large. ModelNoiseScale provides fine control over the initial noise magnitude—use lower values to hew closer to references, higher for more variety. PrimitiveBoolean and Feature Switch controls make it easy to turn reference conditioning and other options on or off.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and ensure the HiDream-O1-Image checkpoint is set in CheckpointLoaderSimple. The VAE will load with the model.
Enter your prompt in the Prompt or User Prompt group (PrimitiveStringMultiline → CLIPTextEncode). Keep prompts clear and specific.

Choose your mode with the Image Edit switch (ComfySwitchNode): Text-to-Image uses EmptyHiDreamO1LatentImage and Size: Text to Image; Image Edit uses LoadImage and Size: Image Edit. If using references, connect up to 10 LoadImage nodes to HiDreamO1ReferenceImages.

Set resolution: pick a trained resolution preset in the Size group (for example, 2048×2048 or 2304×1728). For large inputs, Select the ImageScaleToTotalPixels node and press Ctrl-B to enable safe downscaling.

Tune sampling: pick a sampler in KSamplerSelect or use SamplerCustom; adjust steps and guidance. If outputs drift too much from references, reduce ModelNoiseScale; if they look too similar or flat, increase it slightly.
Run the graph. Inspect results in PreviewAny. When satisfied, use SaveImage to export the final image.
suggestedUseCases: Subject-driven portraits: provide a few clean reference shots via HiDreamO1ReferenceImages to personalize outputs while following a text prompt.
Product visuals: align to brand style with 2–5 style references and generate consistent catalog images at 2048×2048.
Concept art exploration: rapid text-to-image with flexible sampler and scheduler settings for varied ideation.
Style transfer-like guidance: use reference images to steer composition and palette while letting the prompt drive content.
Large-canvas social/marketing assets: create high-res square or landscape images directly at trained sizes.

faqItems.question: How many reference images can I use?
faqItems.answer: Up to 10. Add more LoadImage nodes and connect them to the HiDreamO1ReferenceImages node to include multiple subject/style references.

faqItems.question: What resolutions work best?
faqItems.answer: Use the trained presets provided in the workflow notes, including 2048×2048 (square) and 2304×1728 (landscape). Sticking to these ratios typically yields the sharpest results.

faqItems.question: When should I enable ImageScaleToTotalPixels?
faqItems.answer: Enable it (Select + Ctrl-B) when your input image is very large. It works with ComfyMathExpression to reduce total pixels, preventing VRAM spikes while preserving aspect ratio.

faqItems.question: Do I need a separate VAE?
faqItems.answer: No. CheckpointLoaderSimple loads the HiDream O1 model with its VAE. If you swap VAEs, ensure compatibility, as it can affect color and sharpness.

bccb8f448374.title: Krea 3: Image Edit
bccb8f448374.description: Perform targeted regional edits on an image with Krea 3, changing only the areas you specify while the rest of the picture stays untouched. One image goes in and one edited image comes out. Ideal for e-commerce product restaging, fashion and portrait relighting, and architectural sketch-to-render work.
bccb8f448374.metaDescription: Targeted Krea 3 image edits in ComfyUI: load an image, select a region, describe the change, and export a clean, single edited result.
bccb8f448374.extendedDescription:
This workflow demonstrates precise regional image editing with Krea 3 inside ComfyUI. It starts by loading a single source image with LoadImage (a sample wide_format_digital_render.png is included), then routes it through Krea3ImageNode, which sends the image, your edit instruction, and a targeted region/mask to the Krea 3 image-edit model. The model returns an edited version in which only the specified area is changed while the rest of the pixels are preserved. The final result is saved using SaveImageAdvanced with your chosen filename and output path.

Technically, Krea3ImageNode handles the API call and compositing, preserving the unedited portion of the original and blending the model’s change back into place. You control the edit via a concise text instruction and a region of interest (mask or bounding box, depending on the node version). SaveImageAdvanced provides robust filename templating and path control for organized outputs, while a MarkdownNote in the canvas documents tips and defaults. This setup is ideal when you need one-image-in/one-image-out reliability for tasks like product restaging, portrait relighting, or localized architectural tweaks without re-generating the entire scene.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and review the MarkdownNote for quick tips. Ensure ComfyUI and custom nodes are up to date.
Open the LoadImage node and either keep the provided wide_format_digital_render.png or browse to your own image. Confirm the image feeds into Krea3ImageNode.

In Krea3ImageNode, enter a clear edit instruction (e.g., “replace the sky with a warm sunset” or “brighten the jacket to deep blue”). Define the target area using the node’s region controls (mask or ROI). If the node exposes an API Key field, add your Krea key, or ensure it’s configured as documented for the node.
Optionally adjust available parameters (e.g., edit strength or guidance if present). Keep the region tight and the instruction specific to minimize unintended changes outside your selection.
Configure SaveImageAdvanced with your desired output folder and filename pattern, then Queue Prompt. The edited image will be written to your output directory as a single result.
suggestedUseCases: E-commerce product restaging (swap backgrounds, adjust colors, or change small product details without redoing the whole image).
Fashion and portrait relighting or retouching limited to face, hair, or clothing regions.
Architectural or interior mockups (replace a window view, update a fixture, or change wall finishes in a selected area).
Signage or label swaps on packaging, storefronts, or vehicles.
Minor scene corrections (remove a distracting object, fix blemishes, or clean edges) in a localized region.

faqItems.question: Do I need a Krea API key for this to work?
faqItems.answer: Yes, Krea3ImageNode calls the Krea 3 service. If the node provides an API Key field, paste your key there; otherwise configure it per the node’s documentation (e.g., environment variable or settings panel).

faqItems.question: How do I limit changes to only part of the image?
faqItems.answer: Use Krea3ImageNode’s region controls (mask or region-of-interest). Keep the selection tight around the object you want to modify and write a concise instruction focused only on that area.

faqItems.question: Why is the background changing slightly?
faqItems.answer: Overly broad regions or vague instructions can cause bleed. Shrink the selected area, sharpen your instruction (mention color, material, or lighting), and reduce edit strength if that parameter is available.

faqItems.question: What resolution do I get back, and is my image sent to a server?
faqItems.answer: The node returns a single edited image and typically preserves the input’s aspect ratio. The image and edit request are sent to the Krea API for processing—review Krea’s documentation and privacy policy for details.

bd874c5e02d6.title: Generate UGC Video With Voice Clone
bd874c5e02d6.description: Upload an image to generate AI prompts and synthesize speech. Create a final video with accurate lip sync using Eleven Labs and LTX Video.
bd874c5e02d6.metaDescription: ComfyUI workflow: auto-generate script from an image, clone voice with ElevenLabs, and create lip-synced UGC video using LTX‑2.3.
bd874c5e02d6.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI tutorial workflow turns a single image into a short, lip‑synced UGC-style video with cloned or selected voice. It chains three stages: prompt creation from your uploaded image, speech synthesis with ElevenLabs, and video generation with LTX‑2.3. The Create Prompt group routes the image from LoadImage into GeminiNode to auto-generate two texts: a performance-ready speech script (with expression tags) and a scene description. RegexExtract parses the Gemini response to separate the “speech” and “scene” sections cleanly for downstream nodes.

For audio, you can pick a preset voice via ElevenLabsVoiceSelector or bring your own tone with ElevenLabsInstantVoiceClone, then synthesize the final narration in ElevenLabsTextToSpeech and optionally save it with SaveAudioMP3. The Create Video group feeds the scene description and the audio into the LTX‑2.3 video node (UUID: 98fb87e2-23b5-4ecb-aacc-365912414a12) to produce a talking-style video with accurate lip sync, previewed by PreviewAny and written with SaveVideo. This setup is practical for rapid UGC, product explainers, testimonials, or social posts because it automates script writing from an image and guarantees voice-to-lips alignment through ElevenLabs + LTX.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and open the MarkdownNote for on-canvas tips. Confirm you have API keys set for Gemini (in GeminiNode) and ElevenLabs (in ElevenLabs nodes).

In Load Image, upload your reference image. Run the Create Prompt group to let GeminiNode generate both a speech script (with expression tags) and a scene description. RegexExtract will split these into separate outputs.

Choose a voice: either pick a preset in ElevenLabsVoiceSelector or clone a new one with ElevenLabsInstantVoiceClone (upload a clean 1–2 minute sample). Connect the chosen voice output to ElevenLabsTextToSpeech.
Generate narration: paste or pass the speech prompt into ElevenLabsTextToSpeech and run it. Use PreviewAny to audition the audio. Optionally, write it to disk with SaveAudioMP3.

Create the video: feed the scene description and the generated audio into the LTX‑2.3 video node (UUID: 98fb87e2-23b5-4ecb-aacc-365912414a12) inside the Create Video group. Adjust duration or other available parameters as needed.

Run the final graph. Inspect the result in PreviewAny, then export with SaveVideo. If running locally and you want sharper output, place the LTX upscaler model (ltx-2.3-spatial-upscaler-x2-1.1.safetensors) in your latent_upscale_models folder before rendering.
suggestedUseCases: UGC-style product demos: turn a product image into a short spoken walkthrough with brand-aligned voice.
Testimonials and reviews: generate a talking-head style clip from a customer photo with a friendly, cloned voice.
Social promos: quickly draft scripts from campaign visuals and render lip-synced shorts for TikTok/Reels.
Educational snippets: create narrator-led explainers from illustrative images with expressive TTS.
Creator voice packs: clone your voice once, then reuse it across multiple image-to-video posts.

faqItems.question: Do I need API keys to run this workflow?
faqItems.answer: Yes. Provide a valid Gemini API key in GeminiNode for prompt generation and an ElevenLabs API key in the ElevenLabs nodes for voice selection/cloning and TTS. Without Gemini, you can bypass that step by manually writing the speech and scene prompts.

faqItems.question: How does the workflow keep lips in sync with the audio?
faqItems.answer: The generated narration from ElevenLabsTextToSpeech is fed directly into the LTX‑2.3 video node, which uses the audio to align mouth movements. Keeping the final TTS file as the exact audio source ensures accurate lip sync.

faqItems.question: Can I bring my own pre-recorded narration instead of TTS?
faqItems.answer: Yes. Use LoadAudio to input your narration and connect it where the TTS audio would go in the Create Video group. Skip the ElevenLabsTextToSpeech step in that case.

faqItems.question: What does RegexExtract do in this graph?
faqItems.answer: GeminiNode returns both a speech script and a scene description. RegexExtract parses that response into two clean outputs—one for ElevenLabsTextToSpeech (speech prompt) and one for the LTX‑2.3 video node (scene prompt)—to keep the pipeline reliable.

bdb2c0ea519b.title: Eleven v4: Text to Speech
bdb2c0ea519b.description: Generate expressive speech from text with Eleven v4, the quality-focused ElevenLabs model. Direct the performance with audio tags such as [whispers] or [excited] written into the script, or upload a voice sample to clone a voice and narrate the script in it. One audio file is output. Ideal for audiobooks, narration, and character voiceovers.
bdb2c0ea519b.metaDescription: ComfyUI ElevenLabs v4 TTS workflow with inline performance tags and optional instant voice cloning. Generate one polished audio file from your script.
bdb2c0ea519b.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow turns written scripts into expressive speech using ElevenLabs’ Eleven v4 model. It’s designed around two clear paths: use a preset voice from your ElevenLabs library or instantly clone a voice from an audio sample. The core generation happens in the ElevenLabsTextToSpeech node, which reads your script (written in a Note/MarkdownNote) and applies performance directions you embed as inline tags like [whispers], [excited], [laughs], [sighs], [sarcastic], and [crying]. SaveAudioAdvanced then writes a single audio file to disk.

Technically, Option 1 (Use Preset Voice) routes a selection from ElevenLabsVoiceSelector into ElevenLabsTextToSpeech along with your script and the Eleven v4 model choice. Option 2 (Create a Voice Clone) feeds audio from LoadAudio or RecordAudio into ElevenLabsInstantVoiceClone, which returns a temporary voice you can target in the TTS node. Only one option group should be enabled at a time (select the group and press Ctrl-B to un-bypass it). Because Eleven v4 treats the prompt as a performance script, the workflow lets you direct tone and delivery directly in text while keeping the node graph compact and easy to iterate for narration, audiobooks, and character voiceovers.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and ensure your ElevenLabs API key is configured in the ElevenLabs nodes or extension settings.
Open the Note/MarkdownNote node and paste your script. Add performance tags like [whispers], [excited], [laughs], [sighs], [sarcastic], or [crying] right before or after the words you want to affect.

Choose one path: Option 1 (Use Preset Voice) – select that group and press Ctrl-B to enable it, then pick a voice in ElevenLabsVoiceSelector. Option 2 (Create a Voice Clone) – enable that group with Ctrl-B and provide a clean voice sample via LoadAudio or record one with RecordAudio, then connect it to ElevenLabsInstantVoiceClone.

Verify the ElevenLabsTextToSpeech node is receiving your script and the chosen voice (from either VoiceSelector or InstantVoiceClone) and is set to the Eleven v4 model. Adjust any exposed settings as needed.
Queue the workflow to generate audio. When it finishes, SaveAudioAdvanced will write a single audio file to your chosen location.
Review the result and iterate: refine tags and punctuation for pacing, try a different preset voice or a cleaner clone sample, and re-run until the delivery fits your project.
suggestedUseCases: Audiobook chapters with nuanced delivery using inline performance tags.
Narration for explainer videos or tutorials with consistent tone and clarity.
Character voiceovers for trailers, game mods, or animatics using instant voice clones.
Podcast intros/outros and show bumpers with repeatable, branded voice.
Corporate training and e-learning narration with controlled pacing and emphasis.

faqItems.question: Do I need an ElevenLabs API key for this workflow?
faqItems.answer: Yes. The ElevenLabs nodes call the ElevenLabs API. Enter your API key in the node or extension settings before running. If you see authentication errors (e.g., 401), re-check the key and your account permissions.

faqItems.question: How do the performance tags work, and why might they seem to have no effect?
faqItems.answer: Eleven v4 treats your text as a performance script. Place tags like [whispers] or [excited] in square brackets immediately before or after the words you want to affect. If the effect seems subtle, move the tag closer to the specific phrase, simplify surrounding punctuation, and ensure the TTS node is using the Eleven v4 model.

faqItems.question: What makes a good sample for Instant Voice Clone?
faqItems.answer: Use a clean, dry recording of a single speaker with minimal background noise and consistent mic distance. Avoid music or heavy processing. You can import a file with LoadAudio or capture a short, clear recording with RecordAudio. Only clone voices you have the legal right and consent to use.

faqItems.question: How do I control the output file format and quality?
faqItems.answer: Use SaveAudioAdvanced to set the filename, location, and available audio parameters such as format and sample rate. If you plan to edit later, choose a higher-quality setting; for quick previews, use a smaller file format if offered.

faqItems.question: Can I generate very long scripts?
faqItems.answer: Long scripts are possible but may be limited by your ElevenLabs plan and request timeouts. For reliability, split long content into sections in the Note/MarkdownNote, render them sequentially, and combine the results in your audio editor.

bddedcf69e58.title: Arrow 2: Image to SVG
bddedcf69e58.description: Converts an image input into an SVG output.
bddedcf69e58.metaDescription: Convert images to SVG in ComfyUI using QuiverImageToSVGNodeV2. A simple, reliable workflow for logos, icons, and flat graphics.
bddedcf69e58.extendedDescription:
Arrow 2: Image to SVG is a minimal, reliable ComfyUI pipeline for converting raster images into clean, scalable vectors. It loads a PNG/JPG with LoadImage, converts it to vector paths via QuiverImageToSVGNodeV2 (model: Quiver), and writes the final .svg with SaveSVGNode. The result is an SVG file you can scale without quality loss, edit in vector tools, and embed on the web.

Technically, QuiverImageToSVGNodeV2 analyzes edges and regions in the bitmap to generate Bézier path data suitable for an SVG document. You can balance fidelity and file size by adjusting the node’s available controls (e.g., detail/complexity and smoothing, if exposed in your install). This workflow excels on logos, icons, flat illustrations, and high‑contrast artwork; complex photographs will be simplified into broader shapes. Because it’s a compact three-node chain, it’s also easy to script or batch through the ComfyUI API when you need repeatable vectorization at scale.
howToUse: Load the workflow into ComfyUI and confirm the QuiverImageToSVGNodeV2 node is available (install the Quiver package if it’s missing, then restart ComfyUI).
Open the LoadImage node and select your source image (PNG or JPG). For best results, start with clean, high-contrast artwork and minimal noise.

Select QuiverImageToSVGNodeV2 and, if your build exposes options, adjust detail/complexity and smoothing to balance accuracy with SVG simplicity. Higher detail yields more paths and larger files; lower detail simplifies shapes.
In SaveSVGNode, set the output directory and filename for the .svg. Decide on a naming scheme if you plan to batch multiple images.
Queue and run the workflow. When it finishes, open the SVG in a viewer or vector editor (e.g., Inkscape, Illustrator) to inspect the paths.
Iterate as needed: if the SVG is too noisy, reduce detail or pre-clean the source (crop, increase contrast, remove background); if it’s too simple, increase detail and re-run.
suggestedUseCases: Rebuilding logos and icons as crisp, scalable vectors for responsive web and print.
Converting flat illustrations or UI glyphs into editable SVGs for design systems.
Preparing cut-ready vectors for vinyl cutters or laser engravers that accept SVG.
Vectorizing hand-drawn or scanned line art for further refinement in a vector editor.
Creating lightweight, infinitely scalable graphics for slide decks and infographics.

faqItems.question: What kinds of images produce the best SVG results?
faqItems.answer: Logos, icons, flat illustrations, and high-contrast artwork work best. Photos or highly textured images will be simplified into larger shapes. For single-color output, start with a monochrome or high-contrast source.

faqItems.question: Will colors be preserved in the SVG?
faqItems.answer: The node outputs multi-path SVGs. Color handling depends on your image and the node’s available settings in your install. If you need a single-color result, pre-process the source (e.g., threshold to black and white) before vectorization.

faqItems.question: My SVG is too heavy or looks noisy. How can I optimize it?
faqItems.answer: Lower the node’s detail/complexity, increase smoothing if available, and clean the source (remove background, crop, boost contrast). After export, you can further simplify paths in a vector editor or run the SVG through an optimizer to reduce file size.

faqItems.question: I see a missing model or node error. How do I fix it?
faqItems.answer: Ensure the Quiver package that provides QuiverImageToSVGNodeV2 is installed and the Quiver model is available. Restart ComfyUI after installation and verify the node names in your workflow match the installed nodes.

be07722555ff.title: Flux.1 Outpaint
be07722555ff.description: Extend images beyond boundaries using Flux.1 outpainting.
be07722555ff.metaDescription: Extend images beyond boundaries with Flux.1 Outpaint in ComfyUI. Perfect for creating larger scenes and enhancing image contexts.
be07722555ff.extendedDescription:
The Flux.1 Outpaint workflow in ComfyUI is designed to extend images beyond their original boundaries, a process known as outpainting. This technique is particularly useful for enhancing images by adding context or creating a larger scene from an existing image. The workflow utilizes several key nodes and models, including the Flux.1 model for outpainting, which is guided by the FluxGuidance node. The process begins with loading the necessary models and the image to be outpainted, followed by padding the image using the ImagePadForOutpaint node to prepare it for expansion. The KSampler node is then used to iteratively generate new image sections, while the VAEDecode and UNETLoader nodes work together to ensure the generated content blends seamlessly with the original image.

This workflow is particularly useful because it leverages advanced AI models to maintain the aesthetic and thematic consistency of the original image while expanding its boundaries. The use of the CLIPTextEncode node allows for the incorporation of textual prompts, guiding the outpainting process to align with specific themes or styles. This makes the workflow versatile for various applications, from artistic image creation to practical uses in design and media production.
howToUse: Load the Flux.1 Outpaint workflow in ComfyUI.
Import the image you wish to extend using the LoadImage node.
Ensure the necessary models are loaded, including Flux.1 and related text encoders.
Use the ImagePadForOutpaint node to prepare the image for outpainting.
Run the workflow to generate the extended image using KSampler and VAEDecode nodes.
Save the final outpainted image with the SaveImage node.
suggestedUseCases: Enhancing landscape photography by extending horizons.
Creating panoramic images from standard-sized photos.
Adding contextual elements to product images for marketing.
Expanding artwork for digital displays or print media.
Generating immersive backgrounds for virtual environments.

faqItems.question: What is outpainting?
faqItems.answer: Outpainting is the process of extending an image beyond its original boundaries by generating new content that blends seamlessly with the existing image.

faqItems.question: Do I need specific hardware to run this workflow?
faqItems.answer: While no specific hardware is required, a GPU with sufficient VRAM will significantly speed up the processing time and improve performance.

faqItems.question: Can I control the style of the outpainted area?
faqItems.answer: Yes, you can guide the style of the outpainted area using textual prompts via the CLIPTextEncode node to influence the thematic outcome.

faqItems.question: Is this workflow suitable for all types of images?
faqItems.answer: The workflow is best suited for images where the context can be naturally extended, such as landscapes or abstract art, but may require adjustments for complex or highly detailed images.

be0889296f65.title: VFX Utilities
be0889296f65.description: Generate production-ready VFX utility passes from any image or plate in seconds. This workflow creates alphas, depth, and normal maps using prompt-based and point-based segmentation, giving you the core tools for relighting, compositing, and look development without needing a full CG render.

be81dd6a1a51.title: Qwen Image Edit
be81dd6a1a51.description: Edit images with precise bilingual text editing and dual semantic/appearance editing capabilities using Qwen-Image-Edit's 20B MMDiT model.
be81dd6a1a51.metaDescription: Edit images with bilingual text and dual semantic/appearance capabilities using Qwen-Image-Edit's 20B MMDiT model for precise results.
be81dd6a1a51.extendedDescription: The Qwen Image Edit workflow is designed to provide precise and versatile image editing capabilities, leveraging the power of the Qwen-Image-Edit's 20B MMDiT model. This workflow allows users to perform bilingual text editing and dual semantic/appearance editing on images, making it a powerful tool for both creative and practical applications. By incorporating nodes such as SaveImage, LoadImage, and ImageScaleToTotalPixels, the workflow ensures that images are processed efficiently without compromising on quality. The MarkdownNote node provides a convenient way to annotate and document your editing process, enhancing the workflow's usability. This workflow is particularly useful for users who need to edit images with specific text requirements or who wish to alter the semantic content and appearance of images simultaneously.
howToUse: Load the Qwen Image Edit workflow in ComfyUI.
Import your image using the LoadImage node.
Adjust the image size with the ImageScaleToTotalPixels node to ensure optimal processing.
Use the Qwen-Image-Edit node to apply bilingual text and semantic/appearance edits.
Review and document your changes using the MarkdownNote node.
Save the edited image with the SaveImage node.
suggestedUseCases: Creating bilingual marketing materials with precise text placement.
Editing product images to change both appearance and semantic content for e-commerce.
Designing educational content that requires dual language support.
Enhancing social media posts with tailored text and visual edits.
Developing creative projects that involve complex image transformations.

faqItems.question: What is the Qwen-Image-Edit model used for?
faqItems.answer: The Qwen-Image-Edit model is used for precise bilingual text editing and dual semantic/appearance editing in images, leveraging a 20B MMDiT model for high-quality results.

faqItems.question: How can I ensure optimal image processing?
faqItems.answer: Use the ImageScaleToTotalPixels node to adjust the image size, preventing poor output results from excessively large input images.

faqItems.question: Can I document my editing process?
faqItems.answer: Yes, the MarkdownNote node allows you to annotate and document your editing process within the workflow.

faqItems.question: Is this workflow suitable for social media content creation?
faqItems.answer: Absolutely, the workflow's ability to edit both text and appearance makes it ideal for creating engaging and tailored social media content.

bea767ed39db.title: Topaz: Image Enhance Wonder 3.5
bea767ed39db.description: Upscale and enhance a single image using Topaz's Wonder 3.5 generative model, which adds fine detail, reduces noise, and sharpens text and structured graphics while offering Low, Medium, and High enhancement strengths. The workflow takes 1 input image and produces 1 enhanced output alongside a side-by-side comparison view. Ideal for restoring old or compressed photos, improving product shots and marketing visuals, and preparing low-resolution images for print or large-format display.
bea767ed39db.metaDescription: Compare Topaz Wonder 3.5 Low, Medium, and High enhancement strengths side-by-side to choose the best balance of detail, noise, and text clarity.
bea767ed39db.extendedDescription:
This workflow compares an original image against a Topaz Wonder 3.5–enhanced result using a simple, controlled A/B setup. The LoadImage node provides the source, TopazImageEnhanceV2 applies Wonder 3.5 with a selectable enhancement strength (Low, Medium, or High), and ImageCompare renders a side-by-side view so you can judge fine detail, noise handling, and text/edge clarity. SaveImageAdvanced captures outputs so you can review results across runs.

Methodologically, you hold the model and input constant and vary only the enhancement strength across sequential runs. Low generally preserves natural texture and grain while reducing noise modestly; Medium aims for a balanced boost in detail and denoising; High pushes aggressive detail synthesis, stronger sharpening, and more assertive noise removal. Expect sharper text and structured graphics at higher strengths, but watch for oversharpening, altered grain, or fabricated micro-texture—especially on skin and smooth gradients. Use the A/B view to decide which trade-off best suits your subject and output requirements.
howToUse: Load your source image with the LoadImage node.
Open TopazImageEnhanceV2 and confirm the Wonder 3.5 model is selected; choose an enhancement strength (Low, Medium, or High).
Run the workflow. Use ImageCompare to review the original versus the enhanced output at 100% zoom and at the target display/print size.
Save the result with SaveImageAdvanced, adding the chosen strength to the filename or subfolder for easy tracking.
Repeat the run with a different strength using the same input. Save each version with a clear label (e.g., _low, _medium, _high).
Evaluate trade-offs: check text legibility, edge halos, skin texture, noise patterns, and any signs of fabricated detail. Select the setting that fits your use case.
suggestedUseCases: Photo restoration: find the strength that cleans compression noise while preserving film grain and natural skin texture.
E-commerce/product shots: balance crisp edges and label/text clarity without introducing sharpening halos.
Large-format print and signage: push detail and text sharpness as far as acceptable for viewing distance.
UI screenshots, documents, and technical diagrams: maximize legibility of small text and thin lines.
Upscaling social or web-compressed images: recover detail while preventing plastic or overprocessed looks.

faqItems.question: What exactly is being compared in this workflow?
faqItems.answer: You compare the original image against an enhanced/upscaled version produced by Topaz Wonder 3.5, varying only the enhancement strength (Low, Medium, High) across sequential runs to see how detail, noise, and text clarity change.

faqItems.question: How do Low, Medium, and High strengths differ in practice?
faqItems.answer: Low makes subtle, conservative changes that preserve texture and grain while reducing noise. Medium aims for a balanced increase in detail and sharper edges. High applies the strongest denoise/sharpen/detail synthesis, which can boost text and structured graphics but may introduce oversharpening or invented micro-texture on some photos.

faqItems.question: How can I ensure a fair, repeatable comparison?
faqItems.answer: Keep the input image and model constant, change only the strength, and review outputs at the same zoom level. Save each result with a strength label using SaveImageAdvanced so you can compare versions consistently and revisit choices later.

faqItems.question: Can I compare all three strengths side-by-side at once?
faqItems.answer: By default, the workflow compares original vs enhanced for a single strength. To view all three simultaneously, run and save each strength sequentially, then compare the saved files in your viewer. If you want a multi-branch comparison inside ComfyUI, duplicate the TopazImageEnhanceV2 branch and add additional ImageCompare nodes.

bed989744195.title: Video Face Swap
bed989744195.description: The best open source video face swap workflow. Upload a driving video and a picture of your characters face. This LTX 2.3 lora was trained by @Alissonerdx.
bed989744195.metaDescription: ComfyUI video face swap with LTX 2.3 LoRA. Load a video and face image, stabilize with ReservedRegionFrameComposer, and export via VHS_VideoCombine.
bed989744195.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow performs a video face swap by applying a single reference face image to every frame of a driving video, then recombining the frames into a final clip. The pipeline starts with VHS_LoadVideo to decode the source video into frames and LoadImage to bring in your reference face. A custom face-swap node (dc72113f-8276-4a5a-af12-85d6bec89ed5) drives the actual face transfer using the LTX 2.3 LoRA trained by @Alissonerdx. PrimitiveFloat and PrimitiveInt nodes expose key controls (such as effect strength, region size, or frame step), while ImageResizeKJv2 aligns the reference face scale to your target footage.

To stabilize results and keep the background intact, the workflow composites the generated face back onto each original frame with ReservedRegionFrameComposer. This node lets you define a consistent “reserved” region for the face and blend it with feathered edges, reducing temporal jitter and preserving hair, lighting, and scene motion. ComfyMathExpression is used to derive dynamic values (for example, region size from video resolution), keeping settings in sync with whatever you load. For quality checks, ImageConcanate can assemble side-by-side previews of original vs. swapped frames. Finally, the processed frames are encoded to a video using VHS_VideoCombine or CreateVideo, and the result is written out with SaveVideo.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI. Ensure Video Helper Suite nodes are installed (VHS_LoadVideo, VHS_VideoCombine) and place the LTX 2.3 LoRA file in ComfyUI/models/loras. Restart ComfyUI so nodes and models are detected.
Connect your inputs: point VHS_LoadVideo to your driving video and LoadImage to a clear, front-facing reference image. Verify the video resolution/FPS in the VHS_LoadVideo node preview or metadata.

Set alignment and region: use ImageResizeKJv2 to roughly match the reference face size to the target face. In ReservedRegionFrameComposer, adjust the face region position/size and feather so the new face sits naturally and blends smoothly with the original frame.

Tune effect intensity: adjust any PrimitiveFloat/PrimitiveInt controls exposed for LoRA strength, blend/opacity, or frame step. ComfyMathExpression values can help keep region scaling proportional to the video resolution.
Preview a short segment: queue a small frame range to confirm alignment and blending. Use ImageConcanate to compare original vs. swapped frames and refine region size, feather, or strength if needed.

Export the final video: run the full queue to process all frames, then combine them with VHS_VideoCombine or CreateVideo. Save the output with SaveVideo. If you need original audio, configure VHS_VideoCombine to mux audio or add it afterward in a video editor.
suggestedUseCases: Character continuity for talking-head or interview content while preserving the original performance and timing.
Previsualization and animatics where you need to test different actors or characters in existing footage.
Privacy-friendly edits by swapping identifiable faces with a consented or generic face for internal reviews.
Meme and remix videos with side-by-side comparisons using ImageConcanate for quick iterations.
Brand/influencer content where a consistent on-screen identity is needed across varied source clips.

faqItems.question: What models or add-ons do I need to run this workflow?
faqItems.answer: Install Video Helper Suite (for VHS_LoadVideo and VHS_VideoCombine) and place the LTX 2.3 LoRA by @Alissonerdx into ComfyUI/models/loras. The custom face-swap node (dc72113f-8276-4a5a-af12-85d6bec89ed5) applies the LoRA during inference, so you don’t need to manually add samplers in this template.

faqItems.question: How do I reduce flicker or a “swimming” face across frames?
faqItems.answer: Keep the ReservedRegionFrameComposer region stable around the target face and increase feathering for smoother edges. Use a high-quality, front-facing reference image with similar lighting to the driving video. Avoid aggressive frame skipping; process every frame for best temporal consistency.

faqItems.question: Can I keep the original audio from the driving video?
faqItems.answer: Yes, route frames through VHS_VideoCombine and enable or supply the original audio if the node configuration supports it. If your setup doesn’t mux audio in ComfyUI, export the video and add audio back in a video editor.

faqItems.question: What should I do if the face is misaligned or too big/small?
faqItems.answer: Adjust the region size/position in ReservedRegionFrameComposer and rescale the reference face with ImageResizeKJv2. Use PrimitiveFloat/PrimitiveInt controls (and ComfyMathExpression where provided) to keep the region proportional to the video resolution, then preview a short segment before exporting.

bf82f1e42e83.title: HY 3D 2.1
bf82f1e42e83.description: Generate 3D models from single images using Hunyuan3D 2.1.
bf82f1e42e83.metaDescription: Convert 2D images to 3D models with the HY 3D 2.1 workflow using Hunyuan3D 2.1 for detailed and efficient 3D rendering.
bf82f1e42e83.extendedDescription:
The HY 3D 2.1 workflow is designed to transform single 2D images into detailed 3D models using the Hunyuan3D 2.1 model by Tencent. This workflow leverages a series of specialized nodes to process an image and convert it into a 3D mesh. The process begins with the 'ImageOnlyCheckpointLoader' and 'LoadImage' nodes, which prepare the image for 3D transformation. The 'ModelSamplingAuraFlow' node then applies the Hunyuan3D model to generate a latent representation of the image in 3D space. This latent data is further processed by the 'EmptyLatentHunyuan3Dv2' and 'Hunyuan3Dv2Conditioning' nodes to refine the 3D structure.

The workflow continues with the 'KSampler' node, which samples the latent data to ensure the 3D model is as detailed and accurate as possible. The 'VAEDecodeHunyuan3D' node decodes this sampled data into a voxel representation, which is then converted into a mesh using the 'VoxelToMesh' node. Finally, the 'SaveGLB' node exports the 3D model in GLB format, ready for use in various applications. This workflow is particularly useful for artists and developers looking to create 3D content from existing 2D assets, offering a streamlined process that minimizes manual modeling efforts.
howToUse: Load the HY 3D 2.1 workflow in ComfyUI.
Use the 'ImageOnlyCheckpointLoader' node to load the Hunyuan3D 2.1 model.
Upload your 2D image using the 'LoadImage' node.
Initiate the model processing with the 'ModelSamplingAuraFlow' node.
Refine and sample the 3D model using 'KSampler' and 'VAEDecodeHunyuan3D' nodes.
Export the final 3D model using the 'SaveGLB' node.
suggestedUseCases: Creating 3D assets for video games from concept art.
Generating 3D models for virtual reality environments.
Developing 3D printable objects from 2D designs.
Producing 3D visualizations for architectural projects.
Enhancing digital marketing materials with 3D imagery.

faqItems.question: What type of images work best with this workflow?
faqItems.answer: High-resolution images with clear details and defined edges are ideal for generating accurate 3D models.

faqItems.question: Can I use this workflow for commercial projects?
faqItems.answer: Yes, as long as you comply with the licensing terms of the Hunyuan3D model and any other resources used.

faqItems.question: What file format is the final 3D model saved in?
faqItems.answer: The final 3D model is saved in the GLB format, which is widely supported for 3D applications.

faqItems.question: Do I need any prior 3D modeling experience to use this workflow?
faqItems.answer: No prior 3D modeling experience is required. The workflow is designed to be user-friendly and intuitive.

bfba92751be8.title: 2.2 Creator - Diffusion Guidance
bfba92751be8.description: Learn how to guide diffusion for precise image editing with inpainting and controlnet using Z Image Turbo.
bfba92751be8.metaDescription: Guide diffusion for precise image editing using inpainting and ControlNet with Z Image Turbo in ComfyUI.
bfba92751be8.extendedDescription:
The '2.2 Creator - Diffusion Guidance' workflow in ComfyUI is designed to enhance image editing precision by integrating inpainting and ControlNet techniques. At the core of this workflow is the Z Image Turbo model, which facilitates efficient and accurate diffusion processes. The workflow employs a variety of nodes, such as CLIPLoader and VAELoader, to load and process images, while nodes like DifferentialDiffusion and InpaintModelConditioning are used to guide the diffusion process with spatially varying changes. This makes it particularly useful for tasks that require detailed image editing without the need for model retraining.

The workflow leverages ControlNet to provide structural guidance, such as canny edges or depth maps, to ensure that the diffusion process adheres to desired structural elements. This is achieved through nodes like ZImageFunControlnet and Controlnet Preprocessor. By using per-pixel 'strength' maps, the workflow allows for smooth and gradual changes, making it ideal for applications that demand high precision and control, such as inpainting specific image areas while maintaining the integrity of the surrounding context.
howToUse: Load the '2.2 Creator - Diffusion Guidance' workflow in ComfyUI.
Use the LoadImage node to import the image you wish to edit.
Right-click on the Load Image node and select 'Open in Mask Editor' to create a mask over the area you want to inpaint.
Configure the ControlNet Preprocessor to extract necessary features like edges or depth for guidance.
Adjust the KSampler and ModelSamplingAuraFlow settings to fine-tune the inpainting strength and diffusion process.
Run the workflow to apply the guided diffusion and save the edited image using the SaveImage node.
suggestedUseCases: Enhancing portraits by editing specific facial features while preserving the overall look.
Restoring old photographs by inpainting damaged areas with high precision.
Creating artistic effects by selectively altering parts of an image.
Generating variations of an image with controlled structural changes.
Improving image compositions by seamlessly integrating new elements.

faqItems.question: What is the role of the ControlNet in this workflow?
faqItems.answer: ControlNet provides structural guidance to the diffusion process by using features like edges or depth maps to guide the image editing, ensuring that the changes adhere to desired structural elements.

faqItems.question: How does Differential Diffusion enhance inpainting?
faqItems.answer: Differential Diffusion uses per-pixel 'strength' maps to apply smooth, gradual, and spatially varying changes, allowing for precise inpainting without retraining the model.

faqItems.question: Can I use this workflow for batch processing?
faqItems.answer: While this workflow is primarily designed for single-image editing, you can adapt it for batch processing by automating the image loading and mask creation steps.

faqItems.question: What are the recommended settings for KSampler during inpainting?
faqItems.answer: For inpainting, it is recommended to set the KSampler denoise parameter between 0.5 and 1.0, and the ModelSampling shift between 3.0 and 10.0, depending on the desired level of detail and smoothness.

bff96549e689.title: Meshy T2.5: Text to Model (Smart Topology)
bff96549e689.description: Generate a game-ready 3D model from a text prompt with Meshy T2.5. Meshy T2.5 builds the mesh at the triangle budget you set instead of generating a dense mesh and retopologizing it afterwards, so the result drops straight into a game engine. No input files required. Ideal for props, environment dressing and low-poly game assets that need a predictable triangle count.
bff96549e689.metaDescription: Generate game-ready 3D models from text with Meshy T2.5 Smart Topology in ComfyUI. Set a triangle budget and export GLB—no retopology or input files required.
bff96549e689.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI tutorial workflow shows how to generate a game-ready 3D asset directly from a text prompt using Meshy T2.5 Smart Topology. The core of the graph is the MeshyTextToModelSmartTopologyNode, which sends your prompt and a target_polycount to Meshy’s API and returns a mesh that’s built to approximately that triangle budget from the start. Because the topology is planned during generation, you skip the usual high-poly-to-retopo pipeline and get an asset you can drop straight into an engine.

Technically, the node produces a mesh payload that flows into SaveGLB, which writes a .glb file to disk. The MarkdownNote node embeds inline guidance inside the workflow so you can quickly recall best practices. With no input images or reference files required, this setup is ideal for props, environment dressing, and low‑poly game assets where a predictable triangle count matters.
howToUse: Load the workflow JSON in ComfyUI (Drag-and-drop the .json file into the canvas or use the Load button).
Open the MeshyTextToModelSmartTopologyNode and paste your Meshy API key if required by your setup (or ensure it’s configured globally).
Enter a clear text prompt describing the object (shape, materials, style) and set target_polycount to your desired triangle budget (e.g., 2,000 for mobile props, 10,000 for hero props).
Optionally refine the prompt for constraints like “single closed mesh,” “no base/stand,” or “low-poly, clean edges” to guide topology and silhouette.
Click Queue Prompt to run. The node will contact the Meshy T2.5 Smart Topology model; generation time depends on complexity and queue.
When complete, the SaveGLB node writes the result to the configured path. Import the .glb into Blender, Unity, or Unreal and verify scale, orientation, and shading.
suggestedUseCases: Low-poly game props for mobile and VR where a strict triangle budget is required.
Environment dressing assets (crates, barrels, signage, foliage clumps) with predictable performance costs.
Rapid prototyping and grayboxing—fast placeholders that are already engine-ready.
Stylized asset packs that must maintain consistent topology density across a scene.
Educational demos to teach budget-aware modeling workflows without manual retopology.

faqItems.question: What does target_polycount control?
faqItems.answer: It sets the approximate number of triangles in the final mesh. Meshy T2.5 Smart Topology builds topology to that budget during generation, so the output is close to your target and ready for real-time use. If you need more detail, increase the value; for leaner assets, decrease it.

faqItems.question: Do I need input images or a base mesh?
faqItems.answer: No. This workflow is text-to-3D only. Provide a descriptive prompt, and the MeshyTextToModelSmartTopologyNode generates the model. If you require highly specific forms, include precise shape cues and materials in the prompt.

faqItems.question: What format is exported, and will materials be included?
faqItems.answer: The SaveGLB node writes a .glb file. GLB supports embedded materials and textures; any materials returned by Meshy will be saved with the model. You can import the GLB directly into Blender, Unity, or Unreal.

faqItems.question: Can I get all-quad topology or exact triangle counts?
faqItems.answer: Outputs are triangle-based and budget-aware, not all-quad. The triangle count is approximate—expect small variances. If you need strict quad topology, retopologize the result in a DCC tool after import.

faqItems.question: My asset’s scale or orientation seems off—what should I do?
faqItems.answer: GLB import settings vary by tool. If scale or axis orientation isn’t what you expect, adjust on import (unit scale, up-axis) or apply transforms after loading. Most DCCs and engines provide import presets to standardize this.

c0198b907108.title: FireRed Image Edit 1.1: Image Edit
c0198b907108.description: Upload an image and a text prompt to edit it. Generate a modified image with enhanced identity consistency, multi-element fusion, or professional photo restoration.
c0198b907108.metaDescription: Edit images with FireRed Image Edit 1.1 for enhanced identity consistency and professional restoration using AI-driven text prompts.
