cc1f3ddd8be3.title: Layer Decomposition: Qwen-Image-Layered
cc1f3ddd8be3.description: Decompose an image into editable RGBA layers for high-fidelity recolor, replace, resize, and reposition workflows using Qwen-Image-Layered.
cc1f3ddd8be3.metaDescription: Decompose images into editable RGBA layers in ComfyUI with Qwen-Image-Layered for precise recolor, replace, resize, and reposition workflows.
cc1f3ddd8be3.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI tutorial workflow demonstrates how to decompose any input image into clean, editable RGBA layers using the Qwen-Image-Layered model. It routes your image through LoadImage and ImageScaleToMaxDimension to normalize size (640 px recommended, 1024 px for higher fidelity), then passes the scaled image into a pair of custom nodes (IDs f754a936-daaf-4b6e-9658-41fdc54d301d and 1ea4fa01-a81b-4420-a03c-f60019e69a92) that run Qwen-Image-Layered to infer object-level mattes and produce a stack of per-part layers with alpha. A PrimitiveStringMultiline node optionally supplies a brief text description of the scene to bias or name the resulting layers, and SaveImage writes out the individual PNGs (with transparency) plus any previews to your ComfyUI/output folder. MarkdownNote nodes in the graph provide quick inline tips and links, and the core logic is packaged as a reusable Subgraph so you can drop the layer-extraction block into other pipelines (recolor, background replace, resize/reposition, etc.).

Technically, the model isolates semantic regions and edge-accurate mattes, returning one RGBA image per detected part along with masks. The custom Qwen-Image-Layered nodes handle inference and post-processing: the first applies the model to the scaled input, while the second organizes outputs into clean layers ready for downstream editing. For best results, keep inputs at or below 640 px on the longest side to balance quality and speed; 1024 px yields crisper edges at a noticeable runtime cost. If your node exposes sampler-like controls, the default steps=50 and CFG=4.0 are tuned for stable mask quality—raising steps improves separation fidelity but will increase runtime substantially. The result is a practical, repeatable way to recolor, replace, resize, and reposition elements non-destructively across design, product, and video workflows.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and verify required models/custom nodes are installed. Update ComfyUI to the latest version and ensure the Qwen-Image-Layered weights are available.
Open the LoadImage node and select your source image. Use ImageScaleToMaxDimension to set the longest side to 640 px (recommended) or 1024 px for higher-res results.
Optionally add a short scene description in the PrimitiveStringMultiline node (e.g., "red sneakers on white background, laces, sole, logo") to guide layer naming/separation.

Inspect the Qwen-Image-Layered subgraph (nodes f754a936-daaf-4b6e-9658-41fdc54d301d and 1ea4fa01-a81b-4420-a03c-f60019e69a92). If exposed, keep steps at 50 and CFG at 4.0 for balanced quality/speed; raise steps for cleaner edges if needed.
Run the workflow. The model will decompose the image into RGBA layers and masks. SaveImage will output per-layer PNGs (with alpha) and any previews to ComfyUI/output.
Open the exported PNG layers in your editor (Photoshop, Figma, After Effects, etc.) to recolor, replace backgrounds, resize, or reposition elements non-destructively.
suggestedUseCases: E-commerce product workflows: isolate components (logo, fabric, sole) for fast recolors and variant generation.
Creative compositing: remove/replace backgrounds and reposition objects while preserving realistic edges and transparency.
Design mockups and packaging: separate labels, caps, and containers for targeted edits without re-masking.

faqItems.answer: Use 640 px on the longest side for a good balance of quality and speed. For sharper edges, use 1024 px, but expect longer processing time and higher VRAM use. The ImageScaleToMaxDimension node in the graph handles this automatically.

faqItems.question: Why is it running slowly, and how do steps/CFG affect results?
faqItems.answer: Qwen-Image-Layered is compute-heavy. If your node exposes sampler-like controls, the defaults (steps: 50, CFG: 4.0) are chosen for stable mattes. Increasing steps can refine edges and separation but will increase runtime, often roughly proportionally. Lower steps to speed up drafts, then raise for a final pass.

faqItems.question: Where do the exported layers go and what format are they?
faqItems.answer: SaveImage writes outputs to ComfyUI/output by default. Each layer is exported as a PNG with an alpha channel (RGBA). Many workflows also include a quick preview image for inspection.

LoadImage nodes bring your still references into the graph, and SaveVideo encodes the generated frames (and accompanying audio from the generator) into a final video file.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and confirm the ByteDance2ReferenceNode is available. Open the graph and locate the LoadImage nodes, the central ByteDance2ReferenceNode, and the SaveVideo node.

Add up to 20 image references using the LoadImage nodes (e.g., character faces, product shots, brand elements). Connect these to the image inputs on ByteDance2ReferenceNode and arrange/label them so key references appear first.

Inside ByteDance2ReferenceNode, add up to 6 motion reference videos and up to 6 audio clips using the node’s media inputs (file pickers or list inputs). Order them to match your intended narrative flow and set per-modality weights to balance identity/style (images), motion (videos), and rhythm/lip-sync (audio).

Set core generation settings in ByteDance2ReferenceNode: target duration between 4–30 seconds, frame rate, resolution, and a fixed seed for repeatability. Start with a moderate resolution and frame rate to preview quickly, then raise them for final output.

Click Queue/Execute to generate a preview. Review character consistency, motion pacing, and audio sync; adjust reference ordering and weights if needed. Reduce conflicts by lowering the influence of competing references or removing outliers.

When satisfied, increase quality (resolution/bitrate/FPS if supported), then use the SaveVideo node to encode the final clip. Choose an output path and ensure SaveVideo receives the generated frames (and the audio stream from ByteDance2ReferenceNode) before rendering.
suggestedUseCases: E-commerce product reels that keep brand colors, logos, and product angles consistent while syncing cuts to a soundtrack.
Character-driven short episodes where a hero’s face and outfit remain stable across shots, with lip-synced dialogue pulled from voice tracks.
Ad montages that borrow motion from reference edits and maintain a unified visual style from a brand moodboard.
Talking-head explainers composed from a small set of portrait photos and a clean voiceover, with natural mouth movements.
Stylistic recaps or teasers that blend archival stills with guiding motion clips and music beats.

faqItems.question: How many references should I start with?
faqItems.answer: Begin with a small, curated set: 3–6 strong images for identity/style, 1–2 motion clips, and a single clean audio track. Add more only if you need additional cues. Too many overlapping references can cause conflicts and visual jitter.

faqItems.question: How do I keep the character consistent throughout the clip?
faqItems.answer: Use clear, front-facing images with consistent lighting and aspect ratio, place your best identity shots early in the list, and increase the image-reference influence in ByteDance2ReferenceNode. Avoid mixing drastically different hairstyles, angles, or outfits unless you intend to change appearance.

faqItems.question: My audio drifts or lip-sync looks off. What can I do?
faqItems.answer: Use a single, clean vocal track without heavy reverb or background music for best lip-sync. Ensure your target duration and FPS match your audio plan; if the audio is longer than the selected duration, trim it to fit. Re-queue with a fixed seed after adjustments for consistent comparisons.

faqItems.question: What affects performance and render time?
faqItems.answer: Resolution, frame rate, duration, and the number of references all increase compute and memory use. For faster previews, lower resolution and FPS, shorten duration, and limit references. When satisfied with motion and sync, scale up quality for the final render.

cd398cebf8f2.title: Chatter Box: Voice Cloning with TTS
cd398cebf8f2.description: Upload a short voice clip and input text to generate new speech in the cloned voice.
cd398cebf8f2.metaDescription: Clone a voice from a short clip and generate new speech using text with the Chatter Box TTS workflow. Simple, efficient voice cloning.
cd398cebf8f2.extendedDescription:
The 'Chatter Box: Voice Cloning with TTS' workflow is designed to clone a voice from a short audio clip and generate new speech using text-to-speech (TTS) technology. This workflow utilizes the Chatter Box model, which is specifically tailored for voice cloning tasks. By leveraging the FL_ChatterboxTTS node, users can input a short voice recording, typically between 5 to 10 seconds, and a text prompt to produce speech in the same voice as the input clip. The process is streamlined and efficient, making it accessible for both technical and non-technical users.

Technically, the workflow begins with the **LoadAudio** node, which ingests the user's audio file. This is followed by the **FL_ChatterboxTTS** node, which processes the audio to identify and replicate the unique characteristics of the voice. The text input is then converted into speech that mimics the original voice. The final output is saved using the **SaveAudioMP3** node, allowing for easy access and sharing. The workflow also includes a **MarkdownNote** node for documentation purposes, ensuring that users can keep track of their inputs and outputs. This workflow is particularly useful for content creators, educators, and developers looking to personalize audio content with minimal effort.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and locate the **LoadAudio** node.
Upload a short voice clip (5-10 seconds) to the **LoadAudio** node.
Enter the desired text in the **FL_ChatterboxTTS** node to generate speech.
Run the workflow to process the audio and text input.
Find the generated speech saved as an MP3 file via the **SaveAudioMP3** node.
Review any notes or instructions in the **MarkdownNote** node for additional guidance.
suggestedUseCases: Creating personalized voiceovers for videos or presentations.
Developing voice-based characters for games or animations.
Producing custom audio messages for automated customer service systems.
Generating unique voice content for podcasts or audiobooks.
Experimenting with voice cloning technology for educational purposes.

faqItems.question: What is the minimum length of the voice clip needed for cloning?
faqItems.answer: A voice clip of 5-10 seconds is typically sufficient for effective voice cloning.

faqItems.question: Can I use this workflow for commercial projects?
faqItems.answer: Yes, as long as you have the rights to use the original voice clip, you can use the generated audio for commercial purposes.

faqItems.question: What file format is the generated audio saved in?
faqItems.answer: The generated audio is saved in MP3 format, making it easy to use and share across various platforms.

faqItems.question: Does this workflow support multiple languages?
faqItems.answer: The workflow can support multiple languages, depending on the capabilities of the Chatter Box model used.

faqItems.question: What types of images can I enhance with this workflow?

faqItems.question: Can I adjust the output size of the enhanced image?

ce8809866ba7.title: Wan Animate 2 Distilled: Motion Transfer
ce8809866ba7.description: Animate a still character using a driving video with Wan Animate 2, transferring motion directly from video frames without any pose extraction or skeleton preprocessing. The output preserves the reference character's identity while generating a fresh background and camera movement from your text prompt. This distilled version delivers efficient, high-fidelity motion generation with strong identity preservation, ideal for motion transfer, action mimicry, and character animation replacement projects.
ce8809866ba7.metaDescription: Animate a still character using Wan Animate 2 by transferring motion from a driving video. No pose extraction; prompt-controlled background; identity preserved.
ce8809866ba7.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI tutorial workflow shows how to animate a still character image using the motion from any driving video with Wan Animate 2. The core "Motion Transfer (Wan Animate 2)" subgraph feeds a reference image (identity) and per-frame motion from a driving clip directly into a Wan-based inference node, transferring movement without any pose/keypoint extraction or skeleton preprocessing. A prompt (PrimitiveStringMultiline) guides background style and camera movement, while identity is preserved from the reference image.

Technically, the pipeline starts with LoadImage (reference) and LoadVideo (driving clip). GetVideoComponents provides FPS and frame count for assembly, and GetImageSize plus ComfyMathExpression help keep dimensions consistent across the graph. The Wan Animate 2 inference path (custom nodes with IDs 11706f8a-428d-4ef9-b24f-863f651c1b0b and 7aac4913-f6e2-463e-9ca4-7f9f18363819 inside the subgraph 79280513-53b2-4417-93f8-f3e116bb6736) generates per-frame images that preserve the character’s look while mimicking the driving motion. Frames are collected via BatchImagesNode, previewed with PreviewAny, and rendered to a video using CreateVideo (syncing FPS from GetVideoComponents) before being written to disk with SaveVideo. This distilled setup is efficient, identity-stable, and ideal for motion transfer, action mimicry, and character replacement work.
howToUse: Open the workflow in ComfyUI and ensure the Wan Animate 2 model is available (see ModelScope/Hugging Face links in the notes). The subgraph named "Motion Transfer (Wan Animate 2)" contains the core inference path.
Load your assets: drop a clean reference character image into the LoadImage node and your driving clip into the LoadVideo node. GetVideoComponents will read FPS and frame count for final assembly.
Set your text prompt in PrimitiveStringMultiline to describe background, lighting, and camera motion. Keep this prompt consistent if you later duplicate the motion subgraph to extend length.

Match sizes: use GetImageSize (from the reference) and any provided ComfyMathExpression to keep width/height consistent across the graph. Aim for an aspect ratio close to the driving video to reduce cropping or stretching.

Run the graph to preview frames in PreviewAny. If the provided subgraph is bypassed, select it and press Ctrl+B to enable. For longer videos, select the "Motion Transfer (Wan Animate 2)" subgraph, press Ctrl+C then Ctrl+Shift+V to duplicate it, and link each subgraph’s image output into the BatchImagesNode in order.
CreateVideo assembles the frames at the driving video’s FPS (from GetVideoComponents), and SaveVideo writes the final MP4. Adjust prompt or size and re-run until you’re satisfied.
suggestedUseCases: Character replacement: Make a mascot or illustrated character replicate a live actor’s movements.
Action mimicry for social clips: Transfer trending dance or sport motions to stylized characters.
Previsualization: Block out motion for animation pitches using a single still reference.
Cosplay/VTuber intros: Animate a static avatar performing specific gestures from a sample video.
Product or brand spots: Bring static brand characters to life for short promotional sequences.

faqItems.question: Which nodes and models does this workflow rely on?
faqItems.answer: It uses LoadImage, LoadVideo, GetVideoComponents, GetImageSize, ComfyMathExpression, BatchImagesNode, PreviewAny, CreateVideo, and SaveVideo. The core is the "Motion Transfer (Wan Animate 2)" subgraph (ID 79280513-53b2-4417-93f8-f3e116bb6736) containing Wan Animate 2 inference nodes (IDs 11706f8a-428d-4ef9-b24f-863f651c1b0b and 7aac4913-f6e2-463e-9ca4-7f9f18363819). Model weights are available via ModelScope or Hugging Face under Comfy-Org/Wan-Animate-2.

faqItems.question: How do I make longer videos if my driving clip is long?
faqItems.answer: ComfyUI’s native loop support is still under review. To extend length, manually duplicate the "Motion Transfer (Wan Animate 2)" subgraph: select it, Ctrl+C, then Ctrl+Shift+V. Ensure each duplicate uses the same prompt and size, and chain each subgraph’s output into BatchImagesNode in sequence. Keep duplicating until you cover your desired duration.

faqItems.question: How do I preserve identity while getting the background I want?
faqItems.answer: Use a clean, high-resolution reference image (clear face, consistent clothing, minimal occlusion). Keep the aspect ratio close to the driving video. Describe only background, lighting, and camera movement in the prompt—avoid text that alters the character’s appearance. This workflow intentionally generates a new background from the prompt; it does not reuse the driving video’s original background.

faqItems.question: Can I keep the original background from the driving video?
faqItems.answer: Not in this distilled setup. Wan Animate 2 generates fresh backgrounds guided by your prompt. To retain the original background, you’d need a compositing step (e.g., segment the generated character and overlay onto the source video) or a modified workflow that performs background/foreground separation.

cea88b0db7a4.title: Seedance2.5 Draft: Text to Video
cea88b0db7a4.description: Generate draft preview videos from text prompts using Seedance 2.5's two-phase draft mode: stage one turns your prompt into a fast, low-cost 480p preview plus a reusable draft task ID, and stage two renders the 1080p final from that ID. Ideal for storyboard testing, rapid creative iteration, and budget-conscious production workflows.
cea88b0db7a4.metaDescription: ComfyUI Seedance 2.5 Draft workflow: iterate fast with 480p text-to-video previews, save the draft task ID, then render the approved concept in 1080p.
cea88b0db7a4.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI tutorial workflow demonstrates Seedance 2.5’s two-phase Draft mode for fast, low-cost text-to-video iteration. In Stage 1, the ByteDance2TextToVideoNode submits your prompt to Seedance in Draft mode to generate a quick 480p preview and returns a reusable draft task_id. The preview is written to disk by SaveVideo, and the task_id is persisted with SaveText so you can finalize the exact same draft later without re-running the creative step. Inline MarkdownNote blocks in the graph outline each stage and what to tweak.

Stage 2 promotes that draft to a full-quality 1080p render using ByteDance2DraftToFinalVideoNode. By feeding it the saved task_id (via a direct connection or by pasting the value), the final pass reproduces the motion and composition you approved in Draft while upgrading resolution and quality. This split keeps ideation inexpensive and fast, then commits compute only when you’re confident—ideal for storyboarding, client reviews, and budget-conscious production. The core nodes used are ByteDance2TextToVideoNode (Draft generation), SaveText (store task_id), ByteDance2DraftToFinalVideoNode (final render from draft), SaveVideo (write preview/final to disk), and MarkdownNote (embedded instructions).
howToUse: Load the Seedance2.5 Draft: Text to Video workflow in ComfyUI. Review the MarkdownNote boxes for an overview of Stage 1 (draft) and Stage 2 (final).

Open the ByteDance2TextToVideoNode in Stage 1. Enter your text prompt and ensure your Seedance/ByteDance API credentials are configured for the node. Adjust any exposed options (e.g., length or aspect) as needed, keeping the node in Draft/preview mode.

Run Stage 1. When it finishes, check the 480p preview saved by the connected SaveVideo node. The node also returns a draft task_id; confirm that SaveText wrote this ID to a file (or copy it from the node’s output).

In Stage 2, supply the same draft task_id to ByteDance2DraftToFinalVideoNode (either via the connection from SaveText or by pasting the ID). Set your output path/filename in the Stage 2 SaveVideo node.
Run Stage 2 to render the 1080p final. When complete, open the saved file from the SaveVideo output path and review the upscale of your approved draft.
Iterate efficiently: if you want creative changes, modify the prompt and re-run Stage 1 to generate a new draft and task_id. Use Stage 2 only to finalize drafts you intend to keep.
suggestedUseCases: Storyboard and pre-visualization: validate pacing, framing, and motion with fast drafts before full-quality delivery.
Client approvals: share low-cost previews for feedback, then finalize only the approved draft with the stored task_id.
A/B prompt testing: compare multiple creative directions in 480p and promote the best to 1080p.
Budget-controlled production: minimize spend by separating ideation (Draft) from high-resolution renders (Final).
Team pipelines: archive draft task_ids with SaveText so producers can finalize selected concepts later without re-running creative generation.

faqItems.question: What is the draft task_id and why is it important?
faqItems.answer: The draft task_id uniquely identifies the Seedance 2.5 draft you generated in Stage 1. Stage 2 uses that ID in ByteDance2DraftToFinalVideoNode to render the exact same draft at 1080p. Keep it saved with SaveText or copy it somewhere safe.

faqItems.question: Do I need a prompt again for Stage 2?
faqItems.answer: No. Stage 2 renders from the draft task_id returned by Stage 1, so you don’t need to re-enter the prompt. If you change the prompt, create a new draft in Stage 1 to get a new task_id.

faqItems.question: Why does my final look slightly different from the preview?
faqItems.answer: The final should match the approved draft’s composition and motion but will be rendered at 1080p. Minor differences can arise from scaling and encoding. If results diverge significantly, confirm you used the correct draft task_id and re-run Stage 2.

faqItems.question: How do I troubleshoot failed final renders?
faqItems.answer: Common causes are an invalid or expired task_id, missing API credentials, or a blocked output path. Verify the task_id saved by SaveText, confirm the ByteDance/Seedance API key is set, and ensure SaveVideo’s directory is writable. If issues persist, regenerate a new draft in Stage 1.

cf1758be4e23.title: Image Upscale: Bria Increase Resolution
cf1758be4e23.description: Upscale any image to higher resolutions using Bria's dedicated resolution enhancement API, which preserves original content without adding new details or regenerating the image. The workflow accepts a single input image and produces one enhanced, higher-resolution output, supporting JPEG and PNG files in RGB, RGBA, or CMYK color modes up to a maximum area of 8192x8192 pixels. Built-in content moderation scans both the input image and generated output to ensure safe, policy-compliant processing. Ideal for preparing images for print, enlarging photos for digital display, or increasing resolution of assets for professional design work.
cf1758be4e23.metaDescription: ComfyUI tutorial: Upscale images with Bria’s resolution enhancement API. Preserve original content, pass moderation, and export clean high-res results.
cf1758be4e23.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI tutorial workflow shows you how to cleanly upscale a single image using Bria’s dedicated resolution enhancement API. The core BriaIncreaseResolution node takes an input from LoadImage, sends it to the Bria API, and returns a higher-resolution version that preserves the original content without inventing new details or regenerating the scene. It supports JPEG and PNG inputs in RGB, RGBA, or CMYK color modes, and enforces a maximum area of 8192×8192 pixels to keep processing fast and reliable. Built-in content moderation checks both the input and the enhanced output for policy compliance before finalizing results.

Technically, the graph is straightforward and focused: LoadImage feeds your source into BriaIncreaseResolution, where you specify your target dimensions or scale within the allowed limits. ImageCompare then places the original and the upscaled image side-by-side so you can evaluate edge fidelity, text clarity, and fine textures at a glance. Finally, SaveImageAdvanced writes the enhanced output with your preferred filename, folder, and format (PNG for lossless graphics and text, JPEG for smaller photo files), making it a practical tool for print prep, large digital displays, and professional design workflows that need reliable resolution increases without stylistic changes.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and open the BriaIncreaseResolution node. Enter your Bria API credentials if required and confirm your connection settings.
Use LoadImage to select your source file (JPEG or PNG). The node accepts RGB, RGBA, or CMYK color modes within the 8192×8192 pixel area limit.
In BriaIncreaseResolution, set your target size (e.g., 2× or a specific width/height). Keep total area under 8192×8192 and maintain aspect ratio to avoid cropping.
Run the graph. The node will process moderation checks on the input and output and then return a higher-resolution image that preserves the original content.
Inspect results with ImageCompare to verify sharpness on edges, text, and fine patterns. If needed, adjust target size and rerun for optimal clarity.
Export using SaveImageAdvanced. Choose output folder, filename, and format (PNG for lossless graphics/text, JPEG for photos) and save your enhanced image.
suggestedUseCases: Preparing photos and graphics for print layouts (posters, brochures, packaging) without stylistic changes.
Upscaling UI assets, app screenshots, and presentations for crisp display on high-resolution screens.
Enhancing e-commerce product images for marketplaces where higher-resolution listings improve clarity.
Resizing brand assets or raster logos for larger placements when vector files aren’t available.

faqItems.question: Does this workflow add new details or change the style of my image?
faqItems.answer: No. The BriaIncreaseResolution node preserves original content and structure. It enhances resolution and clarity without generating new details or altering the image’s style.

faqItems.question: What are the size limits and how should I choose my target resolution?
faqItems.answer: The maximum area is 8192×8192 pixels. Start with moderate increases (e.g., 2×) and check results in ImageCompare. If you hit the area cap or see diminishing returns, reduce the target size.

faqItems.question: Which file formats and color modes are supported?
faqItems.answer: Inputs and outputs support JPEG and PNG in RGB, RGBA, or CMYK. ComfyUI previews are typically sRGB-based; if you work in CMYK for print, verify color appearance after saving and before final production.

faqItems.question: What happens if my image triggers content moderation?
faqItems.answer: The BriaIncreaseResolution node will not produce a final output if moderation flags the content. Adjust the image to meet policy guidelines and rerun the workflow.
