ea8ffaeb75cc.title: Anima Lllite: Image Inpainting
ea8ffaeb75cc.description: Inpaint anime images with Anima LLLite, a lightweight ControlNet variant that applies low-rank corrections for precise mask-based editing. Input 1 image and receive 1 inpainted output plus a comparison view. Ideal for fixing character details, removing unwanted objects from anime scenes, and seamless background restoration.
ea8ffaeb75cc.metaDescription: Compare original vs Anima LLLite anime inpainting. Mask-based edits, optional resize, and a side-by-side view to evaluate seams, lines, and color fidelity.
ea8ffaeb75cc.extendedDescription:
This workflow compares the original anime image to an inpainted result produced by Anima LLLite, a lightweight ControlNet-style module that applies low‑rank corrections for precise, mask‑bounded edits. You load an image, paint a mask over the area to change, and the Anima LLLite node (custom node id: 147b517e-5ea6-4fba-84f7-46851be6e4ce) regenerates only the masked region while preserving surrounding lines, colors, and composition. The ImageCompare node then presents a side‑by‑side view so you can judge seam quality, line fidelity, and color consistency.

Methodologically, the pipeline is straightforward: LoadImage → Painter (draw mask) → MaskPreview (verify coverage) → optional ResizeImageMaskNode (keep oversized inputs within a workable resolution, e.g., near 1024x1024) → Anima LLLite inpaint → SaveImage and ImageCompare. The key differences to look for in the comparison are how tightly the edit stays within the mask, whether anime line art remains crisp at boundaries, and how well textures and shading are reconstructed. Because this is a mask‑driven setup, no text prompt is required; results hinge on mask quality, input resolution, and the anime‑tuned prior in Anima LLLite.
howToUse: Load your anime image with LoadImage. If it’s very large (e.g., >1024x1024), connect ResizeImageMaskNode to downscale both image and mask together.
Use Painter to draw the inpaint mask over the exact region you want to change (details, removals, or fixes). Check coverage in MaskPreview.
Run the Anima LLLite inpaint node (custom id: 147b517e-5ea6-4fba-84f7-46851be6e4ce) to regenerate only the masked area while preserving surrounding content.
Open ImageCompare to review original vs inpainted output. Inspect edges along the mask, line continuity, shading, and color consistency.
If seams or artifacts appear, refine the mask (tighten edges or adjust coverage) and rerun. SaveImage will keep outputs so you can compare iterations.
For large edits, try a smaller mask or split the task into multiple passes, comparing each pass in ImageCompare to maintain stable style and lines.
suggestedUseCases: Fixing character details (eyes, hair strands, accessories) without disturbing nearby line art.
Removing unwanted objects, speech bubbles, or UI elements from anime scenes or frames.
Seamless background restoration after taking out a character or prop.
Touching up color leaks, aliasing, or compression artifacts in localized regions.
Cleaning manga panels while preserving inked lines and screentone boundaries.

faqItems.question: What exactly is being compared in this workflow?
faqItems.answer: The ImageCompare node shows the original input versus the inpainted result from Anima LLLite. You can also iterate with different masks or resolutions and compare saved outputs across runs.

faqItems.question: How does Anima LLLite differ from a full ControlNet inpainting setup?
faqItems.answer: Anima LLLite uses lightweight, low‑rank corrections targeted at anime content, focusing changes inside the mask and nearby boundaries. It aims for efficient, localized edits with strong line preservation, which is often faster and simpler to configure than heavier, full ControlNet stacks.

faqItems.question: When should I use ResizeImageMaskNode, and how does resizing affect results?
faqItems.answer: Use it when your input is oversized (e.g., above ~1024x1024) to keep memory and speed manageable and to maintain stable edits. Resizing can slightly soften fine lines; if that happens, try a modest downscale, inpaint, then upscale after, or run multiple smaller, targeted masks.

faqItems.question: Can I use this on non‑anime photos?
faqItems.answer: It may work, but the model is tuned for anime line art and flat shading. For photoreal images, expect less reliable edge and texture reconstruction; use a photoreal‑oriented inpainting model for best results.

eb2a6b1dc4fa.title: Remove Background: Bria Local
eb2a6b1dc4fa.description: Upload a video to remove the background. Generate a new video with a transparent or solid color background.
eb2a6b1dc4fa.metaDescription: Remove video backgrounds in ComfyUI with BRIA. Load a clip, segment the subject, and export with a transparent or solid color background.
eb2a6b1dc4fa.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow removes video backgrounds using the BRIA model and outputs a clean foreground on either a transparent or solid color background. It chains three core nodes: LoadVideo to ingest your source clip, BriaRemoveVideoBackground to generate a high-quality alpha matte and composite the subject, and SaveVideo to render the final result. The BriaRemoveVideoBackground node performs semantic segmentation on each frame to separate foreground from background and either preserves transparency (alpha channel) or fills the background with a user-selected color.

Technically, the workflow passes decoded frames from LoadVideo into BriaRemoveVideoBackground, which computes a per-frame matte and composites according to your background mode. The processed frames are then passed to SaveVideo to encode the output at your chosen location and container. For transparent outputs, use a video format that supports an alpha channel (e.g., WebM with VP9/alpha, if supported on your system). If alpha isn’t available or you plan to edit further, choose a solid background color that’s easy to key later. This minimal, focused graph is fast to iterate and ideal for quick removals without manual rotoscoping.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and confirm the three nodes are present: LoadVideo → BriaRemoveVideoBackground → SaveVideo.
In LoadVideo, select your input clip. Short, well-lit clips with a clear subject against the background produce the best results.

Open BriaRemoveVideoBackground and choose your background mode: Transparent (alpha) or Solid Color. If Solid Color, set a clean key-friendly color (e.g., pure green or blue). Adjust any available edge/feather or refinement controls to reduce halos.

Configure SaveVideo with an output path and container. For transparency, choose a format that supports alpha (e.g., WebM with VP9/alpha if your ffmpeg build supports it). If alpha isn’t available, export with a solid color background for later keying.
Click Queue Prompt to run the workflow. Monitor progress in the ComfyUI interface; processing time scales with resolution and clip length.
Review the output. If you see edge artifacts or flicker, increase refinement in BriaRemoveVideoBackground, try a simpler solid color, or reduce input resolution for faster iterations.
suggestedUseCases: Social video and shorts: quickly place creators over branded or animated backgrounds.
E-commerce product videos: remove cluttered backgrounds to create clean, consistent catalog visuals.
Marketing explainers: composite presenters onto slides or motion graphics without green screen.
Virtual backdrops: generate transparent cutouts for live overlays or post-production scenes.
App demos and tutorials: isolate hands or devices for focused, distraction-free compositions.

faqItems.question: Does this workflow require the internet or an API key?
faqItems.answer: The “Bria Local” variant is designed to run with locally installed BRIA models. If your BriaRemoveVideoBackground node is configured for API usage, you’ll need a BRIA account and key. Check the node’s settings in your environment to confirm which mode you’re using.

faqItems.question: Which export formats support transparency?
faqItems.answer: MP4 does not support an alpha channel. Use a format that supports transparency, such as WebM with VP9/alpha (if your ffmpeg build and SaveVideo configuration support it). If alpha export isn’t available, set a solid key color and chroma key it in your NLE.

faqItems.question: How can I reduce edge halos and flicker around the subject?
faqItems.answer: Increase mask refinement/feathering in BriaRemoveVideoBackground, avoid low-light or motion-blur-heavy footage, and prefer solid, contrasting backgrounds. If needed, slightly downscale the input to stabilize edges, then upscale after compositing.

faqItems.question: What hardware is recommended for faster processing?
faqItems.answer: A GPU-accelerated setup is recommended for video background removal. On CPU-only systems, expect longer processing times—consider shorter clips or lower resolutions for quicker iterations.

eb53769b541b.title: Seedance 2.0 Mini: Text to Video
eb53769b541b.description: Generate cinematic videos from text prompts with Dreamina’s Seedance 2.0 Mini, supporting AI camera controls and consistent character generation across scenes. This workflow takes only prompt input and produces 1 video output. Ideal for AI filmmaking, branded content creation, and multi-shot storytelling projects.
eb53769b541b.metaDescription: ComfyUI tutorial: Generate cinematic text-to-video with Dreamina’s Seedance 2.0 Mini using ByteDance2TextToVideoNode and SaveVideo, with seeds and AI camera control.
eb53769b541b.extendedDescription:
Seedance 2.0 Mini: Text to Video is a minimal, focused ComfyUI workflow that turns a plain-language prompt into a finished video in one pass. It centers on a single generation node—ByteDance2TextToVideoNode—to call Dreamina’s Seedance 2.0 Mini API, and a SaveVideo node to write the result to disk. Because generation happens via API, your local machine mainly handles orchestration and saving, not heavy rendering. The node accepts your text prompt and key generation settings (such as duration, aspect ratio/resolution, FPS, and seed) and returns a ready-to-save clip.

Technically, the ByteDance2TextToVideoNode encapsulates model inference: it submits your prompt and parameters to Seedance 2.0 Mini, which handles motion, subject fidelity, and scene composition. The model supports AI camera behavior (e.g., dolly, pan, orbit-like motion) through prompt cues and/or any dedicated camera fields exposed by the node. For character continuity across multiple shots, keep a stable character description and reuse the same seed between runs. The downstream SaveVideo node then encodes the returned video stream to a file format supported by your ComfyUI/FFmpeg setup, typically MP4 or WebM.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI. Confirm the graph contains ByteDance2TextToVideoNode feeding into SaveVideo.
Open ByteDance2TextToVideoNode and enter your API credentials if required by your setup (key/token or environment config).
Write a clear text prompt describing subject, setting, mood, and motion. Add camera cues (e.g., “slow dolly in,” “orbiting shot”) in the prompt or any camera-specific fields provided by the node.
Set core parameters: duration (seconds), FPS, resolution/aspect ratio, and a seed. Use the same seed and consistent character description to maintain identity across multiple runs.
Optionally refine with negative cues (if the node exposes a negative prompt or quality controls) to avoid unwanted artifacts. Keep wording concise and specific.
In SaveVideo, choose the output filename/path and desired container if available. Queue the workflow. Review the result; iterate by adjusting the prompt, camera cues, or seed for refinements.
suggestedUseCases: AI filmmaking previsualization: block shots, test camera moves, and establish tone before full production.
Branded content drafts: quickly generate product hero shots with controlled camera motion and consistent brand characters.
Storyboarding and animatics: produce short animated beats from text to communicate pacing and scene transitions.
Social media clips: turn concise prompts into loopable visuals for posts, teasers, or mood pieces.

faqItems.question: How do I keep a character consistent across multiple shots?
faqItems.answer: Use a stable, detailed character description (e.g., clothing, age, style) and reuse the same seed value in ByteDance2TextToVideoNode across runs. Keep your wording and aspect ratio consistent between shots to reduce drift.

faqItems.question: Where do I control the camera movement?
faqItems.answer: Add camera directions to your prompt (e.g., “handheld close-up,” “slow dolly-in,” “360° orbit”) and use any camera-related fields exposed by ByteDance2TextToVideoNode if available. Seedance 2.0 Mini interprets these cues to drive AI camera behavior.

faqItems.question: What video formats can I save?
faqItems.answer: SaveVideo writes the returned clip to disk using your ComfyUI/FFmpeg setup. Common outputs are MP4 or WebM. Choose the filename/extension in SaveVideo and ensure FFmpeg is installed for MP4.

faqItems.question: Are there limits on duration, resolution, or FPS?
faqItems.answer: Yes—limits depend on the Seedance 2.0 Mini API and the parameters exposed by ByteDance2TextToVideoNode, as well as your API plan. Check your node’s tooltips and the provider’s documentation for current caps and pricing.

eb5de47381db.title: Video Upscale: HitPaw
eb5de47381db.description: Upload a video to enhance and upscale. Generate a restored output with improved clarity, temporal stability, and optional portrait enhancement.
eb5de47381db.metaDescription: ComfyUI tutorial: upscale and restore videos with HitPaw. Improve clarity, reduce flicker, and optionally enhance portraits using a simple 3-node workflow.
eb5de47381db.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow upscales and restores videos using HitPaw’s video enhancement model. It’s built around three nodes: LoadVideo ingests your source clip and exposes frame sequence, resolution, and FPS; HitPawVideoEnhance applies temporal-aware super-resolution and restoration across frames; and SaveVideo encodes the enhanced frames back into a single video file. The HitPawVideoEnhance node focuses on clarity, de-noising, and temporal stability to reduce flicker between frames, with an optional portrait enhancement mode for sharper faces and skin details.

Technically, the pipeline maintains your video’s frame order and timing from LoadVideo, processes each frame with the HitPaw model while using temporal cues to keep details consistent across adjacent frames, then hands the improved sequence to SaveVideo for export. Because the restoration is temporal-aware, you can upscale aggressively (e.g., 2x–4x) while keeping motion smooth and avoiding per-frame shimmer. The result is a higher-resolution, cleaner clip that’s especially effective for people-focused content, archival footage, and general upscaling without introducing noticeable flicker.
howToUse: Load the workflow JSON in ComfyUI and confirm the three-node chain: LoadVideo → HitPawVideoEnhance → SaveVideo.
Open LoadVideo and select your source clip. Verify the detected FPS and resolution so you know the baseline before upscaling.
Configure HitPawVideoEnhance: choose your upscale factor (e.g., 2x or 4x), enable portrait enhancement if the video features faces, and keep temporal/stability options enabled to minimize flicker.
Open SaveVideo and set your preferred output settings (container/codec, FPS, and quality). For motion consistency, keep the FPS the same as the input unless you have a specific reason to change it.
Run the workflow. Preview the output; if you see over-sharpening or residual noise, lower the enhancement strength or try a smaller upscale factor, then re-run.
Export the final video from SaveVideo. If your original had audio, remux the original audio track afterward using a video editor or ffmpeg, as SaveVideo typically outputs video-only.
suggestedUseCases: Upscaling smartphone or social clips to 1080p/4K with reduced noise and steadier motion.
Restoring family archives or old captures to improve clarity while minimizing temporal flicker.
Enhancing talking-head videos and webinars using the portrait mode for cleaner facial details.
Improving product b-roll or stock footage before editing to save time in post.
Cleaning up screen/grab or gameplay footage for clearer UI text and edges.

faqItems.question: Does this workflow keep the audio from my original video?
faqItems.answer: By default, SaveVideo outputs a video-only file. Export the enhanced video and then remux the original audio track using a video editor or a tool like ffmpeg.

faqItems.question: How do I reduce flicker or shimmering between frames?
faqItems.answer: Keep the temporal/stability options enabled in HitPawVideoEnhance and avoid changing FPS between input and output. If artifacts persist, try a smaller upscale factor or lower enhancement strength.

faqItems.question: Do I need a powerful GPU for this to work?
faqItems.answer: The HitPawVideoEnhance node runs the enhancement step for you; processing time mainly scales with video length, resolution, and upscale factor. Local performance affects decoding/encoding but heavy lifting is handled by the enhancement step.

faqItems.question: What input and output formats work best?
faqItems.answer: Common inputs like MP4/MOV work well via LoadVideo. For output, MP4 with H.264/H.265 is a reliable choice in SaveVideo. Keep FPS consistent for smoother motion unless you have a specific target.

The inclusion of multilingual support broadens the usability of this workflow, making it an excellent tool for global applications.

Ensure the f2fdebf6-dfaf-43b6-9eb2-7f70613cfdc1 node is connected to process the input text.

ed1c4eade3a3.title: Seedance 2.0 - Viral Cinemagraph Effect
ed1c4eade3a3.description: A one click workflow to generate a viral cinemagraph frame effect using Seedance 2.0. Upload an image of your character, optionally describe the motion of the scene and click generate. This workflow bypasses the realistic human input ban/limitation. A cinemagraph is a hybrid of a still photo and video, where a static image features a subtle, repeating, and seamless motion.
ed1c4eade3a3.metaDescription: Create a seamless cinemagraph from a single image with Seedance 2.0. Mask the motion area, describe movement, and export a looping video in one click.
ed1c4eade3a3.extendedDescription:
Seedance 2.0 - Viral Cinemagraph Effect turns a single character image into a short, looping cinemagraph with subtle motion. The workflow starts by loading your still using LoadImage (or BatchImagesNode for multiples), then uses a lightweight text pipeline (PrimitiveStringMultiline → RegexReplace → GeminiNode/GeminiNanoBanana2) to interpret your motion description into concise, model-friendly motion hints. A mask-driven pass defines where movement should happen: MaskPreview helps you visualize the region, and MaskToImage converts that mask for downstream use so the subject or selected area animates while the rest of the frame stays perfectly still.

At the core, ByteDance2ReferenceNode applies Seedance 2.0’s reference-based image-to-video motion on just the masked region, preserving identity and composition from your source photo. Frames are assembled with GetVideoComponents and CreateVideo, then you can inspect results with PreviewAny and export via SaveVideo (and SaveImage for any keyframe/mask snapshots). Two custom utility nodes (f4cfd806-6db2-425e-9f50-3eb8fe546a77 and e42b05e2-13fc-4ad5-822d-b89a8a297d35) are included in the graph to support the pre/post steps the workflow needs; they’re prewired and require no manual changes for a one‑click run. The result is a clean, seamless loop ideal for socials, hero headers, and character reveals—precise, controlled motion without rebuilding the entire scene.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and drop your source image into the LoadImage node (use BatchImagesNode if you want to process multiple images).

Describe the motion you want (e.g., "hair gently sways and eyes blink") in the PrimitiveStringMultiline node. The RegexReplace and GeminiNode/GeminiNanoBanana2 will auto-simplify this into concise motion hints.
Define the moving region: use MaskPreview to check the region to animate and adjust as needed, then let MaskToImage convert it for the motion pass so the background stays static.
Open ByteDance2ReferenceNode to review key controls such as motion intensity and loop length (if exposed in your build). Set fps/duration in GetVideoComponents/CreateVideo to match your platform.
Click Queue Prompt/Generate. Monitor intermediate frames with PreviewAny; tweak mask softness or motion intensity if you see edge artifacts or jitter.
Export your result with SaveVideo (MP4) and optionally SaveImage for masks or key frames you want to keep for iteration.
suggestedUseCases: Character portraits with subtle breathing, blinking, or hair movement for social posts and profile headers.
Product hero shots with gentle highlights or background elements looping to draw attention without distraction.
Album/cover art and thumbnails that stand out with minimal, classy motion.
Cinematic mood posts where only water, smoke, or fabric moves to create depth.
Marketing teasers and reveal loops that preserve brand imagery while adding motion.

faqItems.question: How do I control which part of the image moves?
faqItems.answer: Use the mask stage. Preview the animated region with MaskPreview and refine the mask before it’s converted by MaskToImage. Keep edges soft for cleaner blends and ensure the moving region doesn’t intersect high-contrast edges unless that’s intentional.

faqItems.question: My loop has visible pops at the seam—how can I fix it?
faqItems.answer: Reduce motion intensity in ByteDance2ReferenceNode, shorten the duration slightly, and soften the mask edges. Also check fps/duration in GetVideoComponents/CreateVideo so the start and end frames align more naturally. Subtle motion yields smoother loops.

faqItems.question: What image types and resolutions work best?
faqItems.answer: High-quality, well-lit portraits or product shots with a relatively clean background produce the best cinemagraphs. Square and vertical formats are social-friendly; set your desired output size/fps in GetVideoComponents/CreateVideo to match your target platform.

faqItems.question: Do I need to change the custom utility nodes with ID-like names?
faqItems.answer: No. The nodes f4cfd806-6db2-425e-9f50-3eb8fe546a77 and e42b05e2-13fc-4ad5-822d-b89a8a297d35 are preconfigured for this workflow. Leave them as-is unless you know their specific role in your local build.

eda6aeddc2ec.title: ElevenLabs: Speech to Speech
eda6aeddc2ec.description: Upload a source audio file to apply a new voice tone or clone a different voice, generating a modified audio output.
eda6aeddc2ec.metaDescription: ComfyUI Speech-to-Speech with ElevenLabs: convert any audio into a new voice using preset voices or instant voice cloning, and export MP3/Opus easily.
eda6aeddc2ec.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow performs voice conversion using the ElevenLabs Speech-to-Speech API. You provide a source audio clip (via LoadAudio or RecordAudio), choose a target voice (via ElevenLabsVoiceSelector for a preset voice or ElevenLabsInstantVoiceClone to create a new clone), and the ElevenLabsSpeechToSpeech node generates a new recording that preserves the timing and content of the original while changing the vocal timbre to match the selected voice. The output can be saved with SaveAudioMP3 or SaveAudioOpus.

Technically, the pipeline routes your source waveform into ElevenLabsSpeechToSpeech along with a target voice ID. In Option 1, ElevenLabsVoiceSelector queries your ElevenLabs account and outputs a selected voice for direct use. In Option 2, ElevenLabsInstantVoiceClone uploads a clean reference sample and returns a new voice resource that is then fed into the Speech-to-Speech node. The Note node contains guidance, and several nodes are initially bypassed so you can enable only what you need. This design makes it easy to A/B between preset voices and instant clones while keeping file management simple with explicit save nodes.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and read the Note node. Add your ElevenLabs API key where required by the ElevenLabs nodes (node fields or your ComfyUI env/config).
Provide source audio: either import a file with LoadAudio (place your WAV/MP3/OGG file) or record a take with RecordAudio in the Source Audio group.

Choose a target voice: Option 1 (Use Preset Voice) – select a voice in ElevenLabsVoiceSelector. Option 2 (Create a Voice Clone) – supply a clean reference clip to ElevenLabsInstantVoiceClone. Important: some nodes start bypassed; select them and press Ctrl-B to enable.

Wire the chosen voice output (from VoiceSelector or InstantVoiceClone) and the source audio into ElevenLabsSpeechToSpeech. Adjust available voice settings (e.g., stability, similarity boost) in the node to balance timbre accuracy vs. expressiveness.
Queue and run the workflow. Inspect the ElevenLabsSpeechToSpeech output. If the conversion sounds breathy or noisy, try a cleaner/louder source, trim silence, or lower similarity to reduce artifacts.
Save your result using SaveAudioMP3 or SaveAudioOpus. Pick the format based on your delivery needs (MP3 for broad compatibility, Opus for efficient streaming) and set the output path.
suggestedUseCases: Voice anonymization for interviews, user testing, or internal reviews while preserving natural pacing.
Character voice creation for podcasts, machinima, or indie games using a consistent, cloned persona.
Rapid ADR or pickup lines for video projects when the original voice is unavailable.
Multivoice demos for creatives: try the same read with multiple preset voices to pick a direction.
Brand voice prototyping: convert team recordings into a consistent house voice before booking sessions.

faqItems.question: Do I need an ElevenLabs account and API key?
faqItems.answer: Yes. The ElevenLabsVoiceSelector, ElevenLabsInstantVoiceClone, and ElevenLabsSpeechToSpeech nodes call the ElevenLabs API. Add your API key to the nodes or ComfyUI’s configuration as instructed in the Note node.

faqItems.question: What audio works best for cloning and conversion?
faqItems.answer: Use clean, single-speaker recordings with minimal background noise and reverb. Aim for steady levels without clipping, and avoid music. A clear 30–60 second sample is typically enough for Instant Voice Clone.

faqItems.question: What’s the difference between MP3 and Opus outputs?
faqItems.answer: SaveAudioMP3 produces a widely compatible file ideal for general distribution. SaveAudioOpus yields smaller files at similar perceptual quality—useful for web or app playback—though some workflows may require MP3.

faqItems.question: Is the source audio sent to external servers?
faqItems.answer: Yes. Audio for voice selection, cloning, and speech-to-speech is processed by ElevenLabs’ servers via their API. Review ElevenLabs’ terms, privacy policy, and your usage limits on their dashboard.

ef10fc1fe4d3.title: Moonvalley: Motion Transfer
ef10fc1fe4d3.description: Apply motion from one video to another.
ef10fc1fe4d3.metaDescription: Transfer motion from one video to another with the Moonvalley: Motion Transfer workflow using ComfyUI. Ideal for animators and video editors.
ef10fc1fe4d3.extendedDescription:
The 'Moonvalley: Motion Transfer' workflow is designed to seamlessly transfer motion from one video to another using ComfyUI. This workflow leverages the Moonvalley video generation model, which specializes in capturing and replicating intricate motion details. The core of the process involves the 'MoonvalleyVideo2VideoNode', which applies the motion dynamics from a reference video onto a target video. This is particularly useful for animators and video editors who want to imbue static scenes with dynamic motion without the need for extensive manual animation.

Technically, the workflow begins by loading a reference video using the 'LoadVideo' node. This video should be at least 5 seconds long to ensure sufficient motion data is captured. The 'MoonvalleyVideo2VideoNode' then analyzes the motion patterns and applies them to the target video. Finally, the 'SaveVideo' node is used to export the newly animated video. The inclusion of 'MarkdownNote' nodes provides in-line documentation and notes, making the workflow easy to follow and modify. This process is efficient and produces high-quality results, making it a valuable tool for creative professionals.
howToUse: Load your reference video using the 'LoadVideo' node. Ensure the video is at least 5 seconds long for optimal motion capture.
Configure the 'MoonvalleyVideo2VideoNode' to analyze the motion from your reference video.
Connect your target video to the 'MoonvalleyVideo2VideoNode' to apply the captured motion.
Use the 'SaveVideo' node to export the newly animated video.
Review the 'MarkdownNote' nodes for additional tips and documentation within the workflow.
Adjust parameters as needed to refine the motion transfer and achieve the desired effect.
suggestedUseCases: Animating static scenes in films or video projects.
Creating dynamic promotional videos by adding motion to still footage.
Enhancing video game cutscenes with realistic character movements.
Developing educational content with engaging, animated visuals.
Producing artistic video installations that combine static and dynamic elements.

faqItems.question: What types of videos work best for motion transfer?
faqItems.answer: Videos with clear, distinct motion patterns work best. Ensure the reference video is at least 5 seconds long for optimal results.

faqItems.question: Can I use this workflow for live-action videos?
faqItems.answer: Yes, the workflow is suitable for both animated and live-action videos, as long as the motion is clear and distinct.

faqItems.question: How do I adjust the intensity of the motion transfer?
faqItems.answer: You can tweak the parameters within the 'MoonvalleyVideo2VideoNode' to adjust the intensity and style of the motion transfer.

faqItems.question: Is there a way to preview the results before saving the video?
faqItems.answer: Currently, you need to complete the workflow and save the video to review the results. Consider using short video clips for faster iterations.

Input a text prompt in the TextEncodeAceStepAudio1.5 node to guide the music generation.

Researching advancements in AI-driven music composition and audio fidelity.
Comparing model capabilities for educational purposes in AI and music technology courses.

faqItems.question: What are the main differences between the ACE-Step 1.5 model and its smaller variants?
faqItems.answer: The ACE-Step 1.5 model offers enhanced audio understanding and composition capabilities, resulting in richer and more complex music outputs compared to smaller models.

faqItems.question: How does the workflow handle audio generation?

faqItems.question: Can I use this workflow for generating specific music genres?

faqItems.question: What factors should I consider when choosing between the 4B model and smaller variants?

ef37c26c9bbf.title: MiniMax H3: FLF2V
ef37c26c9bbf.description: Generate a video from a first and last frame using MiniMax H3, producing a smooth animation between the two images. You provide 2 images, and the workflow outputs a single video clip. Ideal for creating seamless transitions in animation, visualizing before-and-after transformations, and generating consistent motion for character or scene sequences.
ef37c26c9bbf.metaDescription: Generate a smooth video between two images in ComfyUI using MiniMax H3. Load first/last frames, run the node, and export an MP4 with SaveVideo.
ef37c26c9bbf.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow turns two still images—a defined first frame and last frame—into a single, smoothly animated video using the MiniMax H3 (Hailuo-03) first–last frame API. Two LoadImage nodes feed your start and end images into the MinimaxHailuo03FirstLastFrameNode, which sends them to the MiniMax service to predict the in-between frames. The node returns the generated sequence back to ComfyUI, and SaveVideo encodes it as a video file at your chosen frame rate.

Technically, the MinimaxHailuo03FirstLastFrameNode performs an API call to MiniMax H3’s First–Last Frame to Video endpoint, conditioning motion on the content of both input images to synthesize temporally consistent intermediate frames. Because the motion is guided by your exact start and end frames, you get a coherent transition without training or manual keyframing. This makes the setup ideal for before/after reveals, scene transitions, and quick animatics where you want subject consistency and controlled start/end states.
howToUse: Load the workflow JSON in ComfyUI, then open the two LoadImage nodes and select your First Frame and Last Frame images (use the same aspect ratio and resolution for both).
Open the MinimaxHailuo03FirstLastFrameNode and enter your MiniMax API credentials. Review any generation options the node exposes (e.g., clip length or frame count) and set them to your needs.
Open the SaveVideo node and set your filename pattern and FPS. Confirm the output directory shown in the node matches where you want the file saved.
Queue and run the workflow. The node will upload your two images to MiniMax H3, generate the in-between frames, and pass the result to SaveVideo.
Preview the output video from the path shown in the SaveVideo node. If needed, adjust your start/end frames or the node settings and re-run for a smoother transition.
suggestedUseCases: Before–after reveals for product mockups, design makeovers, or restoration showcases.
Seamless scene or logo transitions for title cards and motion graphics.
Character or pose interpolation between two keyframes for animatics and storyboards.
Environment shifts (e.g., day-to-night or season changes) using two photographs.
UI/UX state transitions that animate between two static screens.

faqItems.question: Do I need an API key to use this workflow?
faqItems.answer: Yes. The MinimaxHailuo03FirstLastFrameNode calls the MiniMax H3 (Hailuo-03) API. Enter your API key in the node’s credential field and ensure your account has access to the First–Last Frame to Video feature.

faqItems.question: How can I get the smoothest results between two frames?
faqItems.answer: Use images with matching resolution and aspect ratio, similar framing and scale of the subject, and consistent lighting and camera angle. Large viewpoint or style jumps are harder to bridge, so pick start and end frames that are visually related.

faqItems.question: What formats and resolutions are supported?
faqItems.answer: LoadImage supports common image formats like PNG and JPG. For best results, use the same dimensions for both inputs. Note that the MiniMax API may impose size limits; if the node or API errors at high resolutions, downscale both inputs equally and try again.

faqItems.question: Where is the video saved and how do I change FPS?
faqItems.answer: The SaveVideo node writes the final clip to the output folder shown in its settings. You can change the playback speed by adjusting the FPS field in SaveVideo before running the workflow.

ef543bd4a773.title: Seedance Playblast2Render
ef543bd4a773.description:
This workflow turns a raw CG playblast into a final rendered shot using Seedance 2.0.

It preserves your animation and camera from the playblast, while Nano Banana Pro generates reference images and multi-angle grids to define asset look and improve consistency. A custom Gemini node builds structured prompts, allowing Seedance to reinterpret the shot with a controlled, production-ready style.

The result is a fast, repeatable pipeline that replaces traditional rendering with AI-driven output while keeping full control over motion and intent.
ef543bd4a773.metaDescription: Turn a CG playblast into a styled, production-ready render with Seedance 2.0. Preserve motion and camera, add references, and export final video in ComfyUI.
ef543bd4a773.extendedDescription:
Seedance Playblast2Render is a ComfyUI workflow that turns a raw CG playblast into a styled, production-ready render using Seedance 2.0. The pipeline preserves your original motion and framing by conditioning the renderer on the playblast video, then layers in controlled art direction through curated references and a structured prompt. VHS_LoadVideo (with VHS_VideoInfo) ingests the playblast and extracts frame rate and duration, while ImageFromBatch+ helps you pick hero frames for style exploration. Nano Banana Pro (via the GeminiNanoBanana2 node) generates multi-angle look boards and reference grids you can assemble with ImageBatchMulti and LoadImage. PreviewImage/PreviewAny nodes are sprinkled throughout so you can confirm each stage before committing to a render.

A custom GeminiNode builds a clean, shot-aware prompt from your notes, guided by included system instructions for Seedance. Those references and the playblast are fed to ByteDance2ReferenceNode to lock in motion, silhouette, and camera, and then rendered in ByteDance2TextToVideoNode. SetNode/GetNode keep shared parameters (like shot names or FPS) synchronized across groups. When you’re happy, SaveVideo writes out the final clip. The result is a repeatable, fast path that replaces a traditional offline render pass with AI-driven output—while keeping full control over timing, camera, and intent.

The workflow is organized into clear groups: LOAD PLAYBLAST, (OPTIONAL) GENERATE STYLE FRAMES, GENERATE INDIVIDUAL ASSETS, GENERATE SHOT AND STYLE DESCRIPTION FOR SEEDANCE, and DIFFUSION RENDERER BASED ON REFERENCE IMAGES AND PLAYBLAST ANIMATION. There’s also a GENERATE FAUX-PLAYBLAST group if you want to test the pipeline without a real playblast. Because it leverages structured prompting (GeminiNode), reference conditioning (ByteDance2ReferenceNode), and reference grids (GeminiNanoBanana2 + ImageBatchMulti), it’s especially strong at keeping character/prop continuity and delivering a consistent look across shots.
howToUse: Load your playblast: In LOAD PLAYBLAST, use VHS_LoadVideo (or LoadVideo) to import the clip. Inspect FPS, frame count, and duration with VHS_VideoInfo. If needed, use CM_FloatToInt/Int to match integer frame counts downstream.

Optionally create style frames: In (OPTIONAL) GENERATE STYLE FRAMES, pick a hero frame with ImageFromBatch+ and assemble look references using ImageBatchMulti and LoadImage. If you’re using Nano Banana Pro, run GeminiNanoBanana2 to produce multi-angle boards; verify results with PreviewImage/PreviewAny.

Author the prompt: In GENERATE SHOT AND STYLE DESCRIPTION FOR SEEDANCE, add your shot notes and asset callouts (MarkdownNote). Run GeminiNode to generate a structured Seedance prompt; if the workflow exposes SetNode/GetNode, store shared parameters (shot name, FPS) for reuse.

Attach references and motion: In the DIFFUSION RENDERER group, connect the playblast output to ByteDance2ReferenceNode to preserve animation and camera. Feed in any Nano Banana Pro grids or loaded reference images (ImageBatchMulti). Tune the reference strength/conditioning parameters as needed in the node UI.

Render with Seedance: Connect ByteDance2ReferenceNode into ByteDance2TextToVideoNode. Ensure frame range, FPS, and seed are set for reproducibility. Use PreviewAny/PreviewImage to review test passes and make adjustments to the prompt, reference strength, or style boards.
Export the result: When satisfied, connect the renderer output to SaveVideo, set your codec/filename, and write out the final shot. Rinse and repeat for the next sequence to maintain consistency.
suggestedUseCases: Look development passes: lock style and continuity across sequences while preserving timing from editorial.
Stylized previs or animatics: upgrade blockouts into presentable, art-directed clips without a full offline render.
Character and prop continuity: use multi-angle grids to keep hero assets on-model from shot to shot.
Pitch, teasers, and indie cinematics: quickly generate compelling visuals from rough animation.
Product or automotive turntables: retain accurate motion paths while applying consistent brand styling.

faqItems.question: How does the workflow preserve my animation and camera?
faqItems.answer: Your playblast video is fed into ByteDance2ReferenceNode as a conditioning source. That node guides ByteDance2TextToVideoNode so timing, motion, and framing from the playblast are respected while Seedance 2.0 reinterprets the appearance with your prompt and references.

faqItems.question: Do I need Nano Banana Pro style grids, or can I use my own references?
faqItems.answer: Both work. GeminiNanoBanana2 can generate multi-angle boards to establish a consistent look, but you can also load your own refs with LoadImage and assemble them with ImageBatchMulti. The key is to provide clear, angle-diverse references for stable asset identity.

faqItems.question: How do I keep shot duration and FPS identical to the playblast?
faqItems.answer: Use VHS_VideoInfo to read the source FPS and frame count, then propagate those values to the renderer. If you encounter fractional values, CM_FloatToInt and Int help align integer frame counts so the output matches the playblast length.

faqItems.question: What should I tweak first if the style is drifting or inconsistent?
faqItems.answer: Increase reference influence in ByteDance2ReferenceNode, simplify or clarify the structured prompt from GeminiNode, and ensure your ImageBatchMulti contains clean, multi-angle references. Also fix the random seed in ByteDance2TextToVideoNode for repeatable results when iterating.

ef5d632ed2c5.title: Video Outpainting
ef5d632ed2c5.description: Video Outpainting using the LTX 2.3 Video Outpainting IC LoRA. Expand your video in any direction!
ef5d632ed2c5.metaDescription: ComfyUI tutorial: Use LTX 2.3 Video Outpainting IC LoRA to expand videos in any direction. Load, trim frames, outpaint, and export with VHS nodes.
ef5d632ed2c5.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow performs video outpainting: it expands the canvas of each frame in your clip and synthesizes believable new content around the original footage. It loads your source video with VHS_LoadVideo, processes the frames with a custom outpainting processor configured to use the LTX 2.3 Video Outpainting IC LoRA, and reassembles the frames into a finished video with VHS_VideoCombine. A MarkdownNote in the graph provides inline guidance.

Technically, the core outpainting step (custom node ID: 2e37ecc9-770a-4ac2-972c-e953901f49d3) pads the frame in your chosen direction(s) and inpaints the newly added regions while preserving the original content. The LTX 2.3 Video Outpainting IC LoRA conditions the diffusion process so the generated edges stay stylistically and semantically consistent from frame to frame. The workflow exposes two key timeline controls: skip_first_frames (trim frames from the start) and frame_count (how many frames to process after the skip). For example, on a 600‑frame clip you can set skip_first_frames: 60 and frame_count: 480 to process frames 60–539. This makes it easy to test short segments before rendering the entire video.

Because it’s built on VHS nodes, you get reliable frame extraction and recombination, plus straightforward control over frame rate and output location. Use this when you need to convert vertical footage to widescreen, add headroom/side padding for reframing, or extend a background to fit new aspect ratios without obvious cropping.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and confirm required components are present: VHS (Video Helper Suite) for VHS_LoadVideo and VHS_VideoCombine, and the custom outpainting node (ID: 2e37ecc9-770a-4ac2-972c-e953901f49d3) configured with the LTX 2.3 Video Outpainting IC LoRA. If the LoRA/model path is unresolved, point the node to the correct file.
Open VHS_LoadVideo and select your source video. Verify the frame rate and resolution are appropriate for your GPU. Large resolutions and very wide expansions increase VRAM usage and render time.
Set skip_first_frames and frame_count to target the exact segment you want to process. Example: For a 600‑frame clip, skip_first_frames: 60 and frame_count: 480 processes frames 60–539.

In the Outpainting Processor (custom node), choose the expansion direction(s) and amount (e.g., left/right/top/bottom padding or target aspect ratio). Adjust generation strength/denoise as needed—smaller padding and moderate strength generally reduce artifacts and flicker.

Open VHS_VideoCombine, set the output fps to match your source (unless you intentionally want a different frame rate), choose an output path/codec, and ensure it’s writing to a location with enough disk space.

Queue the workflow. Review the result. If edges wobble or textures drift, try reducing the padding amount, lowering denoise/strength, or processing in shorter segments (tuning settings per segment) and then stitch the results.
suggestedUseCases: Reframe vertical (9:16) smartphone videos to widescreen (16:9) by outpainting side margins instead of cropping.
Add headroom or side padding to dialogue or interview shots to accommodate captions, lower thirds, or safe framing.
Extend backgrounds and set pieces for VFX comps or motion graphics overlays without losing original subject framing.
Widen establishing shots from narrow or handheld footage to better match a project’s aspect ratio.
Repurpose social content across platforms with different aspect ratio requirements while preserving the main action.

faqItems.question: Does the workflow keep the original audio?
faqItems.answer: No. VHS_VideoCombine outputs a silent video from the processed frames. To restore audio, mux it from the original clip in your video editor or with ffmpeg, e.g., ffmpeg -i processed.mp4 -i source.mp4 -map 0:v -map 1:a -c copy out_with_audio.mp4.

faqItems.question: How do skip_first_frames and frame_count work together?
faqItems.answer: skip_first_frames trims frames from the start, and frame_count limits how many frames are processed after the skip. For a 600‑frame video: skip_first_frames: 60 and frame_count: 480 processes 480 frames starting at frame 60. Use smaller values to test quickly before rendering the entire clip.

faqItems.question: How can I reduce flicker or edge artifacts across frames?
faqItems.answer: Use conservative padding amounts, keep denoise/strength moderate, and ensure fps in VHS_VideoCombine matches the source. If issues persist, process the video in shorter segments with settings tuned to each section, then stitch the segments in your editor.

faqItems.question: What if I run out of GPU memory?
faqItems.answer: VRAM usage scales with resolution, padding size, and frame batch size. Reduce the input resolution, outpaint a smaller margin, or process fewer frames at a time. Close other GPU‑intensive apps and ensure the LoRA/model paths are correctly set to avoid reloading overhead.

ef8586090398.title: 1 Image to Car Product Shots
ef8586090398.description: Upload a photo of your vehicle and generate a studio quality video of the vehicle from multiple angles.
ef8586090398.metaDescription: Transform a single car image into a studio-quality video with ComfyUI's workflow for professional automotive product shots.
ef8586090398.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow is designed to transform a single image of a vehicle into a high-quality video showcasing the car from various angles. By leveraging advanced nodes such as the ByteDanceSeedreamNode and Kling models, the workflow synthesizes a realistic video output that mimics professional studio shots. The process begins with the LoadImage node, which imports the vehicle photo. The ByteDanceSeedreamNode then processes the image, generating multiple frames that simulate different perspectives of the car. These frames are compiled into a seamless video using the CreateVideo node.

What sets this workflow apart is its ability to automate the creation of professional-grade car product videos from just one image. The SaveImage and SaveVideo nodes ensure that both individual frames and the final video are stored efficiently. Additionally, the Reroute and BatchImagesNode facilitate smooth data handling and processing, making this workflow both robust and user-friendly. This technique is particularly useful for automotive marketers and e-commerce platforms looking to enhance their product listings with dynamic visual content.
howToUse: Load the ComfyUI workflow and import your vehicle image using the LoadImage node.
Process the image with the ByteDanceSeedreamNode to generate multiple angles.
Use the CreateVideo node to compile these frames into a cohesive video.
Save individual frames with the SaveImage node if needed.
Export the final video using the SaveVideo node for use in marketing or presentations.
suggestedUseCases: Create dynamic product videos for automotive e-commerce listings.
Enhance marketing materials with professional-grade car videos.
Generate engaging social media content showcasing vehicle features.
Develop virtual showrooms with rotating car displays.
Produce training materials for automotive sales teams.

faqItems.question: What image format should I use for the best results?
faqItems.answer: For optimal processing, use high-resolution images in JPEG or PNG format.

faqItems.question: Can this workflow handle images of vehicles other than cars?
faqItems.answer: While optimized for cars, the workflow can be adapted for other vehicle types with adjustments to the processing nodes.

faqItems.question: How long does it take to generate a video?
faqItems.answer: The time varies based on image resolution and system capabilities, but typically it takes a few minutes to process and compile the video.

faqItems.question: Is there a limit to the number of angles the video can include?
faqItems.answer: The workflow can generate multiple angles, but the number is limited by the processing power and memory available on your system.

ef8902323dfa.title: Ideogram Vector 1: Text to SVG
ef8902323dfa.description: Generate a fully editable SVG from a text prompt with Ideogram Vector 1, optionally guided by up to five reference images, and save it as one vector file. Ideal for logos, posters, flat illustration, patterns and line art that stays crisp at any size and opens directly in a vector editor.
ef8902323dfa.metaDescription: ComfyUI tutorial: Generate clean, editable SVGs from text prompts with Ideogram Vector 1. Optionally guide style with up to five images and save one vector file.
ef8902323dfa.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow turns a plain-language prompt into a fully editable vector using Ideogram’s Vector 1 model. The core of the graph is the IdeogramVectorGenerateApi node, which accepts your text prompt and up to five optional style/reference images (fed via LoadImage nodes) to guide the look and structure of the output. The model returns a single vector composition, which is then written to disk as an SVG via the SaveSVGNode. A MarkdownNote node is included in the graph to summarize usage tips directly inside the workspace.

Technically, the IdeogramVectorGenerateApi node calls Ideogram Vector 1 to synthesize clean paths and shapes rather than pixels, producing scalable line art, logos, flat illustration, and patterns that remain crisp at any size. Using reference images gives the model a visual anchor—useful for matching brand style, line weight, or color blocking. The SaveSVGNode preserves paths and groups so you can open the result immediately in a vector editor (Illustrator, Inkscape, Figma) to adjust strokes, fills, and layout.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and confirm your Ideogram API access is configured for the IdeogramVectorGenerateApi node (check the node’s settings or your environment setup).

Optionally add up to five style/reference images using LoadImage nodes and connect them to the reference inputs on IdeogramVectorGenerateApi. Use the provided academic-svg.png as a starting example if desired.

Open the IdeogramVectorGenerateApi node: write a concise prompt that describes subject, style, line weight, and palette (e.g., “flat vector logo, monoline outline, 2–3 colors, high contrast, minimal”).
Queue/Run the workflow. The IdeogramVectorGenerateApi node will generate a vector composition guided by your prompt (and references if connected).
Review the output and use the SaveSVGNode to write a single .svg file to your chosen folder. Rename the file in the node to keep versions organized.
Open the saved SVG in your preferred vector editor to tweak strokes, colors, grouping, or to integrate the result into a larger design.
suggestedUseCases: Rapid logo and wordmark ideation with clean, editable vectors.
Poster, sticker, and merch graphics that need crisp scaling at print sizes.
Seamless patterns and flat illustrations for web, UI, or packaging.
Monoline icons and line art for infographics or slide decks.
Brand style exploration by guiding generation with existing assets.

faqItems.question: What file format does this workflow produce?
faqItems.answer: It saves a single SVG via the SaveSVGNode. The result contains vector paths/shapes you can edit in tools like Illustrator, Inkscape, or Figma.

faqItems.question: How do I get the cleanest vector results?
faqItems.answer: Write prompts that emphasize vector-friendly traits (e.g., “flat color, minimal, clean lines, monoline, few shapes”). Avoid photoreal terms. Add 1–5 reference images via LoadImage to lock in line weight, palette, or layout.

faqItems.question: Can I control colors or line thickness?
faqItems.answer: Yes—describe palette and stroke style in your prompt (e.g., “2-color palette: black and teal; thin monoline; high contrast”). You can further fine-tune fills and strokes after generation by editing the SVG.

faqItems.question: Do I need an API key or any special setup?
faqItems.answer: You need valid access to Ideogram’s API for the IdeogramVectorGenerateApi node. Configure the key in the node or your environment per the node’s documentation before running the workflow.

f0257c86b3a0.title: LTX 2.3_ID_lora_CelebVHQ
f0257c86b3a0.description: Bring voice consistency to your open source video generation pipeline with Qwen 3 TTS and LTX 2.3 with the CelebHVQ ID-LoRA.
f0257c86b3a0.metaDescription: Create identity-consistent talking videos from a photo using LTX 2.3, CelebVHQ ID-LoRA, and Qwen 3 TTS. Auto-generate prompts, synthesize voice, and render.
f0257c86b3a0.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI tutorial workflow turns a single image into a short, voice-driven video with strong visual identity and perceived lip alignment. It combines Lightricks LTX 2.3 for video generation with an ID-LoRA (CelebVHQ) to keep the subject’s face and styling consistent across frames, while Qwen 3 TTS produces a matching voice track. The pipeline is organized into clear groups: Load Image, Create Prompts, Prompt Extraction, Create Voice, and Create Video.

Under the hood, GeminiNode analyzes your uploaded image (via LoadImage) and drafts two complementary texts: a speech line with expressive cues and a scene/appearance description. RegexExtract then parses these into an ID-LoRA-ready format with three tagged sections: [VISUAL], [SPEECH], and [SOUNDS]. FB_Qwen3TTSCustomVoice uses the [SPEECH] and style hints from [SOUNDS] to synthesize a voice track, saved with SaveAudioMP3. The LTX 2.3 video node (the custom node in this graph) consumes the structured prompt plus your reference image to render a talking video, with the CelebVHQ ID-LoRA improving identity retention in dynamic, in-the-wild scenarios. PreviewAny lets you iterate quickly, and SaveVideo writes the final clip. Local users can optionally load the LTX spatial upscaler (ltx-2.3-spatial-upscaler-x2-1.1.safetensors) for cleaner details at higher resolution.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and place required models locally: LTX 2.3 checkpoint(s), the CelebVHQ ID-LoRA, and optionally the ltx-2.3-spatial-upscaler-x2-1.1.safetensors in latent_upscale_models.
Open the Load Image group and drop in a well-lit, forward-facing photo of your subject (crop to head-and-shoulders for best identity retention).
In Create Prompts, set your GeminiNode credentials/model if needed, then run it. It will propose a scene/appearance description and a speech line with expression tags.

Check Prompt Extraction. RegexExtract splits content into [VISUAL], [SPEECH], and [SOUNDS]. Edit these fields if necessary so the exact words in [SPEECH] match what you want the subject to say, and the style cues in [SOUNDS] reflect the intended voice and ambience.

In Create Voice, open FB_Qwen3TTSCustomVoice. Choose or configure a voice profile or reference, feed it the [SPEECH] text (and style hints), then generate and SaveAudioMP3. Use PreviewAny to confirm pacing and tone.

In Create Video, enable the CelebVHQ ID-LoRA and ensure the structured prompt is passed to the LTX 2.3 node. Adjust duration/resolution to fit your GPU. Run the video render, preview with PreviewAny, and export with SaveVideo. If you enabled the LTX x2 upscaler locally, the workflow will produce a sharper output.
suggestedUseCases: Talking-head explainers or announcements from a single portrait with consistent identity across multiple clips.
Character-driven shorts where the same subject appears in different scenes but maintains facial features and styling.
Voice-driven social posts: generate the speech with Qwen 3 TTS and pair it with an expressive, on-brand visual.
Podcast or newsletter teasers that turn a static host photo into a quick video bite.
Template-based content where a team updates only the [SPEECH] text each week while keeping the same look and voice.

faqItems.question: What does the CelebVHQ ID-LoRA do here?
faqItems.answer: It helps LTX 2.3 preserve the subject’s identity and facial features across frames, especially in dynamic, in-the-wild shots. It works best with a clear, frontal image and a well-structured prompt that separates [VISUAL], [SPEECH], and [SOUNDS].

faqItems.question: How is lip-sync achieved without a separate lip-sync model?
faqItems.answer: The workflow aligns perceived mouth movements by making the [SPEECH] text explicit and pairing it with matching TTS audio. While not frame-perfect lip-sync, using concise lines, clear punctuation, and expression cues improves alignment. You can retime in post if you need exact phoneme matching.

faqItems.question: Can I use a different ID-LoRA (e.g., TalkVid) or my own?
faqItems.answer: Yes. Swap the LoRA in the LTX 2.3 node. CelebVHQ is tuned for in-the-wild motion; TalkVid is typically stronger for close-up, studio-like talking head shots. For custom LoRAs, keep the same structured prompt format and test different strengths.

faqItems.question: Do I need the LTX x2 upscaler model?
faqItems.answer: It’s optional. If you place ltx-2.3-spatial-upscaler-x2-1.1.safetensors in latent_upscale_models, the workflow can render crisper outputs at higher resolution. If VRAM is limited, disable upscaling or render at a lower base resolution.

f052abfce10e.title: LTX-2 Canny to Video
f052abfce10e.description: Generate high-quality videos from edge detection (Canny) guidance with synchronized audio-video generation using LTX-2. Features precise edge control, structural consistency, and efficient performance.
f052abfce10e.metaDescription: Transform edge-detected images into high-quality videos with LTX-2, ensuring precise edge control and structural consistency.
f052abfce10e.extendedDescription:
The 'LTX-2 Canny to Video' workflow is designed to transform edge-detected images into high-quality videos with synchronized audio. Utilizing the LTX-2 model, this workflow leverages the Canny edge detection technique to ensure precise edge control and structural consistency throughout the video. The process begins with the 'LoadVideo' node to import your source video, which is then decomposed into its components using the 'GetVideoComponents' node. The 'Canny' node plays a crucial role by detecting edges in the images, providing a guide for the video generation process.

This workflow is particularly useful for creators who need to maintain the structural integrity of the original footage while enhancing it with AI-generated elements. The LTX-2 model, developed by Lightricks, ensures that the generated video maintains high quality and coherence. The workflow also includes nodes like 'ImageScaleBy' and 'ResizeImageMaskNode' for adjusting image dimensions, and 'SaveVideo' to compile and save the final video. By following the recommended settings and parameters, users can achieve optimal results with minimal manual intervention.
howToUse: Load the workflow and import your source video using the 'LoadVideo' node.
Decompose the video into components with the 'GetVideoComponents' node.
Apply the 'Canny' node to detect edges in the video frames.
Adjust image dimensions using 'ImageScaleBy' and 'ResizeImageMaskNode' as needed.
Generate the video with synchronized audio using the LTX-2 model.
Save the final video with the 'SaveVideo' node.
suggestedUseCases: Creating artistic videos with enhanced edge definition.
Generating animated sequences from static edge-detected images.
Producing consistent video content with AI-enhanced features.
Developing educational content that requires precise visual consistency.
Enhancing video footage with AI-generated elements while maintaining original structure.

faqItems.question: What is the purpose of the Canny node in this workflow?
faqItems.answer: The Canny node detects edges in video frames, providing a guide for the LTX-2 model to generate videos with precise edge control.

faqItems.question: Can I use this workflow with high-resolution videos?
faqItems.answer: Yes, you can use high-resolution settings like 1920x1088, but ensure that width and height are divisible by 64, and frame count by 8+1.

faqItems.question: What happens if I use invalid parameters?
faqItems.answer: The workflow will not produce errors but will adjust to the closest valid parameters to ensure smooth operation.

faqItems.question: How does the LTX-2 model enhance video quality?
faqItems.answer: The LTX-2 model maintains structural consistency and enhances visual details, ensuring high-quality video output.

f16678cfedd4.title: Kling 4.0: Text to Video
f16678cfedd4.description: Generate a ten-second cinematic clip from text alone with Kling 4.0, holding one single continuous shot through a full high-speed chase while also producing native stereo audio. Ideal for short-form spectacle, concept pitches, and motion references where a single unbroken take carries the idea.
f16678cfedd4.metaDescription: ComfyUI tutorial: Generate a 10‑second, single‑take cinematic video from text using Kling 4.0, then save it with audio using SaveVideo.
f16678cfedd4.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow turns a well-crafted text prompt into a 10‑second cinematic video using Kling 4.0. The core of the graph is a single generator node—Kling4TextToVideoNode—that sends your prompt and settings to the Kling model and returns a ready‑to‑save video. A SaveVideo node then writes the result to disk as an MP4, preserving any audio provided by the model. With a focus on single, unbroken takes, it’s ideal for scenes like high‑speed chases or continuous tracking shots where camera motion carries the story.

Technically, the Kling4TextToVideoNode acts as an API client: you supply the descriptive prompt, duration (configured here for 10 seconds), resolution/aspect ratio, and optional controls like seed and audio enablement if exposed by your node build. The node outputs a video asset that includes frames, timing, and—when enabled—native stereo audio from Kling 4.0. SaveVideo handles the file writing step, using the frame rate and container options provided upstream. For best results, include explicit camera direction in your prompt (e.g., “one continuous handheld shot, no cuts”), define environment and pacing, and avoid conflicting instructions that might imply edits.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and ensure the Kling4TextToVideoNode extension is installed. Add your Kling API key in the node’s settings or global config as required.

Open the Kling4TextToVideoNode and write a clear prompt that specifies a single continuous shot (e.g., “one unbroken tracking shot, no cuts”) and the scene details (subject, environment, time of day, motion style).
Set key parameters on the node: duration to 10 seconds, choose resolution/aspect ratio, and optionally set seed, frame rate, and audio enablement if your node exposes those controls.
Queue the workflow. The Kling4TextToVideoNode will request generation from the Kling API; when complete, it forwards the video to SaveVideo.
In SaveVideo, confirm the output path and filename pattern. Run/queue the save step (if separate) and wait for the MP4 to appear in your output folder.
Review the result in a media player. Iterate by refining the prompt (camera path, pacing, environment), adjusting resolution or seed, and re‑queuing until you reach the desired look.
suggestedUseCases: Previsualization for concept pitches where a single moving camera conveys the idea.
Short‑form spectacle or trailer moments emphasizing dynamic, continuous motion.
Motion reference clips for animators, VFX artists, or storyboard refinement.
Product or environment fly‑throughs captured as a single, uninterrupted take.
Social media teasers that benefit from cohesive camera choreography without cuts.

faqItems.question: Do I need an API key to use Kling 4.0 in this workflow?
faqItems.answer: Yes. The Kling4TextToVideoNode communicates with the Kling API and requires a valid API key. Enter it in the node’s settings or your ComfyUI environment as instructed by the extension.

faqItems.question: Is the clip length fixed at 10 seconds?
faqItems.answer: This workflow is configured for 10 seconds. If your Kling node build supports other durations, you can change it in the node. Otherwise, keep prompts scoped to a 10‑second, single‑take action.

faqItems.question: Does the output include audio?
faqItems.answer: Kling 4.0 can return native stereo audio when audio generation is enabled. If the API response includes audio, SaveVideo will write it into the MP4. If not, the clip will be silent.

faqItems.question: How do I ensure a single continuous shot with no cuts?
faqItems.answer: State it explicitly in the prompt (e.g., “one continuous handheld shot, no cuts”) and describe the camera path, pacing, and start/end beats. Avoid instructions that imply edits or angle changes.

faqItems.question: Do I need an API key and where do I put it?

faqItems.question: Can I control voices, SFX, or music style?
faqItems.answer: You can guide outcomes through prompt design (speaker names with quoted lines, short SFX cues like [door slams], and music descriptors like "soft lo-fi"). faqItems.question: What are the limits for duration, resolution, or fps?

faqItems.question: Can I get separate audio stems for dialogue, SFX, and music?

f30541b504b1.title: Seedream 5.0 Flash: Image Edit
f30541b504b1.description: Edit and generate images with Seedream 5.0 Flash, transforming a single input image into one refined output with cinematic lighting, accurate text rendering, and resolutions up to 2K.
f30541b504b1.metaDescription: Edit and upscale a single image with Seedream 5.0 Flash in ComfyUI—cinematic relights, accurate text, and up to 2K output using ByteDanceSeedreamNodeV3.
f30541b504b1.extendedDescription:
Seedream 5.0 Flash: Image Edit is a compact ComfyUI workflow that turns a single input image into one polished, prompt-directed output. It uses LoadImage to bring in your source asset, passes it to ByteDanceSeedreamNodeV3 (Seedream 5.0 Flash) for image-conditioned generation, and saves the result with SaveImageAdvanced. A MarkdownNote in the graph provides quick reminders and links, and the included sample wine_bottle_brand_ref.png makes it easy to test immediately.

Technically, ByteDanceSeedreamNodeV3 performs prompt-guided editing conditioned on your input image. You control what changes with the node’s prompt fields and key parameters like output size (up to a 2K long edge), seed for repeatability, and edit strength/conditioning (naming may vary by node version) to balance preservation of the source vs. creativity. The model is tuned for fast turnaround ("Flash"), cinematic lighting cues, and more reliable text rendering in the output. SaveImageAdvanced then writes files with your chosen naming/subfolder scheme so you can iterate quickly and keep versions organized.

This setup excels at practical single-shot edits—relighting product photos, refining composition, swapping or sharpening label text, and generating high-res hero images—without the overhead of complex masking pipelines. It’s a focused, prompt-first editor that maintains the structure of your input while applying stylistic and textual updates convincingly.
howToUse: Update ComfyUI to the latest version and open the provided workflow. Ensure the ByteDanceSeedreamNodeV3 custom node is installed and configured (API/key or settings per the node’s readme).
Open LoadImage and select your source file (try the included wine_bottle_brand_ref.png to preview the workflow). Confirm it feeds into ByteDanceSeedreamNodeV3.

In ByteDanceSeedreamNodeV3, write a clear prompt describing the desired edit (e.g., cinematic backlighting, glossy glass, brand label with specific text). If available, set negative prompt to block unwanted styles.

Set output dimensions in ByteDanceSeedreamNodeV3. Keep the long edge at or under 2048 for 2K results. Adjust edit strength/conditioning (if exposed) to control how closely the output follows the input image.
Optionally set a fixed seed for reproducible results. Keep prompts concise when requesting exact on-image text; use accurate spelling and quotes around the desired wording.
Configure SaveImageAdvanced (folder, filename pattern) and click Queue Prompt. Review the saved output, tweak prompts/strength/size, and re-run until you reach the desired look.
suggestedUseCases: Product relighting and polish: Turn a flat packshot into a cinematic hero image while preserving bottle shape and label layout.
Branding and label updates: Refine or replace on-image text with cleaner, more legible type while keeping the original composition.
Marketing one-offs: Generate a single, high-res visual (up to 2K) for a banner, thumbnail, or social post without a complex edit pipeline.
Catalog consistency: Harmonize lighting and style across disparate product images using consistent prompt cues.
Concept previews: Try art direction variants (studio backlight, moody rim light, warm highlights) quickly before a full shoot or retouch.

faqItems.question: Do I need an API key or local model files for ByteDanceSeedreamNodeV3?
faqItems.answer: This workflow uses ByteDanceSeedreamNodeV3, which typically accesses Seedream 5.0 Flash via an API. Follow the node’s installation/readme to set credentials or endpoints as required. After configuration, restart ComfyUI and test with the sample image.

faqItems.question: How do I keep the original layout but improve lighting and text?
faqItems.answer: Use a restrained, descriptive prompt (e.g., "cinematic rim lighting, soft reflections") and reduce the edit strength/conditioning parameter if available. Avoid style prompts that imply large structural changes. Keep text requests short and precise to prevent layout drift.

faqItems.question: What settings help with accurate on-image text?
faqItems.answer: Include the exact wording in quotes and avoid competing style terms. Keep the prompt concise, use correct spelling, and run with a fixed seed for consistency. If unwanted extra text appears, add it to the negative prompt and simplify the style language.

faqItems.question: How do I get clean 2K outputs without failures or artifacts?
faqItems.answer: Set width/height so the long edge is ≤ 2048 in ByteDanceSeedreamNodeV3. If the request fails or returns soft results, try slightly smaller sizes (e.g., 1536), simplify the prompt, and reduce edit strength. Use SaveImageAdvanced to version outputs as you iterate.

f3096e2ffb64.title: Video Extend: Seedance 2.5
f3096e2ffb64.description: Extend an existing video forward or backward by generating new segments that seamlessly preserve the original characters, scenes, and aspect ratio. The source video must be 1.9–30 seconds long, and you specify the duration of the new clip (4–30 seconds, default 5), with output delivered as MP4 or MOV. Ideal for continuing unfinished footage, creating extended narrative sequences, and building longer edit chains.
f3096e2ffb64.metaDescription: Extend videos with Seedance 2.5 in ComfyUI—seamless forward/backward continuations that preserve characters and aspect ratio. Output MP4 or MOV, 4–30s.
f3096e2ffb64.extendedDescription:
Video Extend: Seedance 2.5 is a ComfyUI workflow that continues an existing clip forward or backward while preserving characters, scene layout, and aspect ratio. It starts by loading your source footage with LoadVideo, then uses Video Slice to define the context window and the direction of extension (append after the last frame or prepend before the first). ByteDance2ReferenceNodeV2 extracts strong visual cues from the head or tail of your clip so the Seedance model can generate a seamless continuation that looks and feels like the original footage.

Under the hood, the Seedance generator (executed by the model/inference node d9aa59a4-3784-4796-9f1b-5b467fb41fa1) is conditioned by the reference features to maintain character identity and composition across the newly created segment. You choose the new segment length (4–30 seconds, default 5), and SaveVideo writes the result to MP4 or MOV at the source resolution, keeping your aspect ratio intact. A MarkdownNote in the graph provides inline guidance. Input clips should be 1.9–30 seconds long, making this template ideal for extending unfinished shots, building longer edit chains, or crafting narrative bridges without changing the look of your scene.
howToUse: Open the Video Extend: Seedance 2.5 template in ComfyUI and confirm the Seedance model is properly set in the model/inference node (d9aa59a4-3784-4796-9f1b-5b467fb41fa1).
In LoadVideo, select your source clip (1.9–30s). You can test with the provided sloth_bullfight.mp4 to verify the pipeline.

Open Video Slice and choose the extension direction: Forward to continue after the last frame, or Backward to prepend before the first frame. Set the New Segment Duration to 4–30 seconds (default is 5).

Ensure ByteDance2ReferenceNodeV2 is connected to the sliced segment so it can extract reference features from the head/tail frames for identity and scene continuity. Leave its defaults unless you have a reason to adjust them.
In SaveVideo, set your output filename and container (MP4 or MOV). Keep the source resolution to preserve aspect ratio, and match FPS to your workflow or source if the node exposes FPS settings.

Queue the workflow and run it. Review the join between the original and generated segment; if you see drift, try a slightly shorter extension, provide a cleaner source segment (less motion blur), or adjust the slice range to include stronger reference context.
suggestedUseCases: Extending a shot to match a target edit duration without reshoots.
Continuing narrative action past the recorded endpoint to complete a scene.
Creating pre-roll/post-roll segments for social clips while preserving style and identity.
Lengthening B‑roll or background plates to fill timeline gaps in an edit.
Building longer, seamless chains of stylistically consistent shots for montage sequences.

faqItems.question: What are the clip length limits?
faqItems.answer: The source video must be 1.9–30 seconds long. The new segment you generate can be 4–30 seconds (default 5).

faqItems.question: Can I extend a clip backward as well as forward?
faqItems.answer: Yes. In Video Slice, set the direction to Backward to prepend new footage before the first frame, or Forward to continue after the last frame.

faqItems.question: Does the output include audio?
faqItems.answer: No. SaveVideo produces a silent MP4 or MOV. If you need audio, reattach your original track or a new mix in your video editor.

faqItems.question: How do I keep characters and layout consistent?
faqItems.answer: Use clean, stable source footage with consistent framing and lighting. Ensure ByteDance2ReferenceNodeV2 receives the appropriate head/tail frames, keep the extension length reasonable, and consider re-running if subtle variations occur.
